docs.title: Preface
docs.text:
This is Volume 12 of the series Bhāratīya Jñāna Paramparā: Khagola Jyotiṣa: Astronomy. It is a history of astronomy in the Indian subcontinent, from the star lists and ritual calendar of the Vedic texts and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, through the mathematical astronomy of the siddhāntas (Āryabhaṭa, Varāhamihira, Brahmagupta, Bhāskara II), the school of Mādhava and Nīlakaṇṭha in Kerala, and the meeting with Islamic astronomy, to the observatories of Sawai Jai Singh and the reform of the national calendar in 1957.

The Sanskrit word jyotiṣa covers three different things: mathematical astronomy (gaṇita or siddhānta), horoscopic astrology (horā) and the interpretation of omens (saṃhitā). This volume keeps them apart. Its main subject is mathematical astronomy and the calendar. Astrology and omen literature are described in their own chapter, as part of cultural and intellectual history: the volume reports what the texts claimed without endorsing their predictions, which controlled tests have not supported.

The place of Mesopotamian, Greek and Islamic astronomy in the Indian tradition is described as current scholarship understands it, including where scholars disagree. Claims that the ancient texts anticipated modern physics (heliocentrism, gravitation, the speed of light, the age of the universe) are examined as modern readings at the points where the texts give rise to them, and collected in the last chapter. Dates are given as the range accepted in current scholarship, with traditional dates labelled as such.

The volume rests on the standard editions, translations and studies, above all those of David Pingree, Kim Plofker, K. V. Sarma, K. S. Shukla, Yukio Ōhashi and S. R. Sarma, which are collected in the select bibliography; Sanskrit passages are quoted from the editions cited at each point, and the translations follow them. Mathematical topics that arose from astronomy are treated briefly here and more fully in Volume 11, Gaṇita; Purāṇic cosmography and geography are treated in Volume 21, Bhūgola, and the sky-lore of tribal and rural communities in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti.

The sixteen chapters begin with the naked-eye sky, for readers new to astronomy. They give a place to the Jain and Buddhist calendrical texts beside the Vedic, and to the handbooks, tables and families of the working astronomers beside the great treatises. Several chapters include worked computations, which a reader with a little arithmetic can follow step by step. The book ends with the transmission of Indian astronomy, its encounter with European astronomy in the colonial period, its place among the world’s astronomies and its modern readings. Appendices give a worked computation with the Sūryasiddhānta, a table of the principal texts with their editions, a guide to further reading, a glossary and a chronology.

Nikhil Kumar Rajput Ramanujan College, University of Delhi Guru Pūrṇimā, 2026

docs.title: Chapter 1: Introduction: Jyotiṣa and Its History
1.1 The Word and the Field
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word jyotiṣa is derived from jyotis, “light” or “luminary”, and means the knowledge of the heavenly lights: the Sun, the Moon, the planets and the stars. In the classification of Vedic learning it is the last of the six vedāṅgas, the “limbs” or auxiliary sciences of the Veda, alongside phonetics (śikṣā), ritual procedure (kalpa), grammar (vyākaraṇa), etymology (nirukta) and metre (chandas). Its original task was practical and religious: to tell the priest when a sacrifice was to be performed. The earliest surviving text of the discipline, the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, says as much (Chapter 3).

Over the next two thousand years the word came to cover a very wide field. A learned jyotiṣī (also called gaṇaka, “calculator”, daivajña, “knower of fate”, or sāṃvatsara, “calendar-maker”) of the sixth century CE was expected to compute the positions of the planets and the circumstances of eclipses, to cast and interpret horoscopes, to choose auspicious moments, and to interpret omens in the sky, in the weather and in the behaviour of animals. Varāhamihira, writing in the sixth century, describes the science of the lights (jyotiḥśāstra) as resting on three “branches” (skandhas), and gives the name saṃhitā to a work that covers the whole of it (Varāhamihira 1981–1982, 1.9). The second chapter of his Bṛhatsaṃhitā lists the qualifications of the ideal practitioner, who must master all three.

This volume is a history of the first of these branches, mathematical astronomy, and of the calendar it served. The other two branches are not ignored, since they were part of the same profession and were often practised by the same people, but they are treated in a separate chapter (Chapter 15) and described historically.

The title of this volume, Khagola Jyotiṣa, combines the name of the discipline with the word khagola, “sky-sphere”, the term used by the siddhāntas for the celestial sphere on which the motions of the heavenly bodies are described. It is meant to signal the volume’s focus: the mathematical description of the sphere of the heavens and of the bodies that move on it, as opposed to the reading of their supposed influence on human affairs.

docs.title: 1.2 The Three Branches
docs.text:
Figure 1.1. The three branches (skandhas) of jyotiḥśāstra, with some of their sub-genres. The selection of auspicious times (muhūrta) was placed sometimes under horā, sometimes under saṃhitā.

Gaṇita or siddhānta.

The mathematical branch computes the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets from models and parameters, and from these derives the calendar, the times of eclipses, planetary conjunctions and heliacal risings, the lengths of day and night at a given latitude, and the problems of “direction, place and time” (tripraśna). Its texts are of three kinds, distinguished by the epoch from which they count days: the siddhānta (counting from the beginning of the kalpa), the tantra (from the beginning of the current Kali age) and the karaṇa (a handbook counting from a recent epoch) (Pingree 1981). To these were added tables (sāraṇī, koṣṭhaka) and, in south India, the verse tables called vākyas. This is the subject of Chapters 6 to 10 and 12.

Horā.

The horoscopic branch interprets the positions of the planets at a moment, above all the moment of birth (jātaka), and also the moments of setting out on a military expedition (yātrā), of marriage (vivāha) and of asking a question (praśna). The word horā is the Greek hōra, and the whole branch rests on the Hellenistic astrology translated into Sanskrit in the early centuries CE (Chapters 5 and 15).

Saṃhitā.

The branch of omens collects signs in the sky (the motions and colours of planets, comets, halos, eclipses), in the atmosphere (clouds, winds, rain) and on the earth (earthquakes, the behaviour of animals, the appearance of buildings and objects), and states what each portends for kings, kingdoms, crops and people. Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā is the classic text. Its roots lie in Vedic omen lore and, according to Pingree, partly in Mesopotamian omen series (Pingree 1997).

Why this volume separates the three branches

In the tradition the three branches were held together by a single profession and by the belief that the heavens are signs for human affairs. The modern history of science separates them for a simple reason: they stand in different relations to evidence. The predictions of mathematical astronomy (where the Moon will be, when an eclipse will begin) can be tested against the sky, and Indian astronomers did test and revise them. The predictions of horoscopic astrology and of omen texts have been tested in modern controlled studies and have not been confirmed (Chapter 15). Astrology and omen literature are nevertheless part of the history of Indian thought and society, and they drove much of the demand for accurate astronomy. They are described here as history, not as a source of knowledge about the future.

docs.title: 1.3 An Outline of the History
docs.text:
The history of astronomy in India can be divided into broad periods. The dates are approximate, and the boundaries are not sharp.

Vedic period (c. 1500–500 BCE) The Ṛgveda (core hymns c. 1500–1200 BCE) knows a year of twelve months and 360 days, names the Sun, Moon and dawn as deities, and mentions an eclipse in mythic terms (RV 5.40). The later Vedic texts list the twenty-seven or twenty-eight nakṣatras (lunar asterisms) and use them to date rituals (Chapters 3 and 4). Vedāṅga period (second half of the first millennium BCE?) The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa sets out a five-year luni-solar calendar for the ritual. The canonical Jain texts on the sun and moon (Sūryaprajñapti, Candraprajñapti) use a similar scheme within Jain cosmology. The date of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa is disputed (Chapter 3). Contact and transformation (c. 200 BCE–400 CE) Greek astrology and elements of Hellenistic mathematical astronomy reach India, notably through the Western Kṣatrapa kingdom in western India. The twelve-sign zodiac, the seven-day week and the horoscope enter Indian practice (Chapter 5). Classical siddhānta (c. 400–1200 CE) The systems summarised by Varāhamihira in the Pañcasiddhāntikā (epoch 505 CE); Āryabhaṭa’s Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE); Brahmagupta’s Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta (628 CE); Lalla, Vaṭeśvara, Muñjāla and Śrīpati; Bhāskara II’s Siddhāntaśiromaṇi (1150 CE) (Chapters 6 to 9). Regional schools (c. 1200–1700) Handbooks and tables proliferate; the Kerala school of Mādhava (c. 1340–1425), Parameśvara and Nīlakaṇṭha (Tantrasaṅgraha, 1500) revises planetary theory and develops infinite series (Chapter 10). Indo-Islamic interaction (c. 1250–1750) Perso-Arabic astrology enters Sanskrit as tājika from the thirteenth century (Chapter 15); Sanskrit works on the astrolabe (Mahendra Sūri, 1370), translations of Persian tables at the Mughal court, the debates of Kamalākara and Munīśvara, and the observatories of Sawai Jai Singh in the 1720s and 1730s follow (Chapter 11). Colonial and modern period European study of Indian astronomy from the late eighteenth century; the Madras Observatory; the survival of the traditional almanac; the national calendar of 1957 (Chapters 13 and 16).

Two features of this history deserve emphasis at the outset. First, Indian astronomy was never sealed off from its neighbours. It received Mesopotamian and Greek ideas in antiquity, gave its methods to Sasanian Iran and, in the eighth century, to the Islamic world, and received Islamic astronomy again from the fourteenth century onwards. Its originality lies less in being untouched than in what it made of what it received: the sine function, the day-count (ahargaṇa) method of computation, great integer period-relations, and later the infinite series of the Kerala school. Second, the tradition was continuous. The Sūryasiddhānta and the handbooks derived from it were still being used to compute almanacs in the twentieth century, and many almanacs are still computed from them today.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Genres of astronomical writing
docs.text:
Indian astronomy survives almost entirely in Sanskrit verse, in thousands of manuscripts, most of them from the last five centuries. David Pingree’s Census of the Exact Sciences in Sanskrit (Pingree 1970–1994) lists the authors and manuscripts known to him and remains the basic finding aid; his Jyotiḥśāstra (Pingree 1981) is the standard survey of the literature. A few important works were written in other languages: the Yuktibhāṣā of Jyeṣṭhadeva in Malayalam (c. 1530), astronomical and calendrical works in Tamil, and, from the Mughal period, astronomical tables in Persian.

The main genres were:

  • the siddhānta or tantra, a complete treatise covering mean and true motions, the three problems of direction, place and time, eclipses, conjunctions, heliacal risings, the cosmography of the sphere and, often, instruments;

  • the karaṇa, a practical handbook using a recent epoch and simplified rules, such as Brahmagupta’s Khaṇḍakhādyaka (665), Bhāskara II’s Karaṇakutūhala (1183) and Gaṇeśa Daivajña’s Grahalāghava (1520);

  • tables (sāraṇī), which became common from the second millennium; many survive only in manuscript (Montelle and Plofker 2018);

  • commentaries (bhāṣya, ṭīkā, vyākhyā, vāsanā), which explain, give worked examples, supply demonstrations (upapatti, vāsanā) and sometimes correct the parameters of the root text.

docs.title: 1.4.2 Numbers in verse
docs.text:
Because the texts were composed in verse and transmitted by memorisation and copying, astronomers developed ways of writing large numbers in metrical form. Three systems were widely used:

  • Word-numerals (bhūtasaṅkhyā): a word for something that comes in a known number stands for that digit (“moon” for 1, “eye” for 2, “fire” for 3, “Veda” for 4, “sky” or “void” for 0), and the digits are read from the lowest place upwards. This is the commonest system.

  • Āryabhaṭa’s alphabetic notation: the twenty-five “classed” consonants ka to ma stand for 1 to 25, the unclassed consonants ya to ha for 30, 40, …, 100, and the vowels multiply by successive powers of 100. It allowed Āryabhaṭa to state all the revolution numbers of his system in two verses (Gītikāpāda 3–4) (Āryabhaṭa 1976).

  • Kaṭapayādi: each consonant stands for a digit (Table 1.1), so that any word or phrase encodes a number. It was especially popular in Kerala, where the vākyas for the Moon’s position were written in it (Chapter 10).

Table 1.1. The kaṭapayādi values of the consonants. A vowel following a consonant has no value, but a vowel standing alone counts as zero; in a conjunct consonant only the last counts. Digits are read from right to left. 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 0 ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa ta tha da dha na pa pha ba bha ma ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha

docs.title: 1.4.3 Practitioners and their world
docs.text:
Most of the authors whose names survive were Brahmin men, many of them from hereditary families of astronomers in which skill and manuscripts passed from father to son: the family of Bhāskara II in the Deccan, that of Gaṇeśa Daivajña on the western coast, the Kerala Nampūtiri families. Jain monks wrote on astronomy and astrology too (Mahendra Sūri, the author of the first Sanskrit treatise on the astrolabe, was a Jain), and from the fourteenth century Muslim astronomers and patrons, and Persian-reading Hindu scholars, shaped the field. No woman is known as the author of a Sanskrit astronomical treatise, and evidence for women as patrons or copyists of astronomical manuscripts has not been systematically collected; women appear in the record mainly as the subjects of astrological rules (Chapter 15) and as keepers of the many fasts (vratas) whose dates the almanac fixed (Chapter 13). In Bengal, sayings about weather and sowing are attributed to a legendary woman astrologer, Khanā (see Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna). The tradition’s social base was therefore narrow, and its technical knowledge was in large part a family and caste possession. Its patrons were kings, temples and the many households that needed almanacs and horoscopes (Yano 2003).

Astronomers worked for those patrons. Āryabhaṭa says he wrote at Kusumapura (Pāṭaliputra); Brahmagupta wrote under a Cāpa king at Bhillamāla in Rajasthan; Bhāskara II’s grandson was court astrologer to a Yādava king, and the family’s college at Patna (in present-day Maharashtra) was endowed by an inscription of 1207 (Pingree 1978). Mahendra Sūri wrote at the court of Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq, Nityānanda at that of Shāh Jahān, Jagannātha at that of Jai Singh. Figure 1.2 shows where some of them worked.

Figure 1.2. Some places in the history of Indian astronomy named in this volume: Kusumapura (Āryabhaṭa), Bhillamāla (Brahmagupta), Ujjayinī (the prime meridian), Purī (Śatānanda’s Bhāsvatī), Nandigrāma (Keśava and Gaṇeśa Daivajña; position approximate), the Nila valley in Kerala (Parameśvara and the Kerala school), Lahore (astrolabe makers), Pondicherry (Le Gentil), Madras and Kodaikanal (the colonial observatories), and the five observatories of Jai Singh. Positions are plotted by latitude and longitude; the coastline is simplified, islands other than Sri Lanka are omitted, and no political boundaries are shown.

docs.title: 1.5 How Indian Astronomers Worked
docs.text:
The mathematical astronomy of India was above all a science of computation. Its aim was to predict the positions of the heavenly bodies and the times of the phenomena that mattered for the calendar and for astrology; its theories were judged mainly by whether their predictions agreed with what was seen. Pingree, who studied the tradition more widely than anyone, stressed this computational, instrumental character (Pingree 2003). The texts say little about how parameters were obtained, and they rarely record observations. But they do record changes of parameter, and from the seventh century onwards authors discuss the disagreement between computation and observation (dṛk) and correct their parameters by small adjustments (bīja).

Two of the most explicit statements of this principle come from Kerala. Parameśvara (c. 1360–1455) records eclipse observations made over many years and revised the parameters then in use in his Dṛggaṇita (1431). Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī (1444–c. 1545) argued that astronomical parameters must be revised from time to time by observation, because no system remains accurate for ever (Chapter 10). Commentators also supplied demonstrations of rules, called upapatti or vāsanā. Bhāskara II wrote such a commentary (the Vāsanābhāṣya) on his own Siddhāntaśiromaṇi, and the Malayalam Yuktibhāṣā gives long demonstrations for the results of the Kerala school (Sarma et al. 2008). The reasons astronomers gave for their methods, and how they weighed observation against the authority of earlier texts and of scripture, have been examined by Minkowski (2002).

docs.title: 1.6 The Modern Study of Indian Astronomy
docs.text:
Europeans began to study Indian astronomy seriously in the late eighteenth century. The French astronomer Le Gentil had a Tamil eclipse computation demonstrated to him at Pondicherry (Section 13.8), and tables brought to Paris from India started a long debate about the antiquity of Indian astronomy (Section 16.4.1). The nineteenth century produced the first translations, above all Ebenezer Burgess’s annotated Sūryasiddhānta (Burgess 1860), and the first modern synthesis, by George Thibaut (Thibaut 1899). Śaṅkara Bālakṛṣṇa Dīkṣit’s Marathi history of Indian astronomy (1896; English translation (Dikshit 1969–1981)) remains valuable.

In the twentieth century the field was transformed by critical editions and technical studies: Otto Neugebauer and David Pingree on the Pañcasiddhāntikā (Neugebauer and Pingree 1970–1971) and the transmission of Greek astronomy, Pingree’s Census and surveys, Roger Billard’s statistical analysis of the parameters (Billard 1971), K. S. Shukla’s editions of Āryabhaṭa and Bhāskara I (Āryabhaṭa 1976; Shukla 1976; Bhāskara I 1960), K. V. Sarma’s editions of the Kerala texts (Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī 1977) and his history of the Kerala school (Sarma 1972), the history edited by Sen and Shukla (1985), the source-book of Subbarayappa and Sarma (1985), and Kim Plofker’s Mathematics in India (Plofker 2009), which covers astronomy as much as mathematics.

The subject has also been drawn into debates about national identity. Some writers have used astronomical references in the Vedas to argue for very early dates for the Vedic texts, or have presented Indian astronomers as anticipating Copernicus, Newton or modern cosmology. Others, in the opposite direction, have treated Indian astronomy as a mere copy of Greek models. This volume tries to avoid both distortions. Where scholars disagree (on the date of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, on how much of the siddhānta system came from Greece, on whether the Kerala series reached Europe) the disagreement is stated. Claims of “anticipation” are examined on their merits in Chapter 16.

docs.title: 1.7 The Plan of This Volume
docs.text: Chapter 2 describes, for readers new to the subject, the phenomena of the naked-eye sky that Indian astronomy set out to explain. Chapter 3 examines astronomy in the Vedic texts and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, and the calendrical astronomy of the Jain canon and of early Buddhist texts. Chapter 4 is devoted to the nakṣatras and the star positions of the Sūryasiddhānta. Chapter 5 discusses the Mesopotamian and Greek contributions and the formation of the siddhānta systems, as seen through Varāhamihira’s Pañcasiddhāntikā. Chapters 6 to 8 explain how a siddhānta works: its time scales and parameters, its trigonometry and spherical astronomy, including the shadow problems of the gnomon, and the everyday computational tools of the astronomer (Chapter 6), its planetary models (Chapter 7) and its eclipse computations (Chapter 8). Chapters 9 and 10 follow the astronomers and schools from Āryabhaṭa to the seventeenth century. Chapter 11 deals with instruments, the encounter with Islamic astronomy and the observatories of Jai Singh. Chapter 12 turns to the working astronomer: the handbooks and tables from which almanacs were actually computed, with a worked day-count, the profession and its families, the manuscripts, and the correction of parameters by observation. Chapter 13 describes the calendar and almanac; Chapter 14 the great time cycles and the cosmologies of the siddhāntas and Purāṇas; Chapter 15 astrology and omen literature, including the treatment of comets and meteors, in historical perspective. Chapter 16 follows Indian astronomy to the Islamic world, Europe and East Asia, describes the colonial and modern periods (the European debate over the antiquity of Indian astronomy, the Madras Observatory and its Indian assistants, and the last attempts to reform the siddhāntas from within), places Indian astronomy among the other astronomical traditions of the pre-modern world, and examines some common modern misreadings. Appendices give a worked computation with the Sūryasiddhānta, a table of the principal texts and their editions, a guide to further reading, a glossary and a chronology.

docs.title: 1.8 Reading an Astronomical Verse
docs.text:
Two short examples show how numbers were packed into verse and why commentaries were indispensable.

Āryabhaṭa’s alphabet.

The third verse of the Gītikāpāda begins by giving the revolutions of the Sun in a yuga as khyughṛ. In Āryabhaṭa’s notation the consonant kha has the value 2 and ya the value 30; joined to the vowel u, which multiplies by \(100^2\), they give \((2 + 30) \times 10{,}000 = 320{,}000\). The consonant gha has the value 4, and joined to the vowel ṛ, which multiplies by \(100^3\), it gives 4,000,000. The sum is 4,320,000, the number of solar years, and hence of solar revolutions, in Āryabhaṭa’s yuga. Two syllables thus record a seven-digit number; the same verse gives the revolutions of the Moon, the earth’s rotations and the mean revolutions of Saturn, Jupiter and Mars in the same way (the mean planets Mercury and Venus move with the Sun), and the next verse, among others, those of the Moon’s apogee and of the śīghra apices of Mercury and Venus (Āryabhaṭa 1976). The system is extremely compact, but a single miscopied syllable changes a number, and Āryabhaṭa’s successors preferred the more redundant word-numerals.

Word-numerals.

A verse attributed to Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma and quoted by later Kerala authors (Chapter 10) states the circumference of a circle whose diameter is \(9 \times 10^{11}\) (nine nikharvas) in eleven word-numerals: vibudha (“gods”, 33), netra (“eyes”, 2), gaja (“elephants”, of the eight directions, 8), ahi (“serpents”, 8), hutāśana (“fires”, 3), tri (“three”, 3), guṇa (“qualities”, of which there are three, 3), veda (4), bha (“asterisms”, 27), vāraṇa (“elephants”, 8) and bāhu (“arms”, 2). The compound triguṇa thus contributes two numerals, not one. The first word fills the lowest places: vibudha gives the units and tens (33), netra the hundreds (233), and each following word the next place or places, so that after hutāśana, tri and guṇa the number stands at 33,388,233, and veda, bha, vāraṇa and bāhu complete it. Read from the end, the numerals are 2, 8, 27, 4, 3, 3, 3, 8, 8, 2, 33, which written out in full give the thirteen digits of 2,827,433,388,233. Divided by the diameter, this gives \(\pi \approx 3.14159265359\), correct to eleven decimal places (Volume 11, Gaṇita, discusses the verse and its mathematics). Here the words are ordinary Sanskrit nouns, so the verse can still be read as a sentence, and a copyist who preserves the metre is likely to preserve the number. The reader, however, has to know the conventions: “elephants” could be eight (the elephants of the directions) and “gods” thirty-three (the Vedic count). Commentaries explain such conventions.

docs.title: 1.9 Learning and Transmission
docs.text:
Astronomy was learned from a teacher, often a father or uncle, by memorising the root text and working through its rules with a commentary, examples and calculations on a board or in sand. Manuscripts were written on palm leaf in the south and east, on birch bark in Kashmir and the north-west, and increasingly on paper in the second millennium. Since palm leaf and paper decay in the Indian climate, texts survived only if they were copied every few generations, and many works known by name are lost, among them Āryabhaṭa’s midnight system and much of the work of the Kerala astronomer Mādhava. Most surviving astronomical manuscripts are therefore late copies, held today in public and private libraries in India and abroad, many still uncatalogued and unedited (Pingree 1970–1994). Chapter 12 returns to the manuscripts and to the families who kept them.

Copying and commenting were also the means of innovation. A commentator could explain away a difficulty in his root text, supply an alternative rule, or quietly change a parameter; an author of a new handbook could state that his parameters had been corrected by observation. Reading the history of Indian astronomy therefore means reading layers of text, each in conversation with earlier ones.

docs.title: 1.10 Conventions Used in This Volume
docs.text: Sanskrit terms and names are given in the International Alphabet of Sanskrit Transliteration (IAST). Dates are given in the Common Era; where a text gives its own date or epoch, that date is used, and other dates are approximate. Traditional dates are labelled as such. Following a common practice in the history of Indian astronomy, “Sine” with a capital letter means the Indian half-chord \(R\sin\theta\) of a circle of radius \(R\), and “sine” the modern ratio. Sexagesimal numbers are written with a semicolon after the integer part and commas between the sexagesimal places: thus 365;15,31,30 days means \(365 + \tfrac{15}{60} + \tfrac{31}{60^2} + \tfrac{30}{60^3}\) days. Translations of Sanskrit verses are the author’s, following the editions cited; verse numbers vary between editions, and the edition followed is the one cited at each quotation.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Plofker (2009) is the best single introduction. Pingree (1981) surveys the literature and Pingree (1978) the history of the models. Sen and Shukla (1985) and Subbarayappa and Sarma (1985) provide extensive translated extracts. Yano (2003) is a short, reliable account of the calendar, astrology and astronomy together.

docs.title: Chapter 2: The Sky the Astronomers Saw
2.1 Why Begin with the Sky
docs.text: Indian astronomers, like all astronomers before the telescope, worked with what can be seen with the naked eye and measured with simple instruments. To understand what they achieved, and what their models were designed to explain, it helps to know what the sky actually does. This chapter describes, in modern terms but without technical apparatus, the phenomena that the rest of the volume refers to: the daily turning of the sky, the Sun’s yearly path, the Moon’s phases and its wandering path, the motions of the planets, eclipses, and the slow precession of the equinoxes. Readers familiar with elementary astronomy may pass directly to Chapter 3.

docs.title: 2.2 The Daily Turning of the Sky
docs.text:
Watched for a few hours on a clear night, the whole sky turns slowly from east to west around a point in the north, the celestial pole. Stars near the pole circle it without setting; stars farther away rise in the east, cross the sky and set in the west. The height of the pole above the northern horizon equals the observer’s latitude: about \(8^\circ\) at Kanyakumari, \(23^\circ\) at Ujjain, \(28^\circ\) at Delhi, \(34^\circ\) at Srinagar. At the equator the pole lies on the horizon and every star is above the horizon for half of each day. Polaris, the present “pole star”, a star of only moderate brightness, lies less than a degree from the pole; its closeness to the pole is a recent consequence of precession (Section 2.9).

The modern explanation is that the earth rotates on its axis once in about 23 hours 56 minutes (a sidereal day). Āryabhaṭa held this view (Chapter 9); most Indian astronomers, like most Greek and Islamic astronomers, preferred to say that the starry sphere turns around a stationary earth. For the purposes of computation the two descriptions are equivalent.

The circle on the sky directly above the earth’s equator is the celestial equator. A star’s angular distance north or south of it is its declination; its position around the sky, measured along the equator, is its right ascension. The Indian texts work with these equatorial coordinates as well as with coordinates measured along the ecliptic and with the horizon coordinates of altitude and azimuth (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 2.3.1 The ecliptic and the seasons
docs.text:
Against the background of the stars, the Sun moves eastward by about one degree a day, completing a circuit in a year. Its path, the ecliptic, is a great circle inclined to the celestial equator by about \(23\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ\) (the obliquity of the ecliptic). The Sun crosses the equator northward at the vernal equinox (about 20 March), reaches its greatest northern declination at the summer solstice (about 21 June), crosses the equator southward at the autumnal equinox (about 22 September) and reaches its greatest southern declination at the winter solstice (about 21 December). In Indian terms, the half-year from the winter to the summer solstice is uttarāyaṇa, the Sun’s “northern course”, and the other half dakṣiṇāyana.

As the Sun’s declination changes, so do the point of the horizon at which it rises, its height at noon, and the length of daylight. At the equinoxes the Sun rises due east and day and night are nearly equal everywhere. In northern India in June, the Sun rises well north of east and daylight lasts about 14 hours; in December it rises south of east and daylight lasts about 10 hours. The ratio of the longest to the shortest day increases with latitude; it is about 3:2 at a latitude of \(35^\circ\), which is one reason why the 3:2 ratio of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa has been discussed so much (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 2.3.2 The Sun’s unequal motion
docs.text: The Sun’s motion along the ecliptic is not uniform. Because the earth’s orbit is slightly elliptical, the Sun appears to move fastest in early January and slowest in early July, and the seasons are of unequal length: in the northern hemisphere the half-year from the spring to the autumn equinox is about a week longer than the other half. The difference between the Sun’s actual position and the position it would have if it moved uniformly is the “equation of centre”; it never exceeds about two degrees. The siddhāntas represent it with the manda correction (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 2.3.3 Shadows
docs.text: The simplest way to follow the Sun is to watch the shadow of a vertical stick, a gnomon. The shadow is shortest at noon, when it points due north (in most of India, for most of the year), and its noon length changes through the year with the Sun’s height. At the equinoxes the noon shadow of a gnomon of height \(h\) has length \(h\tan\phi\), where \(\phi\) is the latitude, which is how the siddhāntas find the latitude (Chapter 6). In the tropics, south of the Tropic of Cancer, the Sun stands directly overhead at noon on two days a year, and the gnomon then casts no shadow at all.

docs.title: 2.4 Two Kinds of Year
docs.text: The year can be measured in two ways. The tropical year, from one vernal equinox to the next, governs the seasons; it lasts about 365.2422 days. The sidereal year, the time the Sun takes to return to the same position among the stars, lasts about 365.2564 days, some twenty minutes longer. The difference arises because the equinoxes themselves slide slowly westward among the stars (Section 2.9). The Gregorian calendar follows the tropical year. The Indian siddhāntas defined the year sidereally, by the Sun’s return to the beginning of Aśvinī; as a result the Indian solar months have drifted, over the centuries, against the seasons (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 2.5.1 Phases and months
docs.text:
The Moon moves eastward among the stars about thirteen times faster than the Sun, some \(13^\circ\) a day, and so overtakes the Sun about once a month. When it is in the same direction as the Sun it cannot be seen (new moon, amāvāsyā); a day or two later it appears as a thin crescent in the evening sky; a week after new moon it is half lit (first quarter); a fortnight after new moon it is opposite the Sun and fully lit (full moon, pūrṇimā); and then it wanes through last quarter to the next new moon. The interval from one new moon to the next, the synodic month, averages about 29.53 days. The time the Moon takes to return to the same star, the sidereal month, is shorter, about 27.32 days, because in the meantime the Sun has moved on.

Figure 2.1. The Moon’s phases. The half of the Moon facing the Sun (to the left) is always lit; how much of the lit half we see from the earth depends on the Moon’s position in its orbit. At new moon the Moon lies between the earth and the Sun; at full moon it lies opposite the Sun. Seen from north of the orbit, the Moon moves anticlockwise (eastward). Not to scale.

The Indian lunar day, the tithi, is defined by the Moon’s elongation from the Sun: each tithi corresponds to \(12^\circ\) of elongation, so that there are thirty in a synodic month (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 2.5.2 The new crescent
docs.text: The first visibility of the new crescent after conjunction depends on how far the Moon is from the Sun, how high it stands above the horizon after sunset, the season, the observer’s latitude and the clarity of the air. Usually the crescent is first seen one or two evenings after conjunction; under poor conditions it may not be seen until later. Calendars that begin the month with the observed crescent, such as the Islamic calendar in its religious use, therefore cannot be fixed exactly in advance, whereas the Indian calendar, which defines its months by the computed conjunction or opposition, can. The siddhāntas nevertheless treat crescent visibility, in their chapters on the “elevation of the horns” of the Moon (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 2.5.3 The Moon’s irregularities
docs.text: The Moon’s motion is far from uniform. Its orbit is noticeably elliptical, so that its speed varies between about \(12^\circ\) and \(15^\circ\) a day over the anomalistic month of about 27.55 days, from one perigee (closest approach) to the next; the point of perigee itself moves slowly eastward, completing a circuit in about 8.85 years. The Sun’s attraction causes further irregularities, the largest of which (the evection) displaces the Moon by up to about \(1\tfrac{1}{4}^\circ\). Ancient astronomers could model the first irregularity well; the others required later refinements (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 2.5.4 The Moon’s path and its nodes
docs.text: The Moon’s path is inclined to the ecliptic by about \(5^\circ\). It crosses the ecliptic at two points, the nodes, which slide slowly westward around the ecliptic, completing a circuit in about 18.6 years. The Moon is therefore usually a few degrees north or south of the ecliptic, and it can pass close to, or in front of (occult), stars and planets near the ecliptic. The two nodes are the Rāhu and Ketu of Indian astronomy (Chapter 8).

docs.title: 2.6 Eclipses
docs.text:
A lunar eclipse occurs when the full moon passes through the earth’s shadow, and a solar eclipse when the new moon passes in front of the Sun. Because the Moon’s path is inclined to the ecliptic, this happens only when a full or new moon falls close to one of the nodes, so eclipses come in “seasons” about six months apart, when the Sun is near a node. A lunar eclipse is visible from the whole half of the earth where the Moon is above the horizon, and lasts up to a few hours; a total lunar eclipse turns the Moon a dull red rather than making it disappear. A solar eclipse is visible only from a limited part of the earth, and totality, where it occurs, lasts at most a few minutes along a narrow track. This difference is why lunar eclipses were predicted earlier and more successfully than solar ones, which require the computation of parallax for the observer’s position (Chapter 8).

Observing the Sun

Never look directly at the Sun, with or without binoculars or a telescope, including during a partial or annular solar eclipse: permanent damage to the eye can result. Use certified solar viewing filters or a simple pinhole projection. Lunar eclipses are entirely safe to watch with the naked eye.

docs.title: 2.7.1 The five visible planets
docs.text: Five planets are visible to the naked eye: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. Like the Sun and Moon, they move generally eastward among the stars, close to the ecliptic, but each in its own way. Saturn takes about 29.5 years to go round the zodiac, Jupiter about 12 years and Mars about 1.9 years. Mercury and Venus never stray far from the Sun: Mercury is seen only low in the twilight, never more than about \(28^\circ\) from the Sun, and Venus, the brightest of the planets, never more than about \(47^\circ\), appearing for months at a time as the “evening star” or the “morning star”.

docs.title: 2.7.2 The planets’ names
docs.text: Several Sanskrit names of the planets describe how they look or move. Mars is Aṅgāraka, “the glowing coal”, or Lohitāṅga, “red-bodied”, from its reddish colour, which is plain to the naked eye. Saturn is Śanaiścara, “the slow mover”, the slowest of the visible planets. Venus, the brightest object in the sky after the Sun and Moon, is Śukra, “the bright”. Mercury is Budha, “the wise” (in myth the son of the Moon), and Jupiter is Bṛhaspati or Guru, the preceptor of the gods. Rāhu and Ketu, which cannot be seen at all, entered the list of “planets” (grahas) through astrology and the eclipse myth (Chapter 8). The Sun and Moon were counted among the grahas too, which is why there are seven planets of the week and nine of astrology.

docs.title: 2.7.3 Retrograde motion
docs.text:
From time to time each planet slows down, stops, moves westward for a while among the stars, stops again and resumes its eastward motion. For the superior planets (Mars, Jupiter and Saturn) this retrograde motion happens around the time when the planet is opposite the Sun in the sky, which is also when it is brightest; for Mercury and Venus it happens around the time when they pass between the earth and the Sun. Mars retrogrades for about two and a half months, through about \(15^\circ\); Jupiter for about four months, through about \(10^\circ\); Saturn for about four and a half months, through about \(7^\circ\).

Figure 2.2. Schematic path of a superior planet among the stars around the time of its opposition, showing the loop formed by its retrograde motion. The shape and size of the loop vary from one opposition to the next. Not to scale.

The modern explanation is that the earth and the planets all move around the Sun, and the retrograde motion is an effect of viewing a planet from a moving earth: the earth, moving faster on its smaller orbit, overtakes a superior planet, which then appears to move backwards; an inferior planet moving faster on its smaller orbit overtakes the earth. Ancient astronomers, Indian, Greek and Islamic, reproduced the same appearances by placing the planet on an epicycle, a circle carried around the earth; in Indian astronomy this is the śīghra epicycle (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 2.7.4 Synodic and sidereal periods
docs.text: Two kinds of period are therefore needed to describe a planet’s motion. The sidereal period is the time it takes to go once round the zodiac, as seen from the Sun. The synodic period is the time between successive repetitions of the same configuration with the Sun, for example from one opposition to the next; it governs the cycle of visibility, invisibility and retrograde motion. For Mars the synodic period is about 780 days, for Jupiter about 399 days, for Saturn about 378 days, for Venus about 584 days and for Mercury about 116 days.

docs.title: 2.8 The Fixed Stars
docs.text: Most of the bright stars along the zodiac were used by Indian astronomers as junction stars of the nakṣatras (Chapter 4): Aldebaran (Rohiṇī), Regulus (Maghā), Spica (Citrā), Antares (Jyeṣṭhā) and others. Each star rises about four minutes earlier every day, so that over the year the whole zodiac passes through the night sky. A star that has been invisible in the Sun’s glare first reappears in the eastern sky just before dawn; this “heliacal rising” was used in many cultures to mark the seasons, and the siddhāntas computed it for the planets and for certain stars (Chapter 7). Canopus (Agastya), the second brightest star of the night sky, is visible from India low in the south; its heliacal rising was traditionally associated with the end of the rains, and Varāhamihira devotes a chapter of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā to it.

docs.title: 2.9 Precession
docs.text: Over long periods the whole frame of the equator and the poles shifts slowly with respect to the stars. The earth’s axis traces a cone in about 25,800 years, so that the celestial pole moves in a circle among the stars and the equinoxes slide westward along the ecliptic by about \(50”\) a year, one degree in about 72 years. This is the precession of the equinoxes. Its effects are slow but cumulative: in about two thousand years the equinoxes have moved by nearly thirty degrees, about a whole sign of the zodiac. It is the reason why the tropical and sidereal zodiacs now differ by about twenty-four degrees (Chapter 4), why the solstices no longer fall in the nakṣatras mentioned in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa (Chapter 3), and why Indian solar festivals have drifted against the seasons (Chapter 13). Indian astronomers knew of the motion of the solstices and treated it in different ways (Chapter 6).

docs.title: 2.10 What Naked-Eye Astronomy Can Achieve
docs.text: With careful observation and simple instruments, naked-eye astronomers can measure positions in the sky to a few minutes of arc and times to a minute or so. Mean motions, however, can be determined far more precisely than single positions, because an error of a few minutes of arc is spread over all the cycles completed between two observations: a period measured over centuries is far more precise than one measured over a single cycle. This is why the mean periods of ancient astronomy were often excellent, while the predicted positions of the planets at a given moment, which depend on the models of their irregularities, were much less so. The chapters that follow should be read with this in mind: the achievements of Indian astronomy lie both in the accuracy of its long-period parameters and in the ingenuity of its models, and its limitations are those of all astronomy before the telescope.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Neugebauer (1975) explains the phenomena that ancient astronomy had to model; Plofker (2009) relates them to the Indian texts; Montelle (2011) treats eclipses in detail.

docs.title: Chapter 3: Vedic Astronomy and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa
docs.text:
Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, Ārca recension 36 (Yājuṣa 3)

vedā hi yajñārtham abhipravṛttāḥ kālānupūrvā vihitāś ca yajñāḥ tasmād idaṃ kālavidhānaśāstraṃ yo jyotiṣaṃ veda sa veda yajñān

“The Vedas came forth for the sake of the sacrifices, and the sacrifices are prescribed in the order of times. Therefore whoever knows this science of the ordering of time, jyotiṣa, knows the sacrifices.”

docs.title: 3.1 Astronomy in a Ritual Culture
docs.text:
The earliest Indian astronomy is found in texts whose purpose was religious. The Vedic hymns and the prose texts that explain the ritual (the Brāhmaṇas) and regulate it (the Śrautasūtras) needed a calendar: the new- and full-moon offerings (darśapūrṇamāsa) were performed every fortnight; the seasonal offerings (cāturmāsya) every four months; the great year-long sacrificial sessions (sattras such as the gavām ayana, “course of the cows”) were organised around the solstices and the middle day of the year (viṣuvat). The fire was to be installed under particular nakṣatras. Knowing the times was therefore part of knowing the ritual, as the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa says in the verse quoted above.

This chapter surveys what the Vedic texts tell us about the sky, the five-year calendar of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, the related astronomy of the Jain canon, and the long debate about how far astronomical statements in these texts can be used to date them. The nakṣatras themselves are treated in Chapter 4. A fuller account of the Vedic corpus and its chronology is given in Volume 1 of this series. Here, following the series standard, the core of the Ṛgveda is dated c. 1500–1200 BCE and the later Vedic texts c. 1200–500 BCE.

docs.title: 3.2 The Sky in the Ṛgveda
docs.text:
The Ṛgveda is not an astronomical text, but its poets watched the sky. The Sun (Sūrya, Savitṛ) and the Dawn (Uṣas) are among its most frequently praised deities; the Moon is identified, in later hymns, with Soma. Some passages are of direct calendrical interest:

  • A year of twelve months and 360 days. The riddle hymn RV 1.164 speaks of a wheel with twelve spokes on which stand 720 sons in pairs (v. 11) and of a wheel with twelve fellies on which are fixed 360 pegs (v. 48). The usual reading is that the poet is speaking of the year of twelve months and 360 days and nights. A 360-day “civil” year, with the excess days handled by intercalation, remained the ritual norm in the later Vedic texts.

  • An intercalary month? RV 1.25.8 says that Varuṇa knows the twelve months and the one that is born in addition. This has often been read as a reference to an intercalary thirteenth month, which the later Vedic texts certainly know (under names such as saṃsarpa and aṃhaspati).

  • An eclipse. RV 5.40.5–9 tells how the demon Svarbhānu pierced the Sun with darkness and how the seer Atri found the hidden Sun again. This is the earliest Indian description of a solar eclipse. Attempts to identify the eclipse and so date the hymn have produced widely different results and are not reliable.

  • Asterisms. The wedding hymn of Sūryā (RV 10.85.13) mentions the asterisms Aghā and Arjunī, which correspond to the later Maghā and Phalgunī. The word nakṣatra occurs in the Ṛgveda, but the full list of asterisms appears only in later texts.

docs.title: 3.3 The Later Vedic Calendar
docs.text:
The Yajurveda Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas are far richer in calendrical detail (Ōhashi 1993). The Taittirīya Saṃhitā (4.4.10) lists twenty-seven nakṣatras with their presiding deities, beginning with Kṛttikā (the Pleiades). The Atharvaveda (19.7) gives twenty-eight, including Abhijit. The Taittirīya Saṃhitā (4.4.11) also gives the old names of the twelve months, grouped in pairs into the six seasons (ṛtus): Madhu and Mādhava (spring), Śukra and Śuci (summer), Nabhas and Nabhasya (rains), Iṣa and Ūrja (autumn), Sahas and Sahasya (early winter), Tapas and Tapasya (late winter). The later month names (Caitra, Vaiśākha and the rest), taken from the nakṣatra in which the full moon falls, came into use in the late Vedic period and are standard in classical texts.

Table 3.1. The six seasons and the old month names of the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, with the later lunar months to which they roughly correspond Season (ṛtu) Old month names Later months Vasanta (spring) Madhu, Mādhava Caitra, Vaiśākha Grīṣma (summer) Śukra, Śuci Jyaiṣṭha, Āṣāḍha Varṣā (rains) Nabhas, Nabhasya Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada Śarad (autumn) Iṣa, Ūrja Āśvina, Kārttika Hemanta (early winter) Sahas, Sahasya Mārgaśīrṣa, Pauṣa Śiśira (late winter) Tapas, Tapasya Māgha, Phālguna

The texts know the two halves of the year in which the Sun moves northward and southward along the horizon (later called uttarāyaṇa and dakṣiṇāyana), the six seasons, the bright and dark fortnights, and the days of new and full moon. Several passages discuss which full moon is the “mouth” (beginning) of the year, and give different answers. They also show some observational practice. The Śulbasūtras (c. 800–200 BCE for the corpus as a whole, Baudhāyana’s being the earliest), manuals of altar construction attached to the Śrautasūtras, prescribe how to find the east–west line with a gnomon: mark the points where the tip of its shadow touches a circle drawn around it in the morning and in the afternoon, and join them (Ōhashi 1993). The geometry of these manuals, important for the history of mathematics, is discussed in Volume 11.

docs.title: 3.4.1 The text
docs.text:
The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa is the oldest surviving Indian text devoted to astronomy. It survives in two recensions: the Ārca Jyotiṣa, attached to the Ṛgveda, in 36 verses, and the Yājuṣa Jyotiṣa, attached to the Yajurveda, in 43 or 44 verses, most of them shared with the Ārca. (The Ātharvaṇa Jyotiṣa is a different and later work on auspicious times.) The text says that it sets out the knowledge of time of Lagadha, who is otherwise unknown. Its verses are very compressed, the text is corrupt in places, and several verses are still not securely understood. The standard edition, with the translation and notes of T. S. Kuppanna Sastry, is that of K. V. Sarma (Sastry 1985).

A well-known verse (Ārca 35; Yājuṣa 4) compares the science to the crest of the peacock and the jewel of the serpent: yathā śikhā mayūrāṇāṃ nāgānāṃ maṇayo yathā, “as the crests of peacocks, as the jewels of serpents”, so this science stands at the head of the Vedāṅgas. The Ārca recension names jyotiṣa as the subject of the second line, the Yājuṣa gaṇita (“calculation”). The verse is often quoted as praise of mathematics in general; in its context it praises the calendrical science.

The text was not much used once the siddhāntas had replaced its calendar, and its transmission suffered. A commentary by Somākara on the Yājuṣa recension survives and is of help, but it is late and often uncertain. Modern study began in the nineteenth century, with the work of Albrecht Weber, George Thibaut and, in India, Bāl Gaṅgādhar Tilak and Śaṅkara Bālakṛṣṇa Dīkṣit, and many verses were explained only in the twentieth century. Sastry’s translation and notes (Sastry 1985) represent the results of this long effort, but some verses remain obscure, and interpretations of the text’s rules still differ. Readers should therefore treat any precise statement about the text’s content, including the numbers quoted in this chapter, as resting on interpretation. The broad structure of the calendar (the five-year cycle, the 366-day year, the 62 synodic and 67 sidereal months, the tithi, the solstices in Śraviṣṭhā and Āśleṣā) is, however, not in doubt, and it is confirmed by the closely similar scheme of the Jain canonical texts discussed below.

docs.title: 3.4.2 The five-year yuga
docs.text:
The calendar of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa is built on a cycle of five years, called a yuga. (This has nothing to do with the immense yugas of the Purāṇas and siddhāntas, discussed in Chapter 14.) The five years have the names saṃvatsara, parivatsara, idāvatsara, anuvatsara and idvatsara. The cycle begins when the Sun and the Moon are together at the beginning of the asterism Śraviṣṭhā (later called Dhaniṣṭhā) at the winter solstice, at the start of the bright half of the month Māgha. Within the cycle, the text assumes:

\[\begin{align*} 1 \text{ yuga} &= 5 \text{ years} = 1830 \text{ civil days} \\ &= 62 \text{ synodic months} = 1860 \text{ tithis} \\ &= 67 \text{ sidereal months (revolutions of the Moon through the asterisms).} \end{align*}\]

The year therefore has 366 days, and two intercalary months are needed in each cycle to keep the 62 lunar months in step with the five solar years. The tithi, one-thirtieth of a synodic month, appears here for the first time; it became the basic unit of the later Indian calendar (Chapter 13).

Table 3.2. Periods implied by the five-year yuga of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, compared with modern mean values. Period Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa Modern value Year (days) 366 365.2422 (tropical); 365.2564 (sidereal) Synodic month (days) \(1830/62 = 29.516\) 29.5306 Sidereal month (days) \(1830/67 = 27.313\) 27.3217 Days per tithi \(1830/1860 = 0.984\) 0.9843

The month lengths are reasonable, but the year of 366 days is about three-quarters of a day too long. Over a single five-year cycle the calendar would drift by nearly four days against the Sun, and over a few cycles by a fortnight or more. The calendar can only have worked if it was periodically reset by observation of the Sun and Moon, and the text does not tell us how this was done. The Paitāmaha system summarised by Varāhamihira in the sixth century CE still uses this scheme (Chapter 5), but the siddhāntas replaced it.

docs.title: 3.4.3 Other contents
docs.text: Besides the cycle itself, the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa gives rules for finding the nakṣatra of the Moon and the Sun at any new or full moon of the cycle, for finding the tithi, for converting between units, and for the variation of the length of daylight. It states that daylight increases by six muhūrtas between the winter and the summer solstices, so that the longest day is 18 muhūrtas and the shortest 12 (a muhūrta is one-thirtieth of a day, 48 minutes). This gives a ratio of 3:2 between the longest and shortest day. It also describes a water clock that measures the nāḍikā, one-sixtieth of the day (24 minutes). The text places the summer solstice at the middle of the asterism Āśleṣā, opposite the winter solstice at the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā.

docs.title: 3.4.4 A worked example: the length of daylight
docs.text:
The rule for daylight shows how the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa treats a continuously varying quantity. Daylight grows by 6 muhūrtas in the half-year of 183 days from the winter to the summer solstice, so it grows uniformly by \(6/183 = 2/61\) of a muhūrta each day. If \(n\) days have passed since the winter solstice (with \(n \le 183\)), the length of daylight is

\[D(n) = 12 + \frac{2n}{61} \ \text{muhūrtas},\tag{3.4}\]

and in the other half of the year it decreases at the same rate. Thus 61 days after the winter solstice daylight is 14 muhūrtas (11 hours 12 minutes), and at the equinox, about 91 days after the solstice, it is 15 muhūrtas, exactly half the day. The real variation is not linear but follows a curve close to a sine; a linear (“zigzag”) scheme of this kind is characteristic of early Babylonian astronomy as well, and its presence in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa is one of the parallels discussed below. It is nevertheless a reasonable practical rule, and the error it makes in the length of the day is never more than a fraction of a muhūrta.

docs.title: 3.4.5 The yuga in practice
docs.text: On the usual interpretation, the two intercalary months of the cycle were placed at regular intervals, one in the middle of the cycle and one at its end. Each month began at the new or full moon computed from the cycle, and the nakṣatra of the Moon at each of these moments could be read from the rules of the text. For the ritualist the result was a table of the nakṣatras and tithis at which the new- and full-moon offerings and the seasonal rites would fall over five years. The scheme was easy to remember and to use, and its main weakness, the 366-day year, would have been corrected in practice by watching the Sun’s turning points at the solstices and the full moons of the principal months.

docs.title: 3.5 The Date of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa
3.5.1 The argument from the solstice
docs.text:
The position of the solstices among the stars changes slowly because of the precession of the equinoxes, by about one degree in seventy-two years. If the statement that the winter solstice lay at the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā was an observation, it can in principle be dated.

The calculation runs as follows. In the later system of twenty-seven equal nakṣatras counted from Aśvinī, Śraviṣṭhā begins at sidereal longitude \(293^\circ 20'\). Today the winter solstice (tropical longitude \(270^\circ\)) lies near sidereal longitude \(246^\circ\), using the official Indian ayanāṃśa of about \(24^\circ\). The solstice has thus moved back by about \(47^\circ\) since the time of the observation, which at the modern rate of precession (\(50.3”\) a year) corresponds to about 3,400 years, that is, to a date around 1400 BCE. Variants of the calculation, using the junction star of Śraviṣṭhā (usually identified as \(\beta\) Delphini) instead of the equal division, or other assumptions, give dates between about 1400 and 1150 BCE. Sastry and Sarma took this as the date of the text (Sastry 1985). It is important to keep two dates apart: the astronomical epoch implied by the solstice statement (c. 1400–1200 BCE on these calculations) and the date of composition of the text as we have it, which most historians of astronomy now place much later, around 400 BCE or later (Pingree 1973; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 3.5.2 Why the date is disputed
docs.text:
Three difficulties make this result much less secure than it looks (Plofker 2009).

  1. Precision. “At the beginning of Śraviṣṭhā” is a coarse statement. It may refer to a junction star or to the edge of an equal division of the ecliptic that the text does not define, and an uncertainty of a few degrees in the position corresponds to centuries. An error of one whole nakṣatra (\(13^\circ 20'\)) would shift the date by nearly a thousand years.

  2. Tradition. A solstice position, once stated, could be repeated for centuries after it ceased to be true. Indian astronomers did exactly this with other parameters. An old observation does not date the text that preserves it.

  3. Other evidence. The language and style of the verses look later than those of the late Vedic prose texts, and the text has features with close parallels in Mesopotamian astronomy (below). On these grounds Pingree argued that the text, whatever the age of its solstice statement, was composed in the second half of the first millennium BCE (around the fifth or fourth century BCE, or later), perhaps under Achaemenid influence (Pingree 1973).

Scholarly Note: Mesopotamian parallels

Pingree pointed out that the 3:2 ratio of longest to shortest daylight, the use of a water clock to measure it, a linear (“zigzag”) variation of day length through the year, and the schematic 360-day year are all found in the Mesopotamian astronomical compendium MUL.APIN (early first millennium BCE) (Pingree 1973; Hunger and Pingree 1999). A 3:2 ratio is correct for a latitude of about \(35^\circ\) north, which fits Mesopotamia or the far north-west of the subcontinent, not the Gangetic plain. He concluded that these elements reached India from Mesopotamia, probably while the north-west was part of the Achaemenid empire (late sixth to fourth centuries BCE). Others have replied that a 3:2 ratio could be a simple schematic value reached independently, that north-western India is a possible place of composition, and that the core of the five-year cycle is native to the Vedic ritual calendar. Many historians now accept some Mesopotamian input while recognising that the cycle and its Vedic setting are Indian (Plofker 2009). The question remains open.

docs.title: 3.5.3 Earlier dates from Vedic astronomy
docs.text:
Since the late nineteenth century some writers have used astronomical statements in Vedic texts to argue for much earlier dates. B. G. Tilak argued that passages linking the year’s beginning to Mṛgaśiras pointed to a vernal equinox in that asterism around 4000 BCE (Tilak 1893); others have used the statement of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (2.1.2.3) that the Kṛttikās “do not swerve from the eastern direction”, and the order of nakṣatra lists beginning with Kṛttikā, to argue that the Pleiades lay at the equinox, around the third millennium BCE. More recently Kak (1995) has argued that the dimensions of the Vedic fire altars and the structure of the Vedic texts encode detailed astronomical knowledge.

These arguments rest on interpretations that are uncertain: whether a statement records an observation at all, whether it is precise enough to date, whether the asterism meant is the one assumed, and whether ritual statements about the “beginning of the year” refer to the equinox. They also conflict with the linguistic, textual and archaeological evidence on which the accepted chronology of the Vedic corpus rests. They are not accepted by most historians of astronomy or by Vedic philologists. The statement about the Kṛttikās, for instance, may only mean that they rise roughly in the east, which was true for a long period. Such dates are best treated as hypotheses about particular passages, not as a chronology of the texts.

docs.title: 3.6.1 Texts and framework
docs.text:
The canonical texts of the Śvetāmbara Jains include works devoted to the heavens: the Sūryaprajñapti (Prakrit Sūriyapaṇṇatti) and Candraprajñapti (“Exposition of the Sun”, “of the Moon”), and the Jambūdvīpaprajñapti, together with the later Jyotiṣkaraṇḍaka. Their contents are older than their final redaction, which belongs with the fixing of the canon at Valabhī in the fifth century CE, but how much older is uncertain (Pingree 1981; Plofker 2009). George Thibaut’s study of the Sūryaprajñapti (Thibaut 1880) first drew attention to its close agreement with the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa.

Jain astronomy is set within Jain cosmology. The earth is a flat disc of concentric continents and oceans; at the centre of the innermost continent, Jambūdvīpa, stands Mount Meru, around which the heavenly bodies circle at a fixed height. Night falls when the Sun passes behind Meru. Since a single sun circling Meru could not produce the observed alternation of day and night over the whole continent, the texts assume two suns and two moons, which cross the sky on alternate days, and accordingly two sets of twenty-eight nakṣatras. The changing seasons are explained by the Sun’s moving between inner and outer circular paths around Meru. The cosmography as a whole is described in Volume 24, Samanvaya (Chapter 3), and Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā; here the concern is the astronomy it carries.

docs.title: 3.6.2 The paths of the Sun and the length of daylight
docs.text:
The texts describe the Sun’s seasonal movement with arithmetical precision. Each sun moves on one of 184 circular paths (maṇḍalas) around Meru, keeping to one path for each day. Moving outward from the innermost path to the outermost takes 183 days, and moving back another 183, so the year has 366 days, as in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa. Jambūdvīpa is 100,000 yojanas across, and the innermost path lies 180 yojanas inside its rim, so that the diameter of that path is \(100{,}000 - 2 \times 180 = 99{,}640\) yojanas. According to the texts the zone of the paths is \(510\tfrac{48}{61}\) yojanas wide, the fraction being the breadth of the Sun’s disc, so that the outermost path has a diameter of \(99{,}640 + 2 \times 510 = 100{,}660\) yojanas.

On the innermost path, at the summer solstice, the day lasts 18 muhūrtas and the night 12; on the outermost path the proportions are reversed. From one path to the next the day changes by \(\tfrac{2}{61}\) of a muhūrta, and the 183 steps between the extremes make up exactly the six muhūrtas of difference (\(183 \times \tfrac{2}{61} = 6\)). The circumferences of the paths are computed with \(\pi = \sqrt{10}\), the value the Jain texts use throughout (Volume 4, Chapter 10, and Volume 11): the innermost path comes to \(99{,}640 \times \sqrt{10} \approx 315{,}089\) yojanas. Each sun needs two days, or 60 muhūrtas, to go once around Meru, so on that path it moves \(315{,}089 / 60 = 5251\tfrac{29}{60}\) yojanas in a muhūrta. Multiplying this speed by half the length of the longest day, 9 muhūrtas, gives \(47{,}263\tfrac{21}{60}\) yojanas, the distance at which, on that day, the rising Sun first becomes visible to an observer in Bharata, the southern region of Jambūdvīpa in which India lies. The geometry is not that of the siddhāntas, but every number follows by arithmetic from a few stated assumptions. That internal consistency, rather than agreement with measurement, is what the Jain treatment of the heavens aims at.

docs.title: 3.6.3 Months, years and the five-year yuga
docs.text:
Within this framework the calendar is close to that of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa: a five-year yuga of 1830 days, with 62 synodic and 67 sidereal months, the same 3:2 ratio of longest to shortest day, and similar rules for the nakṣatras of the Moon. The Jain texts are more systematic than the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa in naming the units they use. They distinguish five kinds of month, each a fraction of the yuga:

  • the sidereal month (nakṣatra), \(1830/67 = 27\tfrac{21}{67}\) days;

  • the synodic month (cāndra), \(1830/62 = 29\tfrac{32}{62}\) days;

  • the civil or “seasonal” month (ṛtu, also karma), 30 days;

  • the solar month (āditya or sūrya), \(1830/60 = 30\tfrac{1}{2}\) days;

  • the “increased” month (abhivardhita), \(31\tfrac{121}{124}\) days, one-twelfth of a year that contains thirteen synodic months.

Twelve of each make a year of \(327\tfrac{51}{67}\), \(354\tfrac{12}{62}\), 360, 366 and \(383\tfrac{44}{62}\) days respectively. The yuga consists of three ordinary lunar years and two “increased” years, the third and the fifth, and the arithmetic closes exactly: \(3 \times 354\tfrac{12}{62} + 2 \times 383\tfrac{44}{62} = 1830\) days, which is also five solar years of 366 days, sixty-one civil months and sixty solar months. The texts begin the year and the yuga with the month Śrāvaṇa, near the summer solstice, where the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa begins with Māgha at the winter solstice, and they begin their list of nakṣatras with Abhijit rather than Kṛttikā.

docs.title: 3.6.4 The Moon among the nakṣatras
docs.text:
The Jain texts do not treat the nakṣatras as equal. They measure the time for which the Moon is “joined” to each and assign 15 muhūrtas to six of them, 45 to six others, 30 to the remaining fifteen, and \(9\tfrac{27}{67}\) to Abhijit (Table 3.3). The total is \(6 \times 15 + 15 \times 30 + 6 \times 45 + 9\tfrac{27}{67} = 819\tfrac{27}{67}\) muhūrtas, which is exactly the sidereal month of \(27\tfrac{21}{67}\) days. The Sun’s stay with each nakṣatra is obtained by multiplying by \(\tfrac{67}{5}\), the ratio of the Sun’s year of 366 days to the Moon’s sidereal month, and the Sun’s stays then add up to 366 days. The same unequal division is found in other early jyotiṣa texts and survives in some later Brahmanical works; in the Jain canon it serves the computation of the calendar, not astrology alone.

Table 3.3. The unequal nakṣatras of the Jain texts: the time for which the Moon and the Sun are “joined” to each asterism, in days (d) and muhūrtas (m). One day = 30 muhūrtas. Nakṣatras Moon Sun Śatabhiṣaj, Bharaṇī, Ārdrā, Āśleṣā, Svāti, Jyeṣṭhā 15 m 6 d 21 m the remaining fifteen 30 m 13 d 12 m Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Uttaraphalgunī, Viśākhā, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarabhadrapadā 45 m 20 d 3 m Abhijit \(9\tfrac{27}{67}\) m 4 d 6 m

docs.title: 3.6.5 Commentaries and later use
docs.text: The canonical texts were explained in learned commentaries, above all those of Malayagiri in the twelfth century, which work through their computations (Chapter 9). They were not, however, used to compute almanacs once the siddhāntas had spread. Jain communities, like their neighbours, followed the regional luni-solar almanacs, and Jain scholars who wrote on astronomy wrote mostly in the siddhānta tradition. The Jain religious year is accordingly a luni-solar one of the common Indian type: Mahāvīra’s birth is celebrated on the thirteenth tithi of the bright half of Caitra, the festival of Paryuṣaṇa falls in Bhādrapada, and Dīpāvalī commemorates Mahāvīra’s liberation. The Vīra Nirvāṇa era, whose year begins on the day after Dīpāvalī, counts from the traditional date of that event, 527 BCE; most historians place Mahāvīra later, as an older contemporary of the Buddha.

docs.title: 3.7.1 The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna
docs.text:
The fullest early Buddhist source for astronomy is the Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna, one of the stories collected in the Divyāvadāna. It was translated into Chinese in the third century CE, and two early Chinese versions survive, so it existed in some form by then (Mukhopadhyaya 1954). Its frame story is about caste. Ānanda accepts water at a well from Prakṛti, a girl of the outcaste Mātaṅga community, who falls in love with him. To explain her attachment, the Buddha tells of a former life in which Triśaṅku, king of the Mātaṅgas, asked the proud brahmin Puṣkarasārin to give his daughter in marriage to Triśaṅku’s son Śārdūlakarṇa. When the brahmin refuses with contempt, Triśaṅku shows that he knows the Veda and the brahmins’ own sciences better than Puṣkarasārin, and argues that birth creates no natural distinctions among human beings. Most of the astronomy is placed in Triśaṅku’s mouth as part of that demonstration. A Buddhist text thus uses mastery of jyotiṣa to undermine the claim that such knowledge was the birthright of one community.

The astronomical part lists the twenty-eight nakṣatras beginning with Kṛttikā, with the number of their stars, their shapes, their presiding deities and clans (gotra), and the foods and undertakings suited to each. It describes the lengths of day and night through the year in muhūrtas and the shadow of a gnomon; defines measures of length, weight and time; and gives prognostications from the Moon’s position among the nakṣatras, from earthquakes, and for persons born under each asterism. Its calendar is of the same pre-siddhānta type as that of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa and the Jain texts, and Pingree used it as one of the witnesses for Mesopotamian elements in early Indian astronomy (Pingree 1973). The text matters for two reasons. It dates material of the jyotiṣa type independently of the Brahmanical tradition, and it shows that knowledge of the nakṣatras was a shared possession of Brahmins, Buddhists and others, which could be claimed and contested. Through its Chinese translations it also began the eastward travel of Indian astral lore (Chapter 16).

docs.title: 3.7.2 The monastic calendar
docs.text:
Buddhist monastic life was regulated by the lunar calendar. The community assembled for the uposatha (Sanskrit upavasatha) at new and full moon to recite the monastic rules, and lay followers kept the uposatha days, including the eighth day of each fortnight, by taking additional precepts. Because a fortnight could have fourteen or fifteen days, depending on where a tithi was omitted, the monks had to know which. The Pali Vinaya relates that lay followers asked monks which day of the fortnight it was and that the monks were then permitted to learn the reckoning of the fortnight. The Theravāda tradition later fixed a simple rule: in each season of four months the third and seventh fortnights have fourteen days and the others fifteen, giving a season of 118 days and a year of 354 days, close to twelve synodic months (354.4 days).

The rains retreat (Pali vassa, Sanskrit varṣā) of three months begins on the day after the full moon of Āṣāḍha (Pali Āsāḷha) and ends with the pavāraṇā ceremony, after which the kaṭhina robes are given. The Theravāda calendars of Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia remain luni-solar calendars of the Indian type: when an intercalary month is needed it is usually a second Āsāḷha, so that the retreat stays in the rainy season (Chapter 16). Their Buddhist era counts from a traditional date of the Buddha’s final passing, 544/543 BCE, about a century and a half earlier than the date most historians now prefer (c. 400 BCE).

docs.title: 3.8 Other Early Sources
docs.text: Several other texts bridge the gap between the Vedāṅga and the siddhāntas. The Gārgīya Jyotiṣa (or Vṛddhagārgīyasaṃhitā), probably from around the beginning of the Common Era, is a large compilation of omens, nakṣatra lore and calendrical rules, whose contents and date have been re-examined by Geslani et al. (2017). The Pariśiṣṭas (supplements) of the Atharvaveda preserve omen and nakṣatra texts. The Arthaśāstra uses a calendar of the same general type (Section 3.9). With the Jain and Buddhist texts just described, they show the five-year calendar and its associated lore spread across Brahmanical, Buddhist and Jain literature before the arrival of Greek astronomy (Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 3.9 Time-Reckoning in the Early State
docs.text: The Arthaśāstra, the treatise on statecraft attributed by tradition to Kauṭilya (its present form is composite, c. 50 BCE–300 CE), shows the calendar in administrative use. Its chapter on the measurement of space and time defines units of time from the smallest (tuṭa, lava, nimeṣa) up to the nālikā and muhūrta, describes a water clock, and gives the lengths of a gnomon’s shadow at different times of day. It describes a year of twelve months with intercalation and speaks of different kinds of month (solar, lunar, sidereal and others) used for different purposes, such as the payment of servants and the reckoning of revenue. The calendar is of the same pre-siddhānta type as that of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, adapted to the needs of an administration. Like the Vedic texts, the Arthaśāstra also expects the king to employ astrologers and to heed omens, while warning, in a well-known verse, against excessive reliance on the stars (Chapter 15).

docs.title: 3.10 Evidence of Observation
docs.text: How much observation lay behind the Vedic and Vedāṅga calendar? The texts do not record observations in the way that the Babylonian Diaries do, but they presuppose them. The ritual required knowing when the Sun reached its northern and southern turning points, which could be found by watching the sunrise point on the horizon or the noon shadow of a gnomon; the full and new moons and the asterisms near the Moon were watched night by night; and the length of daylight was measured with water clocks. Ōhashi (1993) collected the textual evidence for these practices and concluded that systematic, if simple, observation was part of Vedic ritual life; its precision, however, was limited.

docs.title: 3.11 Assessment
docs.text: The Vedic and Vedāṅga period produced a functioning luni-solar ritual calendar based on the Sun’s annual course and the Moon’s course among the nakṣatras; the concept of the tithi; a scheme of intercalation; a schematic account of the variation of daylight; the use of the gnomon and the water clock; and a set of named asterisms that remained the frame of Indian lunar astronomy. It did not yet have a theory of the planets, a geometrical model of the sky, or a way of predicting eclipses. Those came with the siddhāntas, after contact with Greek astronomy, as the next chapters describe.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: The text and translation of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa are in Sastry (1985). Plofker (2009) gives a balanced account of Vedic and Vedāṅga astronomy and the dating debate; Ōhashi (1993) surveys the evidence for observation; Pingree (1973) states the case for Mesopotamian influence.

docs.title: Chapter 4: The Nakṣatras: India’s Lunar Asterisms
4.1 Stations of the Moon
docs.text:
The Moon completes a circuit of the stars in about \(27\tfrac{1}{3}\) days (the sidereal month). An observer who notes, night by night, which group of stars the Moon is near will soon have a set of twenty-seven or twenty-eight “stations”. Several ancient peoples made such lists: the Indian nakṣatras, the Chinese xiu (“lodges”), and the Arabic manāzil al-qamar (“stations of the Moon”). In India the nakṣatras were the first frame of reference for the positions of the Moon and the Sun, and they have remained central to the calendar, to ritual and to astrology ever since.

The word nakṣatra in the Ṛgveda means simply “star” or “heavenly light”. By the later Vedic period it had acquired the technical sense of one of the twenty-seven or twenty-eight asterisms along the Moon’s path, each with a name, a presiding deity and a ritual character. In the Vedic texts the asterisms are groups of stars of unequal extent. In the siddhāntas they became twenty-seven equal divisions of the ecliptic, each of \(13^\circ 20'\) (\(800'\) of arc), each still associated with a principal star.

docs.title: 4.2.1 The Vedic lists
docs.text: The oldest complete lists are in the Yajurveda Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas, especially the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (4.4.10) and Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa, and in the Atharvaveda (19.7). These lists begin with Kṛttikā, the Pleiades, and give a deity for each asterism (Agni for Kṛttikā, Prajāpati for Rohiṇī, Soma for Mṛgaśiras, Rudra for Ārdrā, and so on). Some lists have twenty-seven members, others twenty-eight, the extra one being Abhijit. The names and deities differ in detail from the later standard list: Puṣya appears as Tiṣya, Āśleṣā as Āśreṣā, Mūla as Vicṛtau, Śravaṇa as Śroṇā, and the deities of a few asterisms differ.

docs.title: 4.2.2 The siddhānta list
docs.text:
In the siddhāntas, from the fifth century CE onwards, the list begins with Aśvinī, and the first point of Aśvinī is the starting point of the sidereal zodiac, the first point of the sign Meṣa (Aries). The change of starting point is discussed below. Table 4.1 gives the standard list.

docs.title: 4.2.3 Abhijit
docs.text:
Abhijit, the twenty-eighth asterism of some Vedic lists, is usually identified with Vega (\(\alpha\) Lyrae), which lies about sixty degrees north of the ecliptic, far from the Moon’s path. Its presence in a lunar list is therefore odd, and it may reflect an older system in which bright stars marked the Moon’s general region rather than its exact path. The siddhāntas dropped Abhijit from the equal division of twenty-seven, though some later systems give it a narrow segment within Uttarāṣāḍhā and Śravaṇa for ritual and astrological purposes.
