docs.title: 4.3 Junction Stars and Their Coordinates
docs.text:
Each nakṣatra of the siddhāntas has a principal or “junction” star (yogatārā), used for observing conjunctions of the Moon and planets with the asterism. The Sūryasiddhānta (chapter 8) and other texts give the position of each junction star by two coordinates, usually called dhruvaka and vikṣepa. These are not the ecliptic longitude and latitude of modern astronomy: the dhruvaka is the point at which the circle through the star and the celestial pole meets the ecliptic, and the vikṣepa is the distance of the star from the ecliptic measured along that circle. Burgess recognised this “polar” system in his commentary on the Sūryasiddhānta (Burgess 1860).

Identifying the junction stars with stars of modern catalogues has occupied scholars since the eighteenth century. The coordinates given in the texts are rounded, differ from one text to another, and in some cases were computed rather than observed. Pingree and Morrissey compared the coordinates in a range of texts and showed how uncertain some of the identifications are (Pingree and Morrissey 1989). For bright, isolated stars such as Aldebaran, Regulus, Spica, Antares and Altair the identification is secure; for faint or crowded asterisms (Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, Viśākhā, Śatabhiṣaj) more than one candidate has been proposed. Identifications should therefore be quoted with their uncertainty, not as settled facts.

docs.title: 4.3.1 Stars near the Moon’s path
docs.text: Several junction stars lie close enough to the ecliptic to be hidden (occulted) by the Moon from time to time, and to be approached closely by the planets: Aldebaran (Rohiṇī), Regulus (Maghā), Spica (Citrā) and Antares (Jyeṣṭhā) among the bright ones, and the Pleiades (Kṛttikā). The siddhāntas compute the conjunctions of the Moon and planets with the junction stars, using the stars’ coordinates. One configuration attracted special attention: the group of stars of Rohiṇī was imagined as a cart (śakaṭa), and the passage of a planet through it, the “splitting of Rohiṇī’s cart” (rohiṇīśakaṭabheda), was treated as a portent of disaster. The Sūryasiddhānta discusses which planets can pass through it, given their latitudes, and the omen literature describes its consequences, an example of the close interweaving of computation and divination (Burgess 1860; Varāhamihira 1981–1982).

docs.title: 4.3.2 The star catalogue of the Sūryasiddhānta
docs.text:
The eighth chapter of the Sūryasiddhānta is the nearest thing to a star catalogue in classical Sanskrit astronomy, and it shows both what the astronomers recorded and what they left unsaid (Burgess 1860). It gives the positions in a compressed form. For each nakṣatra it states the “portion” (bhoga) of the junction star, its distance from the beginning of its own division of \(13^\circ 20'\), in units of ten minutes of arc; adding the divisions already passed gives the star’s dhruva. Rohiṇī’s portion, for example, is 57 units, or \(9^\circ 30'\), so its dhruva is \(40^\circ + 9^\circ 30' = 49^\circ 30'\). A few positions are given instead by reference to a neighbour: Uttarāṣāḍhā lies in the middle of the division of Pūrvāṣāḍhā, Abhijit at its end, Śravaṇa at the end of Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Śraviṣṭhā where the third and fourth quarters of Śravaṇa meet. The latitudes (vikṣepa) follow in a separate list of whole and half degrees, from \(0^\circ\) for Puṣya, Maghā and Revatī to \(37^\circ\) north for Svāti and \(60^\circ\) north for Abhijit. Almost all the positions are round numbers: whole degrees or simple fractions, not the minutes of arc of an observing record.

The same chapter answers a question that the bare list leaves open: which star of a group is the junction star. Its rule is descriptive. The northern star of the pair is the junction star of the two Phalgunīs, the two Bhādrapadās and the two Āṣāḍhās, and of Viśākhā, Aśvinī and Mṛgaśiras; the middle star of Jyeṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Anurādhā and Puṣya; the southern star of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Maghā and Revatī; the eastern star of Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Mūla and Āśleṣā; Hasta and Śraviṣṭhā are described by their western stars; for the rest the brightest star of the group is meant. A rule of this kind presupposes that the reader already knows the shape of each group in the sky, which is exactly the knowledge that has to be reconstructed today, and it is one reason why identifications differ for the faint and crowded groups.

Besides the junction stars, the chapter places a handful of bright stars away from the zodiac, chosen for their ritual and astrological importance: Agastya (Canopus) at the end of Mithuna, \(80^\circ\) south; Mṛgavyādha, the “deer-hunter” (Sirius), in the twentieth degree of Mithuna, \(40^\circ\) south; Agni and Brahmahṛdaya (the latter usually identified with Capella) in the twenty-second degree of Vṛṣabha, \(8^\circ\) and \(30^\circ\) north; Prajāpati five degrees east of Brahmahṛdaya, \(38^\circ\) north; and Apāṃvatsa and Āpas a little north of Citrā. It also gives the numerical form of the “splitting of Rohiṇī’s cart” described above: a planet in the seventeenth degree of Vṛṣabha with a southern latitude of more than two degrees passes through the cart. Canopus, low in the southern sky of north India, mattered because its heliacal rising in early autumn was associated with the end of the rains, and the Bṛhatsaṃhitā devotes a chapter to it (Chapter 15).

That chapter, on the “course of Agastya”, shows how a single star could join myth, ritual and computation. The first half of its twenty-one verses retells the deeds of the sage Agastya, who drank the ocean and humbled the Vindhya mountain, and describe the autumn scene at the star’s rising: the waters, muddied by the rains, become clear again, “like the hearts of the good”, and water poisoned by serpents becomes wholesome. The king is to offer a libation (argha) to the star in the southern quarter at the end of the night, as the darkness begins to break, with flowers, fruits, gems, cloth, a cow and a bull, and the star’s colour and brightness at its rising are read as omens for health, rain and harvest. But one verse is astronomical. The learned, Varāhamihira says, should announce the date of the first appearance for each place by calculation; at Ujjayinī it falls when the true Sun is still seven degrees short of Kanyā, at a longitude of about \(143^\circ\). At the end of the chapter he records an older rule, introduced with “it is said” (kila): the star is seen when the Sun is in Hasta, and sets when the Sun reaches Rohiṇī.

The two rules can be compared with the sky. Canopus never rises more than about \(14^\circ\) above the horizon at Ujjain, so its first visibility before dawn depends on how dark the sky must be and how high the star must stand to be seen. A modern computation for the sixth century, assuming that the star becomes visible when it is two to six degrees high while the Sun is ten to fourteen degrees below the horizon, puts the first morning appearance when the Sun’s sidereal longitude (counted from a zero point that places Spica at \(180^\circ\)) is between about \(138^\circ\) and \(151^\circ\). Varāhamihira’s \(143^\circ\) falls well within this range, and his insistence on computing the date separately for each place is correct, since the star’s altitude, and with it the date of first visibility, changes quickly with latitude. The older rule, with the Sun in Hasta (\(160^\circ\) to \(173^\circ 20'\)), would put the first appearance at Ujjain between about one and five weeks too late.

A second, independent star list entered Sanskrit with the astrolabe (Chapter 11). The rete of an astrolabe carries pointers for bright stars, and the user must know where they are. Malayendu Sūri’s commentary on Mahendra Sūri’s Yantrarāja, written in the late fourteenth century, accordingly gives Persian and Sanskrit names for thirty-two stars, with data for setting them on the instrument. These stars and their positions came from the Islamic tradition, and so largely from Ptolemy’s catalogue, not from the Sūryasiddhānta, and they include stars far from the zodiac that had no place in the nakṣatra system. From the fourteenth century, therefore, two star lists of different origin coexisted in Sanskrit, a small instance of the meeting of traditions described in Chapter 11.

docs.title: 4.3.3 Reading the coordinates: a worked example
docs.text:
Because the coordinates are polar (Section 4.3), a star far from the ecliptic can have a dhruva very different from its ecliptic longitude. Svāti, usually identified with Arcturus, is the clearest case. The Sūryasiddhānta gives it dhruva \(199^\circ\) and vikṣepa \(37^\circ\) north. Read naively as an ecliptic longitude, \(199^\circ\) would put Arcturus \(19^\circ\) east of Spica, at \(180^\circ\); in the sky the two stars have almost the same longitude.

The conversion follows the definition. With the Sūryasiddhānta’s obliquity of \(24^\circ\), the point of the ecliptic at \(199^\circ\) has a declination of \(-7^\circ 37'\) and a right ascension of \(197^\circ 28'\). The star lies on the same circle through the poles, \(37^\circ\) further north, at declination \(+29^\circ 23'\) and the same right ascension. Converting these equatorial coordinates into ecliptic ones in the usual way gives a longitude of \(182^\circ 42'\) and a latitude of \(+33^\circ 41'\). The same conversion for Citrā (dhruva \(180^\circ\), vikṣepa \(2^\circ\) south) gives \(180^\circ 49'\) and \(-1^\circ 50'\). In the text’s own coordinates, therefore, Arcturus is \(1^\circ 53'\) east of Spica and \(33^\circ 41'\) from the ecliptic. Computed from modern data for 500 CE, including the large proper motion of Arcturus, it was \(0^\circ 23'\) east of Spica and \(31^\circ 46'\) from the ecliptic. The text is thus about \(1\tfrac{1}{2}^\circ\) out in longitude and \(2^\circ\) in latitude, an accuracy typical of the list as a whole.

The modern longitudes are counted from a zero point that makes Spica agree with the converted value, since the text’s zero point is not a star. Table 4.2 extends the comparison to ten bright stars. Three features stand out. First, the conversion matters most for stars far from the ecliptic and away from the solstitial points: for Svāti it moves the longitude by more than \(16^\circ\), for Brahmahṛdaya by more than \(8^\circ\), while for Rohiṇī, Maghā and Citrā it changes little. Secondly, after conversion the longitudes of the bright zodiacal stars agree with the modern values to within one to four degrees, and the latitudes of those near the ecliptic to within a degree; the far northern and southern stars fare worse: Mṛgavyādha is five degrees out in longitude, and Brahmahṛdaya’s latitude is six degrees too large if the star is Capella. Thirdly, the errors differ from star to star by several degrees, so they cannot be removed by moving the zero point or by assuming another date; they look like the errors of rounded values taken from different sources or corrected at different times, which is also the conclusion suggested by the variation of the coordinates between texts (Pingree and Morrissey 1989).

One consequence concerns the modern ayanāṃśa. The Citrā-pakṣa definition adopted by the Calendar Reform Committee (below) places Spica at an ecliptic longitude of exactly \(180^\circ\). The Sūryasiddhānta’s \(180^\circ\) for Citrā is a polar longitude, which corresponds to an ecliptic longitude about \(49'\) larger. The modern convention was inspired by the text but does not reproduce it exactly, which illustrates the point made below: there is no uniquely “correct” sidereal zero point to be recovered from the sources.

docs.title: 4.4 From Kṛttikā to Aśvinī: Precession and the Zodiac
docs.text: The equinoxes and solstices move westward among the stars by about \(1^\circ\) in 72 years, so the nakṣatra in which the Sun stands at a given season changes over the centuries. This explains why lists that begin the year at different asterisms may come from different periods, and it is the basis of the dating arguments discussed in Chapter 3.

docs.title: 4.4.1 The sidereal zodiac
docs.text:
Indian astronomers of the siddhānta period counted longitudes from a fixed point among the stars, the beginning of Aśvinī, which they took to be the same as the beginning of the sign Meṣa. This is a sidereal zodiac. The Greek and modern Western zodiac is tropical: it is counted from the vernal equinox, which moves against the stars. The difference between the two, the ayanāṃśa, grows by about \(50”\) a year.

The siddhāntas place the end of Revatī, and hence the beginning of Aśvinī and of the zodiac, close to the star \(\zeta\) Piscium, the junction star of Revatī. The vernal equinox coincided with this region of the sky around the fifth or sixth century CE. In other words, the classical astronomers fixed their sidereal zero point at about the place where the equinox stood in their own time. The exact year in which the two zodiacs “coincided” depends on the definition adopted and is debated.

docs.title: 4.4.2 The ayanāṃśa today
docs.text:
Different schools adopted different definitions of the sidereal zero point, and hence different values of the ayanāṃśa. The Calendar Reform Committee of 1955 recommended, for religious calendars, the definition associated with N. C. Lahiri (the “Citrā-pakṣa” ayanāṃśa), in which the star Citrā (Spica) has a sidereal longitude of exactly \(180^\circ\) (Calendar Reform Committee 1955). On this definition the ayanāṃśa was about \(23^\circ 51'\) in 2000 and about \(24^\circ 12'\) in 2025. Other definitions in use among astrologers (associated with B. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnamurti, among others) differ from it by up to about a degree and a half. These differences are matters of convention, not of observation: there is no physically privileged sidereal zero point.

The practical consequence is that the Indian solar months and the dates of solar festivals have drifted against the seasons. Makara Saṅkrānti, the Sun’s entry into sidereal Capricorn, falls today on 14 or 15 January, more than three weeks after the winter solstice that it once marked (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 4.5 Nakṣatras and Signs
docs.text:
When the twelve signs of the zodiac (rāśis) entered India with Greek astrology (Chapter 5), the two divisions of the ecliptic were combined. A sign of \(30^\circ\) contains \(2\tfrac{1}{4}\) nakṣatras, or nine quarters (pādas) of \(3^\circ 20'\), and since both systems start from the same point, the beginning of Aśvinī and of Meṣa, a sign begins at a nakṣatra boundary every \(120^\circ\), that is, at the beginnings of Meṣa, Siṃha and Dhanus; the other signs begin at the boundary of a quarter. Table 4.3 shows the correspondence, which follows by simple arithmetic.

Table 4.3. The twelve signs and the nakṣatras (with quarters) that they contain Sign Western Nakṣatras contained Meṣa Aries Aśvinī; Bharaṇī; Kṛttikā 1 Vṛṣabha Taurus Kṛttikā 2–4; Rohiṇī; Mṛgaśiras 1–2 Mithuna Gemini Mṛgaśiras 3–4; Ārdrā; Punarvasu 1–3 Karka Cancer Punarvasu 4; Puṣya; Āśleṣā Siṃha Leo Maghā; Pūrvaphalgunī; Uttaraphalgunī 1 Kanyā Virgo Uttaraphalgunī 2–4; Hasta; Citrā 1–2 Tulā Libra Citrā 3–4; Svāti; Viśākhā 1–3 Vṛścika Scorpio Viśākhā 4; Anurādhā; Jyeṣṭhā Dhanus Sagittarius Mūla; Pūrvāṣāḍhā; Uttarāṣāḍhā 1 Makara Capricorn Uttarāṣāḍhā 2–4; Śravaṇa; Dhaniṣṭhā 1–2 Kumbha Aquarius Dhaniṣṭhā 3–4; Śatabhiṣaj; Pūrvabhādrapadā 1–3 Mīna Pisces Pūrvabhādrapadā 4; Uttarabhādrapadā; Revatī

The Sanskrit names of the signs are translations of the Greek ones (Meṣa, “ram”, for Aries; Vṛṣabha, “bull”, for Taurus; Mithuna, “couple”, for Gemini; and so on), and the Greek names themselves were also used in Sanskrit for a time (Chapter 5). Because the Indian signs are sidereal, they no longer coincide with the Western tropical signs of the same names: the Sun now enters sidereal Meṣa around 14 April, about three and a half weeks after it enters tropical Aries at the March equinox.

docs.title: 4.6 Finding the Moon’s Nakṣatra
docs.text:
Given the Moon’s sidereal longitude, its nakṣatra and quarter follow by division:

\[\text{nakṣatra} = \left\lfloor \frac{\lambda_M}{13^\circ 20'} \right\rfloor + 1, \qquad \text{pāda} = \left\lfloor \frac{\lambda_M \bmod 13^\circ 20'}{3^\circ 20'} \right\rfloor + 1 .\tag{4.1}\]

For example, if the Moon’s sidereal longitude is \(200^\circ 45'\), then \(200^\circ 45' / 13^\circ 20' = 15.06\), so the Moon is in the sixteenth nakṣatra, Viśākhā, which begins at \(200^\circ\); it is \(45'\) into it, in the first quarter. Since the Moon moves on average about \(13^\circ 10'\) a day relative to the stars, it will leave Viśākhā, \(12^\circ 35'\) further on, in a little under a day. The almanac gives, for each day, the nakṣatra current at sunrise and the time at which it ends, computed from the Moon’s true (not mean) motion; because that motion varies between about \(12^\circ\) and \(15^\circ\) a day, a nakṣatra can last from about 21 to 27 hours.

docs.title: 4.7.1 Calendar and ritual
docs.text: The nakṣatra of the Moon on a given day is one of the five elements of the almanac (pañcāṅga), and the names of the lunar months derive from the nakṣatras near which the full moon falls: Caitra from Citrā, Vaiśākha from Viśākhā, Jyaiṣṭha from Jyeṣṭhā, Āṣāḍha from Āṣāḍhā, Śrāvaṇa from Śravaṇa, Bhādrapada from Bhādrapadā, Āśvina from Aśvinī, Kārttika from Kṛttikā, Mārgaśīrṣa from Mṛgaśiras, Pauṣa from Puṣya, Māgha from Maghā, and Phālguna from Phalgunī. Vedic ritual texts prescribe particular nakṣatras for installing the sacred fires and for other rites, and the domestic ritual manuals (gṛhyasūtras) prescribe them for marriage and other life-cycle rites.

docs.title: 4.7.2 The nakṣatras in Vedic ritual
docs.text: The Brāhmaṇas discuss at length under which nakṣatra the sacred fires should be installed (agnyādheya). The Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa considers the Kṛttikās, Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, the Phalgunīs, Hasta and Citrā, giving mythological reasons for and against each; the debate shows both that the nakṣatras were observed and named and that their use was governed by ritual reasoning rather than by astronomy. The Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa prescribes offerings to each nakṣatra and its deity (the nakṣatreṣṭi). In this way the asterisms became a calendar of ritual opportunities long before they became a coordinate system.

docs.title: 4.7.3 Personal life
docs.text: The nakṣatra occupied by the Moon at a person’s birth, the janmanakṣatra, has long been important in Indian personal life. In parts of south India birthdays are still celebrated on the day the Moon returns to the birth nakṣatra rather than on the solar date, and the first syllable of a child’s name was traditionally chosen according to the quarter (pāda) of the birth nakṣatra. Each nakṣatra is divided into four pādas of \(3^\circ 20'\), giving 108 in all; in astrology each pāda corresponds to one ninth of a sign (navāṃśa). The use of the nakṣatras in electing auspicious times (muhūrta), in the planetary periods (daśā) of horoscopy and in matching horoscopes for marriage belongs to astrology and is described in Chapter 15.

docs.title: 4.7.4 Seasons and agriculture
docs.text:
Because the Sun spends about \(13\tfrac{1}{2}\) days in each nakṣatra, the Sun’s nakṣatra provides a fine division of the solar year, and several regional agricultural calendars use it. In Kerala the solar nakṣatra periods (Malayalam ñāṟṟuvela) are traditional markers for sowing and for the expected monsoon rains, the period of the Sun in Ārdrā (Tiruvātira) in late June being associated with the rains. Proverbs linking rain in particular nakṣatras with good or bad harvests are found in many Indian languages, among them the Bengali sayings ascribed to Khanā and the Hindi sayings ascribed to Ghāgh and Bhaḍḍarī (Volume 15, Kṛṣi and Jīva Vijñāna). The Bṛhatsaṃhitā of Varāhamihira includes nakṣatra-based rules for forecasting rain (Chapter 15). Such traditions record long experience of the monsoon calendar, but they were never systematically tested, and the folk beliefs attached to them (for example, that rain in Svāti produces pearls in oysters) are poetic conventions rather than observations.

The sky-knowledge of Adivasi and other rural communities outside the Sanskrit and Tamil written traditions is a different matter. Many communities have their own names and stories for the Pleiades, Orion, the Great Bear and the Milky Way, and use them to tell the time at night and to mark the seasons of sowing and harvest. This knowledge has been documented systematically only recently and for a few regions, notably among the Gond, Kolam and Banjara of central India; it is described in Volume 23, Jana–Jāti, and is not treated further in this volume, which follows the written astronomical tradition.

docs.title: 4.7.5 Myth
docs.text: The Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata tell that the nakṣatras were twenty-seven daughters of Dakṣa, all married to the Moon (Soma). The Moon favoured Rohiṇī; the other wives complained to their father, whose curse made the Moon waste away, and the curse was softened so that the Moon waxes again each month. The story ties the Moon’s monthly circuit of the asterisms to its waxing and waning: the Moon wastes and recovers because of its conduct towards its twenty-seven wives.

docs.title: 4.8 The Seven Sages and Their “Motion”
docs.text:
Not every star that mattered lay on the Moon’s path. From the later Vedic period the seven bright stars of the Great Bear (Ursa Major) were identified with the Seven Sages (saptarṣi): Marīci, Vasiṣṭha, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha and Kratu. Beside Vasiṣṭha (Mizar) shines the faint Arundhatī (Alcor), named after his wife. The domestic ritual manuals tell the bride and groom to look at the pole star (dhruva) and at Arundhatī after the wedding, as emblems of constancy and fidelity; the older history of the asterism in the Ṛgveda is discussed in Volume 1, Veda Prakāśa.

A doctrine found in the Purāṇas, and set out by Varāhamihira in the chapter of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā on “the course of the Seven Sages” (saptarṣicāra) on the authority of Vṛddhagarga, holds that the Sages move through the nakṣatras, staying a hundred years in each, so that they complete the circuit of twenty-seven in 2700 years. Varāhamihira states that the Sages were in Maghā when Yudhiṣṭhira ruled the earth, and that the Śaka era began 2526 years after that king’s time (Varāhamihira 1981–1982). This would place Yudhiṣṭhira in the twenty-fifth century BCE, not at the beginning of the Kali age in 3102 BCE, where other traditions put the events of the Mahābhārata: the traditional chronologies of the epic age were themselves not consistent (Chapter 14).

The Purāṇas define the Sages’ “position” as the nakṣatra that lies on a line through the two stars of the group that rise first, but no such motion exists. The stars of the Great Bear share in the slow precessional shift of all the stars, about one degree in seventy-two years, so that such a line would pass from one nakṣatra of \(13^\circ 20'\) to the next in roughly 960 years, not a hundred; otherwise their places among the nakṣatras are fixed. The siddhānta astronomers did not include the Sages’ motion in their computations. The doctrine belongs to the omen and chronological literature, where it served as a measure of long periods.

It also became an era. In Kashmir and the neighbouring hill states years were counted in the Saptarṣi or Laukika (“popular”) era, in cycles of a hundred years corresponding to the Sages’ stay in one nakṣatra. The hundreds were usually omitted, so that a date gives only the year within the current century. The era’s epoch corresponds to 3076 BCE, and Kalhaṇa’s chronicle of Kashmir, the Rājataraṅgiṇī, completed in the Laukika year [42]24 (1148–49 CE), dates its events by it (Sewell and Dikshit 1896). A computed epoch and an imaginary motion thus supplied a working calendar for one of India’s most important historical works.

docs.title: 4.9 The Lunar Mansions in Other Cultures
docs.text:
The Chinese system of twenty-eight lodges (xiu) is attested from at least the fifth century BCE. Its divisions are unequal and are measured along the celestial equator from “determinative stars”. Several xiu share stars with nakṣatras (the Pleiades, Spica, Antares), but many do not. The Arabic system of twenty-eight lunar stations (manāzil) appears in pre-Islamic Arabian weather lore and was later systematised; its relation to the Indian list has been debated, and an Indian contribution to its later astronomical form has been suggested but not established. The question whether the Indian and Chinese systems share a common origin, influenced one another, or arose independently was argued vigorously in the nineteenth century and is not settled; the evidence is compatible with independent development from the same observable fact, the Moon’s monthly circuit of the stars (Pingree 1981).

In the eleventh century al-Bīrūnī described the Indian lunar stations at length in his book on India, comparing them with the Arabic stations (al-Bīrūnī 1888). Indian nakṣatra lore also travelled with Buddhism to Central and East Asia, through texts such as the Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna (Section 3.7).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the identifications of the junction stars see Pingree and Morrissey (1989) and Burgess (1860); for the Vedic lists, Ōhashi (1993); for the ayanāṃśa question, Calendar Reform Committee (1955); for the place of the nakṣatras in the calendar, Sewell and Dikshit (1896).

docs.title: Chapter 5: Contact and Transformation: The Formation of Siddhānta Astronomy
5.1 The Problem of Origins
docs.text:
Between the five-year calendar of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa and the Āryabhaṭīya of 499 CE lies a transformation. The earlier astronomy had no planetary theory, no geometrical model of the heavens, no trigonometry and no method of predicting eclipses. The Āryabhaṭīya, and the systems summarised by Varāhamihira a few years later, have all of these: a spherical earth at the centre of a spherical cosmos, a zodiac of twelve signs divided into degrees and minutes, epicyclic models for the Sun, Moon and five planets, a table of sines, and complete procedures for eclipses. Almost nothing survives from the centuries in which this change took place, and historians have had to reconstruct it from fragments, from the later texts, and from comparison with Mesopotamian and Greek astronomy.

This chapter describes what is known about that transformation and the debate about it. Its conclusion, in brief, is that Greek astrology and elements of Hellenistic mathematical astronomy reached India in the early centuries CE and were decisive for the new science; and that what Indian astronomers made of them, from the sine function to the great integer cycles, was original and distinctive.

docs.title: 5.2 Mesopotamian Elements
docs.text:
Chapter 3 described the parallels between the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa and the Mesopotamian compendium MUL.APIN (Pingree 1973). Some of the oldest layers of Indian omen literature also have Mesopotamian counterparts, and Pingree argued that a part of the omen material of the Gārgīya Jyotiṣa and of the Atharvavedic supplements descends from the great Mesopotamian omen series Enūma Anu Enlil, transmitted through the Achaemenid empire (Pingree 1997). The sexagesimal subdivision of the day into sixty nāḍikās, each of sixty vināḍikās, may belong to the same stream.

Later, a second wave of Babylonian mathematical astronomy reached India indirectly, through Greek intermediaries. The Vasiṣṭha system summarised by Varāhamihira (below) uses arithmetical methods for the Moon and planets that closely resemble the linear and step-function schemes of Seleucid-period Babylonian astronomy, which Greek astronomers had also adopted (Neugebauer and Pingree 1970–1971; Neugebauer 1975).

docs.title: 5.3.1 Routes of contact
docs.text: After Alexander’s campaigns (327–325 BCE) Greek-speaking kingdoms ruled parts of Bactria and north-western India for two centuries, and trade between Roman Egypt and the ports of western India flourished in the first centuries CE. The Western Kṣatrapas, rulers of Gujarat and Mālava with their capital at Ujjayinī, were in close commercial contact with the Roman world. It was in their territory that Greek astrology was translated into Sanskrit, and Ujjayinī later became the meridian city of Indian astronomy.

docs.title: 5.3.2 The Yavanajātaka
docs.text:
The key document is the Yavanajātaka (“Horoscopy of the Greeks”), a Sanskrit verse treatise on Greek horoscopic astrology by Sphujidhvaja. In Pingree’s edition, the text states that it versifies a prose translation made by Yavaneśvara (“lord of the Greeks”) in a year Pingree computed as 149/150 CE, and that the verse version itself was completed in 269/270 CE (Pingree 1978b). The earlier date rests on an emended reading of a damaged verse, and Mak (2013), using newly found manuscripts, has questioned both the reading and Pingree’s account of the text’s history. The verse text belongs at any rate to the third century CE.

The Yavanajātaka introduced into Sanskrit the apparatus of Hellenistic astrology: the twelve signs of the zodiac and their attributes, the horoscopic “places” or houses counted from the ascendant, the planetary lords of signs, the aspects between planets, the decans, and the techniques for judging a nativity. Its final chapter contains rules for computing the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, of a kind that Pingree identified as Greek adaptations of Babylonian methods. The work was followed by the Vṛddhayavanajātaka of Mīnarāja (perhaps fourth century) and by the astrological works of Satya and others that Varāhamihira used two centuries later.

docs.title: 5.3.3 Greek words in Sanskrit astronomy
docs.text:
The clearest evidence of the Greek contribution is linguistic. Varāhamihira, in the opening chapter of his Bṛhajjātaka, gives the Greek names of the signs alongside the Sanskrit ones: kriya (Greek krios, Aries), tāvuri (tauros), jituma (didymoi), kulīra, leya (leōn), pāthona (parthenos), jūka (zygon), kaurpya (skorpios), taukṣika (toxotēs), ākokera (aigokerōs), hṛdroga (hydrochoos) and ittha (ichthyes). Other loanwords became permanent parts of the technical vocabulary of both astrology and astronomy (Table 5.1).

Table 5.1. Some Greek loanwords in Sanskrit astronomy and astrology Sanskrit Greek Meaning in Sanskrit horā hōra half of a sign; horoscopy as a whole kendra kentron cardinal place of a horoscope; anomaly of a planet liptā lepton minute of arc drekkāṇa dekanos one third of a sign (decan) jāmitra diametron the seventh place, opposite the ascendant āpoklima apoklima the “cadent” places of a horoscope paṇaphara epanaphora the “succedent” places

Varāhamihira also gives a learned Sanskrit derivation of horā from ahorātra (“day and night”) by dropping the first and last syllables. This is a scholastic etymology; the word is Greek. The use of kendra, originally the Greek word for the “centre” of an epicycle, for the anomaly of a planet in Indian planetary theory shows that Greek geometrical astronomy, not only astrology, entered the Indian vocabulary.

The seven-day week, with days named after the seven planets in the order Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, also came with Hellenistic astrology; its order derives from the Hellenistic scheme of “planetary hours”, explained in Chapter 13. The Yavanajātaka knows the week. Weekdays begin to appear in Indian inscriptions in the Gupta period.

Indian authors acknowledged their debt. Varāhamihira quotes the view that although the Yavanas are foreigners (mlecchas), this science is well established among them, and they are honoured like seers (Varāhamihira 1981–1982).

docs.title: 5.4.1 Varāhamihira’s compendium
docs.text:
The best view of Indian astronomy just before and around Āryabhaṭa comes from the Pañcasiddhāntikā (“Five Siddhāntas”) of Varāhamihira, whose epoch is 505 CE. Varāhamihira, who worked in the region of Ujjayinī and was active in the first half of the sixth century, summarised five astronomical systems then current, each named after a supposed author: Paitāmaha (“of the Grandfather”, Brahmā), Vāsiṣṭha (of the sage Vasiṣṭha), Romaka (“of the Romans”), Pauliśa (of Pauliśa, probably a Greek “Paulos”) and Saura (“of the Sun”). The text survives in only a few corrupt manuscripts. It was first edited by Thibaut and Sudhākara Dvivedī in 1889; the standard edition, with translation and a mathematical commentary, is that of Neugebauer and Pingree (1970–1971).

Varāhamihira also judged the five systems. He states that the Pauliśa is accurate, that the Romaka is close to it, that the Saura is more accurate still, and that the remaining two, the Paitāmaha and Vāsiṣṭha, are far from the truth (Neugebauer and Pingree 1970–1971).

docs.title: 5.4.2 The five systems
docs.text:
Paitāmaha.

The Paitāmaha system, summarised very briefly, is a version of the five-year calendar of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, with a year of 366 days. Its inclusion shows that the old calendar was still known in the sixth century, and Varāhamihira’s verdict shows that it was obsolete.

Vāsiṣṭha.

The Vāsiṣṭha uses arithmetical methods for the Moon and planets akin to those of late Babylonian astronomy (linear “zigzag” functions and step functions), as transmitted in Greek and Greco-Egyptian astronomy before Ptolemy.

Romaka.

The Romaka has a tropical year of 365;14,48 days (in sexagesimal fractions, that is \(365 + \tfrac{14}{60} + \tfrac{48}{3600}\) days, about 365.2467 days), the value of the Greek astronomer Hipparchus, and a cycle of 2850 years, which is 150 times the nineteen-year (Metonic) luni-solar cycle. Its name, its year and its cycle all point to a Greek source.

Pauliśa.

The Pauliśa, associated with a Greek name, contained methods for the Sun, Moon, eclipses and planets, and Varāhamihira used it extensively. A “Pauliśasiddhānta” was also known to later authors and to al-Bīrūnī, but it is not certain that it was the same text.

Saura.

The Saura is a fully developed siddhānta, with a sidereal year of 365;15,31,30 days (about 365.25875 days), epicyclic models for the planets and procedures for eclipses. It is an earlier form of the Sūryasiddhānta, which survives in a substantially later recension (Chapter 6).

The Pañcasiddhāntikā thus shows Indian astronomy around 500 CE as a field in which older Indian, Babylonian-derived and Greek-derived systems existed side by side, and in which the most accurate of them had already taken the form of the classical siddhānta.

docs.title: 5.5 What Was Borrowed and What Was Made
5.5.1 Pingree’s thesis
docs.text: David Pingree, who did more than anyone to edit and interpret the sources, argued that the mathematical models of the siddhāntas derived from Greek astronomy of the period between Hipparchus (second century BCE) and Ptolemy (second century CE), transmitted to India in the early centuries CE, before Ptolemy’s Almagest became standard in the Greek world. Since that pre-Ptolemaic Greek astronomy is almost entirely lost in Greek, he argued that the Sanskrit texts could be used to recover it (Pingree 1976, 1978a). On this view the Indian epicycle models, without Ptolemy’s equant, preserve an earlier Greek stage of planetary theory, and some Indian parameters go back to Greek ones.

docs.title: 5.5.2 Objections and qualifications
docs.text:
Pingree’s reconstruction has been criticised on several points.

  • Independent observation. Roger Billard’s statistical study of the mean motions in Indian texts showed that the parameters of several systems, including Āryabhaṭa’s, are most accurate close to the dates of the texts themselves, which implies that they were derived or corrected from observations made in India at that time (Billard 1971). Indian astronomers were not simply carrying Greek numbers forward.

  • Absence of direct evidence. No Greek text with the Indian planetary models has been found. The reconstruction of a lost Greek source is plausible but inferential.

  • Distinctive structure. The siddhānta models differ from anything known in Greek astronomy in important respects: the use of the sine instead of the chord; the variable size of the epicycles; the sequential application of the two planetary corrections; the integer revolution numbers in a great cycle; the day-count method; the sidereal frame. The case for a largely independent development was put by Indian historians of astronomy writing in the decades after independence, among them K. S. Shukla and other contributors to the history of Indian astronomy edited by S. N. Sen and Shukla (Sen and Shukla 1985). In broad terms their argument rests on these structural differences, together with Billard’s evidence for Indian observation: the characteristic methods of the siddhāntas have no counterpart in any surviving Greek text, so the planetary models should be regarded as built in India, and the borrowing as limited to a few elements, such as the zodiac of signs, the horoscope and some astrological vocabulary.

docs.title: 5.5.3 A balanced view
docs.text:
Most historians today take a middle position, well expressed by Plofker (2009). The Greek contribution was real and fundamental: the zodiac of signs and degrees, the geometrical model of the sphere, the idea of representing planetary motion by combinations of circles, the horoscope, and a body of technical vocabulary. Babylonian methods came both directly and through Greek intermediaries. But the classical siddhānta was not a translation. Indian astronomers created a new trigonometry based on the half-chord or sine (Chapter 6), a new form of computation based on integer periods and the day-count, new parameters derived from their own observations, and new models with variable epicycles and corrections applied in stages, procedures that some modern analysts interpret as approximating the effects Ptolemy obtained with the equant. Later they developed these further in directions without parallel in Greek astronomy, culminating in the Kerala school.

Table 5.2. Some structural features of Ptolemaic and Indian planetary astronomy: Ptolemy’s Almagest (c. 150 CE) and the Indian siddhāntas (from c. 500 CE). Feature Ptolemy, Almagest Indian siddhāntas Trigonometric function chord, radius 60 sine (jyā); radius \(3438'\) in Āryabhaṭa and the Sūryasiddhānta Frame of longitudes tropical (from the equinox) sidereal (from the beginning of Aśvinī) Mean motions tables of motion from an epoch integer revolutions in a great cycle; day-count (ahargaṇa) First inequality eccentric circle with equant manda epicycle of variable size Second (synodic) inequality epicycle śīghra epicycle of variable size Combination of inequalities single geometrical construction corrections applied in sequence Earth stationary sphere at the centre stationary sphere at the centre (Āryabhaṭa: rotating) Order of the spheres Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn the same

docs.title: 5.5.4 Astrology as the vehicle
docs.text: Why did Greek mathematical astronomy enter India? Pingree’s answer was that it came with astrology. A horoscope requires the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets at the moment of birth, and the ascendant, which depends on the rising times of the signs at the place of birth. Greek astrological manuals therefore included, or presupposed, methods for computing these things, and the Indian astrologers who adopted the horoscope needed them too. The last chapter of the Yavanajātaka, with its rules for planetary positions, illustrates the connection (Pingree 1978b, 1997). If this is right, the demand for horoscopes, not curiosity about the planets for their own sake, was the main force behind the creation of the siddhānta, and the close association of astronomy and astrology in the later tradition (Chapter 15) is a legacy of its origins.

docs.title: 5.5.5 From chord to Sine
docs.text: The most important mathematical change was the replacement of the Greek chord by the Indian half-chord. The Indian choice of radius, \(R = 3438'\) (the number of minutes in a radian), is itself a point of contact. The historian G. J. Toomer argued that Hipparchus’ lost table of chords, from the second century BCE, used the same radius, \(3438'\), and that the Indian Sine tables were derived from it by halving the chords of double arcs (Toomer 1973). Ptolemy, three centuries later, used a radius of 60 parts. If Toomer is right, the Indian Sine table is a transformed descendant of the oldest Greek trigonometry; the transformation, from chord to half-chord, was nevertheless an Indian step, and it made Indian trigonometry simpler and more powerful than its source. The Indian interval of \(3^\circ 45'\) corresponds to chords of arcs at intervals of \(7^\circ 30'\), the interval of Hipparchus’ table as Toomer reconstructed it.

docs.title: 5.5.6 Revisions after Varāhamihira
docs.text: The Romaka and Pauliśa systems did not survive as working systems, but they left traces. Varāhamihira mentions an astronomer Lāṭadeva in connection with them, and later tradition remembered Lāṭadeva as a pupil of Āryabhaṭa. Brahmagupta rejected the Romaka as standing outside the tradition of the smṛtis, since it did not use their yugas and Manu periods; his objection shows that it was still felt to be alien to the Indian scheme of time. The Saura, revised, survived as the Sūryasiddhānta, and its claim to divine revelation, to the asura Maya at the end of the Kṛta age, gave it an authority that no human author’s text could have (Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 5.5.7 Heliocentric origins?
docs.text: The Dutch mathematician B. L. van der Waerden proposed that the Indian planetary models, and especially Āryabhaṭa’s, derived ultimately from a heliocentric Greek system (Waerden 1987). His argument rested on the heliocentric ratios that can be read in the Indian parameters, which, as Section 7.3.3 shows, any accurate geocentric model must contain; the hypothesis has not been accepted by most historians (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 5.6 Other Directions of Exchange
docs.text: Contact did not run in one direction only. Indian astronomy and astrology were known in Sasanian Iran. Under the Sasanian kings, especially in the sixth century, Greek and Indian works on astrology and astronomy were translated into Middle Persian, and the Sasanian royal astronomical tables (the Zīk-i Shahriyārān, known in Arabic as the Zīj al-Shāh) appear to have used Indian parameters and methods alongside Greek ones. Through these Persian intermediaries, as well as directly, Indian elements entered the astronomy and astrology that the Abbasid caliphs inherited (Pingree 1963). Indian astrological material is also found in the Arabic astrological literature of the eighth and ninth centuries, which in turn shaped medieval European astrology. In the eighth century Indian siddhānta astronomy reached Baghdad directly, and Indian astronomy and calendars also travelled to Tang China and across Southeast Asia; these later transmissions are followed in Chapter 16.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Pingree (1978b) and Neugebauer and Pingree (1970–1971) are the essential editions; Pingree (1976) and Pingree (1978a) state Pingree’s thesis; Mak (2013) re-examines the Yavanajātaka; Plofker (2009) gives a balanced assessment; Billard (1971) is the main statistical study of the parameters.

docs.title: Chapter 6: The Siddhānta: Cycles, Mean Motions, Sines and the Sphere
6.1 What a Siddhānta Contains
docs.text:
A siddhānta (“established conclusion”) is a complete treatise of mathematical astronomy. Although the classical siddhāntas differ in their parameters and details, they share a common plan, which is already clear in the Āryabhaṭīya (499 CE) and is fully developed in Brahmagupta’s Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta (628) and in the Sūryasiddhānta. The fourteen chapters of the Sūryasiddhānta, as translated by Burgess, give a good picture of the whole (Burgess 1860):

  1. mean motions of the planets (madhyamādhikāra);

  2. true positions (spaṣṭādhikāra);

  3. direction, place and time (tripraśnādhikāra);

  4. eclipses of the Moon;

  5. eclipses of the Sun (parallax);

  6. the projection (drawing) of eclipses (parilekha);

  7. conjunctions of the planets;

  8. the asterisms and their conjunctions with planets;

  9. heliacal risings and settings;

  10. the elevation of the Moon’s horns (the appearance of the crescent);

  11. the dangerous aspects of the Sun and Moon (pāta);

  12. cosmography (bhūgola);

  13. the armillary sphere and other instruments;

  14. the kinds of time-measure (māna).

Brahmagupta’s work adds chapters on mathematics (arithmetic and algebra, chapters 12 and 18), a long critique of earlier astronomers (chapter 11), and chapters on instruments and on the sphere. The Āryabhaṭīya is far shorter: 121 verses in four parts, of which the first gives the parameters, the second is mathematical, the third deals with time and planetary motion, and the fourth with the sphere and eclipses (Āryabhaṭa 1976).

docs.title: 6.2 The Sūryasiddhānta
docs.text: The Sūryasiddhānta has been the most widely used siddhānta of the last thousand years. It presents itself as a revelation of the Sun to the asura Maya at the end of the Kṛta age, that is, as the ancient teaching of a god. Historically it is a text that was revised over several centuries. Varāhamihira’s “Saura” system (Chapter 5) is an early form of it; the version we have is considerably later. Its parameters, analysed by Billard, fit best around 1000 CE, and its text probably reached its present form between the eighth and eleventh centuries, with later corrections (Billard 1971; Pingree 1981). It was the basis of the “Saura” school of astronomy, dominant in northern India and widely used elsewhere. Burgess’s translation of 1860, made with the help of Indian pandits and with notes by W. D. Whitney, remains a standard reference (Burgess 1860).

docs.title: 6.3 Units of Time
docs.text:
The siddhāntas distinguish between “real” (mūrta) time, which can be measured, and “unreal” (amūrta) time, consisting of units too small to measure. The Sūryasiddhānta (1.11–13) begins real time with the prāṇa (“breath”). Since a sidereal day has 21,600 prāṇas, one prāṇa is the time in which the sky turns through one minute of arc; it lasts four seconds of sidereal time. From it are built:

6 prāṇas = 1 vināḍikā (also called pala) = 24 seconds 60 vināḍikās = 1 nāḍikā (ghaṭikā, daṇḍa) = 24 minutes 60 nāḍikās = 1 sidereal day

A muhūrta is two nāḍikās (48 minutes), and thirty muhūrtas make a day. The Purāṇas and other texts give elaborate lists of smaller units (truṭi, lava, nimeṣa, kāṣṭhā, kalā); these lists disagree with one another, and the smallest units are notional. They show an interest in the subdivision of time, not an ability to measure it.

The siddhāntas also distinguish several kinds of day, month and year according to what is being counted (Burgess 1860):

  • the civil day (sāvana), from sunrise to sunrise;

  • the sidereal day (nākṣatra), one rotation of the sky;

  • the lunar day or tithi (cāndra), one-thirtieth of a synodic month;

  • the solar day (saura), the time in which the Sun moves one degree; thirty of them make a solar month, the Sun’s passage through one sign.

The final chapter of the Sūryasiddhānta lists nine “measures” of time, from the human measures just described to the “divine” and “Brahmā” measures of the cosmic cycles.

docs.title: 6.4.1 The idea
docs.text:
The most distinctive feature of siddhānta astronomy is the way it expresses mean motions. Instead of giving the daily motion of each planet as a fraction, it states how many complete revolutions (bhagaṇas) each planet makes in a very long period, the mahāyuga of 4,320,000 years, and how many civil days that period contains. The mean daily motion of a planet is then simply

\[\text{mean daily motion} = \frac{\text{revolutions in the cycle}}{\text{civil days in the cycle}} \times 360^\circ .\tag{6.1}\]

At the beginning of the cycle (and, depending on the system, at certain points within it) all the mean planets are assumed to be together at the beginning of Aśvinī. The cycles themselves, and their place in the cosmic chronology of the Purāṇas, are discussed in Chapter 14. Here what matters is their computational function: they make every mean motion an exact ratio of two integers.

docs.title: 6.4.2 The revolution numbers
docs.text:
Table 6.1 gives the revolution numbers of Āryabhaṭa and of the Sūryasiddhānta, and the sidereal periods that follow from those of the Sūryasiddhānta (dividing the 1,577,917,828 civil days of its mahāyuga by the number of revolutions). For Mercury and Venus the numbers given are those of their śīghra apex, whose period is the planet’s period around the Sun (Chapter 7); their own mean motion is that of the Sun.

Table 6.1. Revolutions in a mahāyuga of 4,320,000 years, with the sidereal periods derived from the Sūryasiddhānta values and modern mean values. Periods in days. The derived periods agree closely with modern mean values. Two cautions are needed. First, these are mean periods, which can be determined accurately from observations spread over long intervals; they say nothing about how well the models reproduce the actual, irregular motion of a planet. Second, the agreement for the sidereal year is less impressive than it looks: the siddhānta year of about 365.2588 days is some 3.5 minutes longer than the true sidereal year, and about 24 minutes longer than the tropical year. Because the Indian calendar is tied to this sidereal year, its seasons have slowly drifted (Chapter 13).

Other combinations follow from the same numbers. The synodic month of the Sūryasiddhānta is \(1{,}577{,}917{,}828 / (57{,}753{,}336 - 4{,}320{,}000) = 29.530588\) days, against a modern mean value of 29.530589 days; its draconic month (relative to the node) is 27.21225 days, against 27.21222 days.

Āryabhaṭa’s cycles and the conjunction at the Kali epoch

Āryabhaṭa divided his mahāyuga into four equal quarters of 1,080,000 years, unlike the Purāṇic ratio 4:3:2:1. All his revolution numbers for the Sun, Moon and planets are divisible by four. As a result, the mean Sun, Moon and planets return to conjunction at the beginning of every quarter, and in particular at the beginning of the present Kali age. The integer structure of his parameters was designed so that the computation could start from a simple configuration.

docs.text:
Dividing each revolution number by the number of civil days and multiplying by \(360^\circ\) gives the mean daily motion (madhyamagati) of each body. Table 6.2 gives these motions for the Sūryasiddhānta, computed from its parameters and written in sexagesimal form (degrees; minutes, seconds, thirds), as the texts and handbooks express them.

docs.title: 6.4.4 Counting days: the ahargaṇa
docs.text:
To find a planet’s mean position on a given date, the astronomer first computes the number of civil days elapsed since the epoch, the ahargaṇa (“heap of days”). In the siddhāntas the usual epoch is the beginning of the Kali age, which by the conventional reckoning fell at midnight or at sunrise (depending on the school) on 17/18 February 3102 BCE (Julian calendar), at the meridian of Ujjayinī. The ahargaṇa is computed from the elapsed solar years and months, converted into lunar months and civil days using the period relations of the system, with corrections for intercalary months and omitted tithis. The mean longitude is then

\[\bar{\lambda} = \lambda_0 + \frac{R \cdot A}{D} \times 360^\circ \pmod{360^\circ},\tag{6.2}\]

where \(A\) is the ahargaṇa, \(R\) the planet’s revolutions and \(D\) the civil days of the cycle, and \(\lambda_0\) any position at the epoch. Handbooks (karaṇas) simplified the work by starting from a recent epoch and giving the mean positions at that epoch, so that the numbers involved were small. Chapter 12 works through a complete day-count by these rules.

The computed time is that of the prime meridian. For any other place the astronomer applied a correction for the difference in longitude (deśāntara), found from the distance to the meridian and the size of the earth. The prime meridian of Indian astronomy passes through Laṅkā, a notional point on the equator (not the island of Sri Lanka), and through Ujjayinī; the Sūryasiddhānta names other places on it, such as Rohitaka and Kurukṣetra.

Example 6.1 (The correction for terrestrial longitude)

Suppose an almanac is computed for Ujjayinī and is to be used at a place about \(7^\circ\) east of the prime meridian (roughly the longitude of Vārāṇasī). Since the earth turns \(360^\circ\) in a day, \(7^\circ\) of longitude corresponds to \(7/360\) of a day, about 28 minutes, or 70 vināḍikās. Local midnight at the eastern place comes 28 minutes before midnight at Ujjayinī, and in that time the Moon moves about \(13.2^\circ \times 28/1440 \approx 0.26^\circ\), or \(15'\). The Moon’s computed position at local midnight must therefore be reduced by about \(15'\), and the Sun’s by about \(1'\). The siddhāntas obtained the difference in longitude from the distance in yojanas between the place and the prime meridian, measured along the parallel of latitude, or from the difference between the computed and observed times of a lunar eclipse, which is seen at the same moment everywhere.

The Kali epoch itself was not observed: the grand conjunction of the mean planets at that moment follows from the period relations, from which the date was computed backwards. How European scholars first argued over this point is told in Section 16.4.1.

docs.title: 6.4.5 Correcting the parameters
docs.text: Mean motions derived from integer revolutions cannot remain accurate for ever. From the seventh century onwards astronomers applied small corrections, called bīja (“seed”), to the revolution numbers of a standard text to bring its predictions into agreement with observation in their own time. The best-known bīja corrections are those applied to the Sūryasiddhānta and to the Āryabhaṭa system in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Different schools (pakṣas) are distinguished by their parameters: the Brāhma school following Brahmagupta, the Ārya school following Āryabhaṭa, the Ārdharātrika school following Āryabhaṭa’s lost midnight system, and the Saura school following the Sūryasiddhānta (Pingree 1978). Chapter 9 returns to them.

docs.title: 6.5.1 From chord to half-chord
docs.text:
Greek astronomers computed with the chord of an arc. Indian astronomers, from the earliest surviving siddhāntas onwards, used the half-chord, which is the sine of modern trigonometry multiplied by the radius of the circle. They called it ardhajyā (“half bowstring”), or simply jyā or jīvā. They also used the cosine (koṭijyā, the half-chord of the complementary arc) and the versed sine (utkramajyā, \(R - R\cos\theta\)). The adoption of the half-chord, which makes the relations in right-angled triangles direct, is one of the most important Indian contributions to mathematics. The Arabic jīb, a transliteration of jīvā, became Latin sinus and our “sine” (Chapter 16).

Indian texts usually work not with the sine of modern mathematics (a ratio) but with a length, the Sine of an arc in a circle of chosen radius \(R\):

\[\operatorname{Sin}\theta = R\sin\theta .\tag{6.3}\]

Āryabhaṭa and the Sūryasiddhānta take \(R = 3438'\). This is the number of minutes of arc in a radian: a circle of circumference \(21{,}600'\) (that is, \(360^\circ\)) has a radius of \(21{,}600/2\pi \approx 3437.75'\). With this choice an arc and its Sine are measured in the same unit, and for small arcs they are nearly equal.

docs.title: 6.5.2 The table of Sines
docs.text:
Both Āryabhaṭa and the Sūryasiddhānta give Sines for 24 arcs at intervals of \(225'\) (\(3^\circ 45'\)), from \(225'\) to \(5400'\) (\(90^\circ\)). Āryabhaṭa gives them as differences, in a single verse of his alphabetic notation; the Sūryasiddhānta gives the Sines themselves. The values agree with the modern values to within about one unit (Table 6.3).

docs.title: 6.5.3 How the table was made
docs.text:
Āryabhaṭa states a rule (Āryabhaṭīya, Gaṇitapāda 12) for generating the successive Sine differences: each difference is less than the preceding one by the preceding Sine divided by the first Sine (225). In modern notation, if \(\Delta_k\) is the \(k\)-th difference and \(S_k\) the \(k\)-th Sine,

\[\Delta_{k+1} = \Delta_k - \frac{S_k}{225}.\tag{6.4}\]

The rule expresses the fact that the second differences of the Sine are proportional to the Sine itself, with the opposite sign. The exact factor for this interval is \(2(1-\cos 3^\circ 45') \approx 1/233.5\) rather than \(1/225\), so the rule is an approximation, which Āryabhaṭa’s successors refined. The rule is often compared with the differential equation \(y” = -y\) satisfied by the sine; it is better understood as a finite-difference property of the table, which later Kerala astronomers analysed further (Plofker 2009).

Bhāskara I, in his Mahābhāskarīya (early seventh century), gave a remarkable rule for computing the Sine without a table. In modern terms, for an arc \(\theta\) in degrees,

\[\sin\theta \approx \frac{4\theta(180-\theta)}{40500 - \theta(180-\theta)} ,\tag{6.5}\]

which is never in error by more than about \(0.0016\) between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\). Brahmagupta’s rule for interpolating in the table with second differences is given in Section 6.11. The mathematical side of Indian trigonometry, including the infinite series of the Kerala school, is treated in Volume 11.

docs.title: 6.6 The Sphere: Direction, Place and Time
6.6.1 The celestial sphere
docs.text:
The siddhāntas place a spherical earth, at rest, at the centre of the universe, surrounded by the spheres of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and the fixed stars, in that order of distance. (Āryabhaṭa alone made the earth rotate; see Chapter 9.) The celestial sphere turns westward once a sidereal day about the poles; the Sun, Moon and planets move slowly eastward along the ecliptic. The angle between the ecliptic and the equator, the obliquity, is given as \(24^\circ\) by Āryabhaṭa, Brahmagupta and the Sūryasiddhānta; its true value around 500 CE was about \(23^\circ 38'\).

Figure 6.1. The celestial sphere of the siddhāntas, with the equator and the ecliptic inclined to it by the obliquity (taken as \(24^\circ\)).

docs.title: 6.6.2 Some fundamental rules
docs.text:
The chapter on “direction, place and time” solves problems of spherical astronomy by rules equivalent to the formulae of modern spherical trigonometry, though stated with Sines, proportions and right triangles. A few examples, written in modern notation with \(\phi\) the observer’s latitude, \(\epsilon\) the obliquity, \(\lambda\) the Sun’s longitude, \(\delta\) its declination and \(H\) its hour angle:

  • Declination of a point of the ecliptic:

    \[\sin\delta = \sin\epsilon\,\sin\lambda .\tag{6.6}\]

  • Ascensional difference (cara), the amount by which half the day differs from six hours (fifteen nāḍikās):

    \[\sin(\text{cara}) = \tan\phi\,\tan\delta .\tag{6.7}\]

  • Altitude \(a\) of the Sun:

    \[\sin a = \sin\phi\,\sin\delta + \cos\phi\,\cos\delta\,\cos H .\tag{6.8}\]

  • Rising times of the signs at the equator (laṅkodaya) and at the observer’s latitude (svadeśodaya), needed to find the ascendant and to convert between time and longitude.

Example 6.2 (Declination and length of day with the Sine table)

To find the Sun’s declination when its longitude is \(60^\circ\) (the end of Vṛṣabha), the astronomer multiplies the Sine of the longitude, 2978 (Table 6.3), by the Sine of the greatest declination, \(24^\circ\), which the Sūryasiddhānta gives as 1397, and divides by the radius:

\[\operatorname{Sin}\delta = \frac{2978 \times 1397}{3438} \approx 1210 .\]

In the table, 1210 lies between the Sines 1105 (arc \(1125'\)) and 1315 (arc \(1350'\)); interpolating linearly, the arc is about \(1125' + \frac{1210 - 1105}{210} \times 225' \approx 1238'\), or \(20^\circ 38'\). The modern formula \(\sin\delta = \sin 24^\circ \sin 60^\circ\) gives \(20^\circ 37'\).

At Ujjayinī (latitude about \(23^\circ 11'\)), the ascensional difference for this declination follows from \(\sin(\text{cara}) = \tan\phi\tan\delta \approx 0.428 \times 0.376 = 0.161\), so that the cara is about \(9^\circ 16'\) of the equator, or about 37 minutes of time. Half the day is then \(6^{\text{h}} + 37^{\text{m}}\), and the whole day about 13 hours 14 minutes, ignoring refraction and the size of the Sun’s disc.

docs.title: 6.6.3 The rising times of the signs
docs.text:
Because the ecliptic is inclined to the equator, equal arcs of the ecliptic take unequal times to rise above the horizon. At the equator (“at Laṅkā”) the rising time of a sign equals the difference of the right ascensions of its beginning and end. The Sūryasiddhānta gives these rising times in prāṇas (one prāṇa corresponds to one minute of arc of the equator, or four sidereal seconds): 1670 for Meṣa, 1795 for Vṛṣabha and 1935 for Mithuna, the same three numbers in reverse order for the next three signs, and so on symmetrically around the circle (Burgess 1860). The three numbers add up to 5400, a quarter of the 21,600 prāṇas of a sidereal day. Computing the same quantities today with an obliquity of \(24^\circ\) gives about 1669, 1794 and 1938 prāṇas, so the tabulated values are accurate to a few units.

At a place in latitude \(\phi\), the signs of the northern half of the ecliptic rise more slowly and those of the southern half more quickly. The texts obtain the local rising times (svadeśodaya) by subtracting from, or adding to, the equatorial rising times the corresponding parts of the ascensional difference (cara), computed for the latitude of the place. Tables of local rising times are the basis of the computation of the ascendant (lagna) used in horoscopes and of the conversion of time into ecliptic longitude.

Table 6.4. Rising times of the signs at the equator according to the Sūryasiddhānta, in prāṇas, compared with values computed today for an obliquity of \(24^\circ\) Signs Sūryasiddhānta Computed Meṣa, Kanyā, Tulā, Mīna 1670 1669 Vṛṣabha, Siṃha, Vṛścika, Kumbha 1795 1794 Mithuna, Karka, Dhanus, Makara 1935 1938

docs.title: 6.6.4 The gnomon and the latitude
docs.text:
The basic instrument of these chapters is the gnomon (śaṅku), conventionally 12 aṅgulas (“digits”) high, set up on level ground (Chapter 11). The length of its shadow at noon on an equinox, the palabhā or “equinoctial shadow”, gives the latitude:

\[\tan\phi = \frac{\text{equinoctial noon shadow}}{12}.\tag{6.9}\]

From the shadow at any hour, together with the Sun’s declination, the astronomer could find the time of day; conversely, from the time he could predict the shadow. The east–west line was found by the old method of the circle and the two shadow tips (Chapter 3). Texts give long series of such problems, and their solutions are among the most elaborate trigonometry of the siddhāntas (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 6.6.5 Shadow problems: the latitude triangles and a worked example
docs.text:
The chapter on the “three questions” (tripraśna: direction, place and time) is built on one figure. At noon on an equinox the Sun stands on the equator, so its distance from the zenith equals the latitude, and the gnomon, its shadow and the line from the tip of the gnomon to the tip of the shadow form a right triangle with the angle \(\phi\) at the top (Figure 6.2). The gnomon is 12 aṅgulas, the equinoctial shadow (palabhā or akṣabhā) is \(s_0\), and the hypotenuse, the “equinoctial hypotenuse” (palakarṇa or akṣakarṇa), is \(\sqrt{144 + s_0^2}\).

Figure 6.2. The equinoctial shadow at noon (meridian section, drawn to scale for a shadow of 5 aṅgulas). The Sun’s distance from the zenith equals the latitude \(\phi\), and the same angle appears at the tip of the gnomon, so \(\tan\phi = 5/12\) and the hypotenuse is 13.

The latitude triangles.

Many other right triangles in the sphere have the same angles as this one, and the astronomers exploited the similarity systematically. Writing \(R\) for the radius of the Sine table (3438) and naming the sides as the texts do, the following are proportional to gnomon, shadow and hypotenuse:

  • the Sine of the co-latitude (lambajyā), the Sine of the latitude (akṣajyā) and the radius \(R\), so that \(\textit{akṣajyā} = R\,s_0/\textit{palakarṇa}\);

  • the Sine of the Sun’s declination (krāntijyā), the “earth-sine” (kujyā, the ascensional difference measured as a line in the plane of the Sun’s diurnal circle) and the Sine of the amplitude (agrā), the angular distance of the rising point from the east point, so that \(\textit{kujyā} = \textit{krāntijyā}\times s_0/12\) and \(\textit{agrā} = \textit{krāntijyā}\times\textit{palakarṇa}/12\).

Bhāskara II collects such triangles under the name “latitude figures” (akṣakṣetra) and uses them as a kind of master key: whenever three of the quantities are known, a rule of three gives the fourth. The method is equivalent to plane trigonometry applied to well-chosen sections of the sphere, and it explains why so many rules of the tripraśna have the form of a single proportion (Plofker 2009; Burgess 1860).

A worked example.

Take a place where the equinoctial shadow is 5 aṅgulas, so that the equinoctial hypotenuse is exactly 13 (the latitude is \(22^\circ 37'\), close to that of Kolkata). Then

\[\textit{akṣajyā} = \frac{3438 \times 5}{13} \approx 1322, \qquad \textit{lambajyā} = \frac{3438 \times 12}{13} \approx 3174 .\]

Let the Sun’s tropical longitude be \(30^\circ\). Its krāntijyā is \(1397 \times \operatorname{Sin}30^\circ / 3438 = 698\tfrac{1}{2}\), a declination of \(11^\circ 43'\) north. The “day-radius” (dyujyā), the radius of the Sun’s diurnal circle, is \(\sqrt{3438^2 - 698.5^2} \approx 3366\). From the latitude triangles:

  • kujyā \(= 698.5 \times 5/12 \approx 291\), and the Sine of the ascensional difference, carajyā \(= 291 \times 3438/3366 \approx 297\). The arc is about \(298\) prāṇas (\(4^\circ 58'\)), or \(49\tfrac{2}{3}\) palas, so the half-day is 15 ghaṭikās \(49\tfrac{2}{3}\) palas and the whole day about 31 ghaṭikās 39 palas (12 hours 40 minutes);

  • agrā \(= 698.5 \times 13/12 \approx 757\), an amplitude of \(12^\circ 43'\): the Sun rises that far north of the east point, which the astronomer needs in order to check the east–west line or to orient a building on a given day;

  • at noon the Sun’s distance from the zenith is \(22^\circ 37' - 11^\circ 43' = 10^\circ 54'\), so the noon shadow is \(12\tan 10^\circ 54' \approx 2.3\) aṅgulas, pointing north.

The inverse problem: time from a shadow.

The most frequent practical question ran the other way: the shadow has been measured; what time is it? Suppose that on the same day, in the morning, the shadow is found to be exactly as long as the gnomon, 12 aṅgulas. Then the hypotenuse of the shadow (chāyākarṇa) is \(\sqrt{144 + 144} \approx 16.97\), and the Sine of the Sun’s altitude (also called śaṅku, the “great gnomon”) is \(12 \times 3438/16.97 \approx 2431\), an altitude of \(45^\circ\). The texts then enlarge this Sine in the ratio \(R\) : lambajyā and again in the ratio \(R\) : dyujyā, which gives \(2431 \times \frac{3438}{3174} \times \frac{3438}{3366} \approx 2689\tfrac{1}{2}\); from this they take away the carajyā, 297, leaving about \(2392\tfrac{1}{2}\), the Sine of about \(44^\circ 06'\). This is the arc of the diurnal circle that the Sun has climbed above the six-o’clock circle; adding the ascensional difference, \(4^\circ 58'\), gives \(49^\circ 04'\) since sunrise, that is about 8 ghaṭikās 11 palas, or 3 hours 16 minutes. In modern notation the procedure is the solution of equation (6.8) for the hour angle \(H\):

\[\cos H = \frac{\sin a}{\cos\phi\,\cos\delta} - \tan\phi\,\tan\delta ,\]

where the first term is the enlarged Sine and the second is the Sine of the ascensional difference, both divided by \(R\). The modern formula gives the same result: \(H = 45^\circ 54'\) from noon, and the time since sunrise \(94^\circ 58' - 45^\circ 54' = 49^\circ 04'\).

Two points emerge from the example. The gnomon was a clock as well as a direction-finder, and the long shadow chapters of the siddhāntas are, in effect, the theory of a sundial that could be set up anywhere with a stick and a level floor. And every step depends on the equinoctial shadow, the one local constant that a practitioner had to measure, or read from a list of towns, before the rules could be applied; this is why texts and almanacs record the palabhā of the places for which they compute.

docs.title: 6.7 The Shape and Size of the Earth
docs.text:
From Āryabhaṭa onwards the siddhāntas teach that the earth is a sphere, suspended in space without support. Āryabhaṭa states that it is round on all sides, covered with living beings, like the bulb of a kadamba flower with its blossoms. The Sūryasiddhānta (12.32) says that the earth stands in the middle of the cosmic egg, in the sky, holding itself by the supporting power of Brahman. This is a statement, in religious terms, about why the earth does not fall. Brahmagupta and, later, Bhāskara II explained the falling of heavy objects to the earth by an attracting power or nature of the earth (Section 9.6).

The siddhāntas give the size of the earth in yojanas. Āryabhaṭa gives a diameter of 1050 yojanas, and the Sūryasiddhānta a diameter of 1600 yojanas, from which it computes the circumference as \(1600\sqrt{10} \approx 5059\) yojanas. The length of the yojana varied from text to text and is not known precisely, so modern conversions of these figures into kilometres (and claims that they match the modern value) depend on the length assumed. What can be said is that the siddhāntas had a spherical earth of a definite size, used in computing parallax and the correction for terrestrial longitude.

docs.title: 6.8 The Sizes of the Sun and Moon
docs.text: For eclipses and parallax the siddhāntas need the sizes and distances of the Sun and Moon. Āryabhaṭa gives the diameters of the earth, Sun and Moon as 1050, 4410 and 315 yojanas; the Sūryasiddhānta gives 1600, 6500 and 480 yojanas (Āryabhaṭa 1976; Burgess 1860). Both thus make the Sun about four times the size of the earth and the Moon about three-tenths of it. The modern ratios are very different: the Sun’s diameter is about 109 times the earth’s, the Moon’s about 0.27 times. The Moon’s distance, found from its parallax, was estimated reasonably well, in the region of sixty earth-radii (the modern mean distance is about 60.3 earth-radii); the Sun’s distance, whose parallax is far too small to be measured with the naked eye, was greatly underestimated, as it was by Greek and Islamic astronomers. In the siddhāntas the Sun’s distance follows from the principle of equal linear velocities (Chapter 7), not from measurement. The apparent diameters of the Sun and Moon, about half a degree each, were well known, and they are what matter for eclipse computation.

docs.title: 6.9 Precession
docs.text:
The precession of the equinoxes, the slow westward motion of the equinoxes among the stars, is not discussed by Āryabhaṭa or Brahmagupta. The Sūryasiddhānta (3.9–12) describes a “libration” of the starry sphere: the equinoctial point moves back and forth through \(27^\circ\) on either side of the beginning of Aśvinī, completing 600 such oscillations in a mahāyuga. An oscillation therefore takes 7200 years and covers \(108^\circ\), a mean rate of \(54”\) a year. Theories of oscillating precession (“trepidation”) were also held by some Islamic and medieval European astronomers; the true precession is a steady motion of about \(50.3”\) a year, completing a circuit in about 25,800 years.

According to Bhāskara II, Muñjāla (932) gave 199,669 revolutions of the solstices in a kalpa of 4,320 million years, a steady rate of about \(59.9”\) a year. Bhāskara II reports this value alongside the oscillation of the Sūryasiddhānta (Bhāskara II 1861). In practice, Indian almanac-makers have dealt with precession by the ayanāṃśa, the correction between the sidereal and tropical longitudes (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 6.10 Corrections to Time
docs.text: The siddhāntas know that the interval between successive sunrises is not constant. They correct the computed time for two effects. The first, bhujāntara, arises from the Sun’s unequal motion along the ecliptic (its equation of centre). The second, udayāntara, arises from the inclination of the ecliptic to the equator, which makes equal arcs of longitude rise in unequal times; it was introduced into the computation of mean positions by Bhāskara II. Together they correspond to what is now called the equation of time (Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 6.11 The Astronomer’s Computational Tools
docs.text: Indian mathematics grew up largely inside astronomy: the Āryabhaṭīya devotes one of its four parts to mathematics, Brahmagupta’s Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta has two mathematical chapters, and Bhāskara II’s Līlāvatī and Bījagaṇita were treated as parts of his Siddhāntaśiromaṇi. That mathematics, which went far beyond astronomical needs, is the subject of Volume 11. This section describes only the tools that the astronomer used every day, with small worked examples, so that the procedures described in this and the following chapters can be followed in detail (Plofker 2009; Datta and Singh 1962). Besides the Sine, the most constant of them was the right triangle, whose sides are the bhujā (“arm”), the koṭi (“upright”) and the karṇa (“ear”, the hypotenuse); most problems of spherical astronomy were solved not with spherical triangles but by finding plane right triangles inside the sphere and applying proportions between their sides, as the commentaries explain.

docs.title: 6.11.1 Sexagesimal arithmetic and units
docs.text:
Positions on the ecliptic were expressed in signs (rāśis) of \(30^\circ\), degrees (aṃśas or bhāgas), minutes (kalās or liptās) and seconds (vikalās); time in days, nāḍikās and vināḍikās. Whole numbers were written decimally, while fractions were usually sexagesimal, so that a longitude might be written as 4 signs \(13^\circ 25' 40”\), that is, \(133^\circ 25' 40”\).

Example 6.3 (Sexagesimal multiplication)

The Sun’s mean daily motion in the Sūryasiddhānta is about \(0;59,8\) degrees, that is, \(59'\,8”\) (Table 6.2). In 30 days the mean Sun moves \(30 \times 8” = 240” = 4'\) and \(30 \times 59' = 1770'\), together \(1774' = 29^\circ 34'\): about half a degree less than a full sign, which is why the solar months average a little more than thirty days.

Lengths were measured in aṅgulas (“finger-breadths”) and distances in yojanas. In the system of Bhāskara II’s Līlāvatī, 24 aṅgulas make a hasta (cubit), 4 hastas a daṇḍa, 2000 daṇḍas a krośa and 4 krośas a yojana; Āryabhaṭa defines his yojana as 8000 “man-heights”. Because the basic units were not standardised, the length of the yojana is uncertain, and modern estimates range roughly between eight and fifteen kilometres. For the gnomon this does not matter, since only the ratio of shadow to gnomon is used; for the size of the earth and the distances of the planets it means that the siddhānta figures cannot be converted into modern units with any confidence (Section 6.7).

docs.title: 6.11.2 The rule of three
docs.text:
The most frequently used operation is the “rule of three” (trairāśika), the computation of the fourth term of a proportion from the “argument” (pramāṇa), its “fruit” (phala) and the “requisition” (icchā). Thus: if in the 1,577,917,828 civil days of a mahāyuga (pramāṇa) the Moon makes 57,753,336 revolutions (phala), how many does it make in the 1,863,079 days (icchā) elapsed between the Kali epoch and 1 January 2000? The answer is

\[\frac{57{,}753{,}336 \times 1{,}863{,}079}{1{,}577{,}917{,}828} = 68{,}190.51383\ldots \text{ revolutions},\]

and its fractional part, multiplied by 360, gives the Moon’s mean longitude, about \(184.98^\circ\) (Appendix A). Almost every step of a siddhānta computation, from the mean motions to the conversion of time into arc and the corrections for terrestrial longitude, is a rule of three or a chain of them (the “rule of five” and longer rules); the texts also know an “inverse” rule of three for quantities that vary inversely.

docs.title: 6.11.3 Interpolation
docs.text:
A table gives values only at intervals. Between two tabulated Sines the simplest method is linear interpolation. Brahmagupta, in his Khaṇḍakhādyaka (665), gave a better rule that takes account of the change in the differences of the table. If \(f_0\) is the tabulated value at the beginning of the interval, \(\Delta_-\) the difference of the preceding interval, \(\Delta_+\) that of the current interval, and \(t\) the fraction of the interval to be added, then

\[f(t) \approx f_0 + t\,\frac{\Delta_- + \Delta_+}{2} + t^2\,\frac{\Delta_+ - \Delta_-}{2},\tag{6.11}\]

which is equivalent to what is now called second-order interpolation.

Example 6.4 (Interpolating the Sine of \(20^\circ\))

The arc of \(20^\circ\) is \(1200'\). In Table 6.3 the Sines of \(1125'\) and \(1350'\) are 1105 and 1315, so \(\Delta_+ = 210\); the preceding difference is \(\Delta_- = 1105 - 890 = 215\); and \(t = 75/225 = 1/3\). Linear interpolation gives \(1105 + 210/3 = 1175.0\). Brahmagupta’s rule gives \(1105 + \tfrac{1}{3} \times \tfrac{215 + 210}{2} + \tfrac{1}{9} \times \tfrac{210 - 215}{2} \approx 1105 + 70.83 - 0.28 = 1175.6\). The value computed today, \(3438 \sin 20^\circ\), is 1175.9.

docs.title: 6.11.4 Iteration
docs.text:
Many problems cannot be solved in one step, because the quantity sought appears on both sides of the equation. When the present tithi ends depends on the Moon’s speed, which depends on its position at the time sought; the middle of a solar eclipse depends on the parallax, which depends on the time. Indian astronomers handled such problems by iteration (asakṛt, “not once”): compute an approximate answer, recompute the quantities that depend on it, and repeat until the answer no longer changes.

Example 6.5 (The end of a tithi)

Suppose that at sunrise the Moon’s elongation from the Sun is \(293^\circ 49'\), so that the 25th tithi (which ends at \(300^\circ\)) has \(6^\circ 11'\) still to run, and that the Moon is gaining on the Sun at \(12^\circ 12'\) a day. A first estimate of the time remaining is \(6^\circ 11' / 12^\circ 12' \approx 0.507\) days. Suppose that recomputing the true positions for that moment gives an elongation of \(299^\circ 53'\) and a relative speed of \(12^\circ\) a day. The remaining \(7'\) take about \(0.010\) days, so the tithi ends about 0.517 days, or 12 hours 24 minutes, after sunrise; a further repetition changes the result only slightly. (The numbers are illustrative.)

Iterative procedures appear in the siddhāntas for the times of tithis and conjunctions, for the contacts of eclipses, for solar parallax and, in some schools, for combining the manda and śīghra corrections (Chapter 7).

docs.title: 6.11.5 The pulveriser
docs.text: The kuṭṭaka or “pulveriser”, first described by Āryabhaṭa, finds a whole number that leaves given remainders when divided by given numbers, by repeated division as in the Euclidean algorithm. In astronomy such problems arise when the positions of several bodies (or the fractional parts of their revolutions) are known and the number of days elapsed since the epoch is sought; Bhāskara I’s commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya contains many such exercises (Shukla 1976). With the large divisors of the period relations, the pulveriser worked by hand was a serious computation. The method and its worked examples are treated in Volume 11.

docs.title: 6.11.6 Approximation and precision
