docs.text: Indian astronomers were practical about precision. They used \(\sqrt{10}\) for \(\pi\) when it was convenient (the Sūryasiddhānta computes the earth’s circumference this way) and Āryabhaṭa’s \(3.1416\) when it was not; they replaced a Sine by its arc for small angles, and complicated corrections by simpler approximations in handbooks; they rounded parameters to make computation easier. Gaṇeśa Daivajña’s Grahalāghava dispensed with the Sine table altogether in favour of algebraic approximations (Section 12.3). The test was whether the result agreed with the sky well enough for the purpose in hand: a calendar, an eclipse, a horoscope. Where higher precision was needed, as for the Moon’s position in the almanac, more elaborate methods were developed, culminating in the series and tables of the Kerala school (Chapter 10).

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Burgess (1860) is still the most complete annotated translation of a siddhānta in English. Āryabhaṭa (1976) give the Āryabhaṭīya; Plofker (2009) explains the trigonometry and spherical astronomy; Montelle and Plofker (2018) describe the tables and their arithmetic; Pingree (1978) gives the parameters of the schools; Datta and Singh (1962) is the classic source-book of the mathematics.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Planetary Theory: Mean and True Motion
7.1 The Problem
docs.text:
The Sun, Moon and planets do not move uniformly along the ecliptic. The Sun takes longer to pass through some signs than others, so that the seasons are of unequal length. The Moon’s daily motion varies between about twelve and fifteen degrees. The five planets visible to the naked eye (Indian tārāgrahas, “star-planets”) behave more strangely still: from time to time each slows, stops, moves backwards (westward) for a while, stops again and resumes its forward motion. Mercury and Venus never move more than a limited distance from the Sun, appearing alternately as morning and evening stars.

The siddhāntas account for these irregularities by two corrections applied to the mean position computed from the great cycles (Chapter 6). The first, the manda (“slow”) correction, corresponds to what modern astronomy calls the equation of centre: the effect of the elliptical shape of an orbit. The second, the śīghra (“fast”) correction, applied only to the five planets, corresponds to the effect of viewing the planet from a moving earth. The siddhāntas describe both in geocentric terms, as the effects of epicycles, with the bodies arranged around the earth in the same order as in Ptolemy: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn, and beyond them the stars (Table 5.2).

docs.title: 7.2.1 The model
docs.text:
In the manda model a point, the mean planet, moves uniformly around a circle (the deferent, kakṣyā) centred on the earth. The true planet lies on a smaller circle, the manda epicycle, centred on the mean planet. As the mean planet moves forward, the true planet moves around the epicycle in the opposite direction at the same rate, so that the line from the centre of the epicycle to the planet always points in the same direction, towards the apogee (mandocca, “slow apex”). The effect is that the planet moves slowest when it is farthest from the earth, in the direction of the mandocca, and fastest at the opposite point. Āryabhaṭa notes that the same motion can be produced by an eccentric circle, and the equivalence of eccentric and epicycle was standard (Āryabhaṭa 1976).

Figure 7.1. The manda epicycle. The line from the mean planet to the true planet stays parallel to the direction of the apogee (mandocca); the angle \(\mu\) between the lines from the earth to the mean and true planets is the manda correction; \(\bar\lambda\) is the mean longitude. The epicycle is drawn much larger than in the texts.

docs.title: 7.2.2 Epicycle and eccentric
docs.text:
The same motion can be described in two ways. In the epicycle form, the planet moves on a small circle whose centre travels around the earth. In the eccentric form, the planet moves uniformly on a single circle of the same size as the deferent, whose centre is displaced from the earth towards the apogee by a distance equal to the radius of the epicycle. Elementary geometry shows that the two constructions put the planet at exactly the same place at every moment (Figure 7.2). Indian astronomers used both, choosing whichever was more convenient for the problem in hand, and the commentators explain the equivalence. The eccentric form makes clear that the manda correction represents an off-centre orbit; in modern terms the eccentricity of the orbit is about half the ratio of the epicycle radius to the deferent radius.

Figure 7.2. The equivalence of epicycle and eccentric. The planet on the epicycle (solid circles) is at the same place as a planet moving on the dashed eccentric circle, whose centre is displaced from the earth towards the apogee. Not to scale.

docs.title: 7.2.3 The rule
docs.text:
Let \(\bar\lambda\) be the mean longitude and \(\lambda_A\) the longitude of the mandocca. The manda anomaly (mandakendra) is \(\kappa = \bar\lambda - \lambda_A\). If the circumference of the epicycle is \(c\) degrees when that of the deferent is \(360^\circ\), the correction (mandaphala) is, in the form used by Āryabhaṭa and the Sūryasiddhānta,

\[\sin\mu = \frac{c}{360}\,\sin\kappa ,\tag{7.1}\]

and the corrected longitude is \(\bar\lambda - \mu\): the correction is subtractive when the anomaly lies between \(0^\circ\) and \(180^\circ\) (the mean planet has passed the apogee) and additive otherwise. In the texts the rule is stated with Sines: multiply the Sine of the anomaly by the epicycle and divide by 360, and take the arc of the result.

docs.title: 7.2.4 Variable epicycles
docs.text:
A peculiarity of the Indian models is that the epicycles change size. The Sūryasiddhānta gives two values for each epicycle, one at the ends of the odd quadrants of anomaly and one at the ends of the even quadrants, and the size at intermediate points is found by proportion to the Sine of the anomaly. Table 7.1 gives its values. The texts do not explain why the epicycles vary. Modern historians have related the variation, together with the stepwise application of the corrections described below, to the effect that Ptolemy obtained with the equant, a point about which the planet’s angular motion is uniform; this is a modern interpretation of the models, not a statement of their authors (Neugebauer 1975; Plofker 2009).

Table 7.1. Epicycle circumferences in the Sūryasiddhānta, in degrees (deferent \(= 360^\circ\)), at the ends of the even and odd quadrants (Burgess 1860). Body Manda (even / odd) Śīghra (even / odd) Sun \(14 \;/\; 13\tfrac{2}{3}\) — Moon \(32 \;/\; 31\tfrac{2}{3}\) — Mars \(75 \;/\; 72\) \(235 \;/\; 232\) Mercury \(30 \;/\; 28\) \(133 \;/\; 132\) Jupiter \(33 \;/\; 32\) \(70 \;/\; 72\) Venus \(12 \;/\; 11\) \(262 \;/\; 260\) Saturn \(49 \;/\; 48\) \(39 \;/\; 40\)

docs.title: 7.3.1 The model
docs.text:
The second correction accounts for the retrograde motion of the planets and the limited elongation of Mercury and Venus. Here too the planet is placed on an epicycle, the śīghra epicycle, whose radius is large. The point towards which the planet on this epicycle is directed is the śīghrocca (“fast apex”). The śīghra anomaly is the difference between the longitude of the śīghrocca and the (manda-corrected) longitude of the planet.

The role of the Sun in this model is different for the two groups of planets, and it is important to state it correctly.

  • For the superior planets (Mars, Jupiter, Saturn), the mean planet moves around the zodiac with the planet’s own sidereal period (about 687 days, 12 years and 29 years), and the śīghrocca is the mean Sun.

  • For the inferior planets (Mercury and Venus), the mean planet is the mean Sun: it moves around the zodiac in a year. The śīghrocca moves with the planet’s own period around the Sun (about 88 and 225 days). The revolution numbers given for Mercury and Venus in Table 6.1 are those of their śīghroccas.

In modern terms, the śīghra correction is the difference between the planet’s heliocentric and geocentric directions. For a superior planet the epicycle reproduces the earth’s annual motion around the Sun as seen from the planet; for an inferior planet the deferent carries the Sun around the earth and the epicycle carries the planet around the Sun.

docs.title: 7.3.2 The rule
docs.text:
If \(\sigma\) is the śīghra anomaly and \(r = c/360\) is the ratio of the śīghra epicycle to the deferent, the correction \(\psi\) is given by

\[\sin\psi = \frac{r\,\sin\sigma}{K}, \qquad K = \sqrt{(1 + r\cos\sigma)^2 + (r\sin\sigma)^2},\tag{7.2}\]

and the corrected longitude is \(\lambda + \psi\), the planet being displaced towards the śīghrocca. Here \(K\) is the “hypotenuse” (karṇa), the distance of the planet from the earth in units of the deferent radius. Equivalently, \(\tan\psi = r\sin\sigma / (1 + r\cos\sigma)\). Unlike the manda correction, which is small, the śīghra correction can amount to tens of degrees; the division by the hypotenuse is essential.

docs.title: 7.3.3 What the śīghra epicycles encode
docs.text:
The ratios of the śīghra epicycles to the deferent are very close to the ratios of the sizes of the planetary orbits in the heliocentric system: for a superior planet, the radius of the earth’s orbit divided by that of the planet; for an inferior planet, the radius of the planet’s orbit divided by that of the earth (Table 7.2).

Table 7.2. Śīghra epicycle ratios of the Sūryasiddhānta (even quadrant) compared with the corresponding modern ratios of mean orbital radii. Planet Epicycle / 360 Modern ratio Ratio meant Mercury 0.369 0.387 Mercury’s orbit / earth’s orbit Venus 0.728 0.723 Venus’s orbit / earth’s orbit Mars 0.653 0.656 earth’s orbit / Mars’s orbit Jupiter 0.194 0.192 earth’s orbit / Jupiter’s orbit Saturn 0.108 0.105 earth’s orbit / Saturn’s orbit

The ratios can be checked against a simple observable quantity. For an inferior planet, the greatest angular distance from the Sun (the maximum elongation) is reached when the line of sight is tangent to the śīghra epicycle, so that \(\sin(\text{maximum elongation}) = r\). For Venus this gives \(\arcsin 0.728 \approx 46.7^\circ\), and for Mercury \(\arcsin 0.369 \approx 21.7^\circ\). The observed greatest elongations of Venus are about \(45^\circ\) to \(47^\circ\), and those of Mercury, whose orbit is very eccentric, range from about \(18^\circ\) to \(28^\circ\). The śīghra epicycles were thus fixed, directly or indirectly, by observations of exactly this kind.

This agreement is sometimes presented as evidence that Indian astronomers secretly knew the heliocentric system. It is not. Any geocentric model that reproduces the observed retrograde arcs and maximum elongations correctly must contain these ratios, because the size of the retrograde loop and the maximum elongation of an inferior planet are fixed by them. Ptolemy’s epicycles encode the same ratios, as was noticed in the sixteenth century. The Indian epicycles show that the parameters were well fitted to observation; they do not show what Indian astronomers believed about the physical arrangement of the planets. Nīlakaṇṭha’s reinterpretation of the model is described in Section 10.6, and the modern claims built on these ratios in Section 16.6.

docs.title: 7.4 Combining the Corrections
docs.text:
For the Sun and Moon only the manda correction is needed. For the five planets both corrections must be applied, and since each affects the other, the order matters. The Sūryasiddhānta prescribes for the superior planets a sequence of half and full corrections: apply half the śīghra correction to the mean planet, then half the manda correction computed from the result; then compute the full manda correction from this and apply it to the original mean planet; finally compute and apply the full śīghra correction (Burgess 1860). Āryabhaṭa, Brahmagupta and later authors used related but different sequences, and some prescribed iterating a correction until the result no longer changed (Plofker 2009). These procedures are approximate ways of solving the combined geometrical problem, and their differences were a subject of discussion among the schools.

Example 7.1 (A simplified illustration)

The following numbers are not taken from any text; they illustrate a single application of each correction for Jupiter, using the even-quadrant epicycles of Table 7.1. Suppose the mean longitude of Jupiter is \(145^\circ 20'\), its mandocca is at \(171^\circ 18'\), and the mean Sun (the śīghrocca) is at \(78^\circ 45'\).

Manda anomaly:

\[\kappa = 145^\circ 20' - 171^\circ 18' = -25^\circ 58'.\]

With \(c = 33^\circ\), \(\sin\mu = (33/360)\sin(-25^\circ 58') = -0.0401\), so \(\mu \approx -2^\circ 18'\). The mean planet has not yet reached the apogee, so the true planet is ahead of it: the manda-corrected longitude is \(\bar\lambda - \mu \approx 147^\circ 38'\).

Śīghra anomaly: \(\sigma = 78^\circ 45' - 147^\circ 38' = -68^\circ 53'\). With \(r = 70/360 = 0.194\), \(\tan\psi = 0.194\sin\sigma/(1 + 0.194\cos\sigma) = -0.170\), so \(\psi \approx -9^\circ 37'\). The planet is displaced towards the Sun.

True longitude: about \(147^\circ 38' - 9^\circ 37' = 138^\circ 01'\), that is, about \(18^\circ\) in the sign Siṃha (Leo).

docs.title: 7.5 Retrograde Motion and Stations
docs.text: As the śīghra anomaly increases, the true planet moves forward ever more slowly, stops, and moves backwards (vakra, “crooked” motion) until, on the other side of the epicycle, it stops again and resumes direct motion (mārga). The Sūryasiddhānta (2.53–55) gives the values of the śīghra anomaly at which retrogradation begins: \(164^\circ\) for Mars, \(144^\circ\) for Mercury, \(130^\circ\) for Jupiter, \(163^\circ\) for Venus and \(115^\circ\) for Saturn; it ends at the same distance on the other side of \(180^\circ\) (Burgess 1860). Later astronomers computed the stationary points more exactly, using the instantaneous rate of change of the śīghra correction. This led Brahmagupta and, more explicitly, Muñjāla, Bhāskara II and the Kerala astronomers to rules for the “instantaneous” velocity (tātkālika gati) of a planet that involve, in effect, the derivative of the Sine (Plofker 2009). Such rules are sometimes described as “calculus before Newton”; they are better understood as sophisticated rules for the rate of change of particular trigonometric quantities, developed for astronomical purposes, without the general theory of the derivative.

docs.title: 7.6 Latitudes
docs.text: The planets and the Moon do not move exactly on the ecliptic. Their orbits are inclined to it, and they cross it at two points, the nodes (pāta). The siddhāntas compute a planet’s latitude (vikṣepa) from its distance from its ascending node and from the maximum latitude: for the Moon, \(4^\circ 30'\) in Āryabhaṭa and the Sūryasiddhānta (modern mean value about \(5^\circ 09'\)). For the planets the latitude depends on the planet’s distance from the earth, and the texts divide by the śīghra hypotenuse to account for this. The treatment of the latitudes of Mercury and Venus in the classical texts is, however, faulty, because the latitude is computed from the wrong one of the two motions; the error was corrected by Nīlakaṇṭha around 1500 (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 7.7 The Theory of the Moon
docs.text: The Moon is the most demanding body for a calendar-maker, because the tithi, the nakṣatra and the eclipses all depend on its exact position. The classical siddhāntas give the Moon only a manda correction, with a maximum of about five degrees. The real Moon is subject to further inequalities, the largest of which, the evection (first described by Ptolemy), reaches about \(1\tfrac{1}{4}^\circ\). Muñjāla in the tenth century and Bhāskara II in the twelfth added a second lunar correction that has been interpreted as corresponding to the evection, and the Kerala astronomers and the authors of later almanacs introduced further corrections (Pingree 1978; Plofker 2009). Without such corrections the computed time of a tithi or of an eclipse can be in error by an hour or more.

docs.title: 7.8 Heliacal Risings and Settings
docs.text: A planet close to the Sun is lost in its glare. Its first appearance in the morning or evening sky after a period of invisibility is its heliacal rising (udaya), and its last appearance before it disappears again its heliacal setting (asta). These events mattered for the calendar and for astrology (a planet that is “set” was considered weak, and certain rites were avoided while Venus or Jupiter was invisible), and the siddhāntas give rules for predicting them. The rules state, for each body, the minimum distance from the Sun, measured in degrees of time (kālāṃśas), at which it becomes visible. According to the Sūryasiddhānta these are \(12^\circ\) for the Moon, \(17^\circ\) for Mars, \(11^\circ\) for Jupiter and \(15^\circ\) for Saturn; for Venus \(10^\circ\) (or \(8^\circ\) when it is retrograde) and for Mercury \(14^\circ\) (or \(12^\circ\)) (Burgess 1860). Brighter bodies need a smaller distance. The real limits depend also on the observer’s latitude, the season and the clarity of the sky, and the values are conventional approximations. The visibility of the new crescent Moon, important for the calendar and for Islamic practice in India, was treated in a separate chapter of the siddhāntas on the “elevation of the horns” of the Moon.

docs.title: 7.9 Conjunctions and “Planetary War”
docs.text: The siddhāntas also compute the conjunctions of planets with one another and with the junction stars of the nakṣatras. When two of the five planets come very close, the texts speak of a “planetary war” (grahayuddha) and give rules, partly astronomical and partly astrological, for declaring a victor, usually the planet that is brighter or lies to the north. The computation of the moment of conjunction and of the apparent separation of the two planets required their true longitudes and latitudes, their daily motions and an estimate of their apparent diameters, and it is a good example of how astronomical computation served astrological interpretation (Burgess 1860; Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 7.10 Distances and Sizes
docs.text: The siddhāntas also assign sizes to the planetary orbits. A principle found in Āryabhaṭa and the Sūryasiddhānta is that all the heavenly bodies move with the same linear speed, so many yojanas a day, along their orbits; the slower a planet’s angular motion, the larger its orbit. From the size of the Moon’s orbit, estimated from its parallax, the sizes of all the others follow from their periods. The resulting distances (in yojanas) serve to compute parallaxes and apparent diameters, but the principle itself is arbitrary, and the distances it gives for the outer planets bear no relation to the true ones.

docs.title: 7.11 Mercury, the Hardest Planet
docs.text: Mercury posed the greatest difficulties to every pre-telescopic astronomy. It is never far from the Sun and is seen only briefly in the twilight, low on the horizon, so that observations of it are few and imprecise. Its orbit is the most eccentric of the planets, so that its maximum elongations vary widely, and its motion as seen from the earth is correspondingly irregular. Ptolemy needed a special, more complicated model for it. The Indian models treat Mercury in the same way as Venus, with the parameters of Table 7.1, and their predictions for it were the least reliable. In practice this mattered less than one might think: Mercury’s heliacal risings and settings and its conjunctions were of astrological rather than calendrical importance, and errors were hard to detect.

docs.title: 7.12 How Good Were the Models?
docs.text: The siddhānta models reproduce the main features of planetary motion well, and their mean motions were often excellent (Chapter 6). Their true positions were less accurate. For the Sun and for Jupiter the errors were usually small; for Mars, whose orbit is quite eccentric and whose apparent motion is the hardest to model with circles, and for Mercury, which is difficult to observe, they could be large. The errors also grew with time as the mean motions drifted, which is why the bīja corrections and new handbooks were needed. Roger Billard’s analysis of the parameters of many texts showed both that they were fitted to observation near the time of each text and that they deteriorated afterwards (Billard 1971). In this the Indian tradition resembles every other pre-telescopic astronomy: its models were instruments for computation, repeatedly adjusted against the sky.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Pingree (1978) gives a technical account of the models of all the schools; Plofker (2009) explains the computations; Burgess (1860) translates and comments on the rules of the Sūryasiddhānta; Neugebauer (1975) compares Greek and Indian models.

docs.title: Chapter 8: Eclipses: Myth, Geometry and Computation
8.1 Why Eclipses Mattered
docs.text: An eclipse (grahaṇa, “seizing”) was, for the Indian astronomer, both a religious event and a test. Dharmaśāstra texts treat the time of an eclipse as especially powerful: bathing in sacred water, giving gifts and reciting mantras then are highly meritorious, and many land grants recorded in copper-plate inscriptions say they were made on the occasion of an eclipse. Eating and cooking were restricted before and during an eclipse. The almanac therefore had to announce eclipses in advance, with their times. At the same time an eclipse was the most public check on an astronomical system. If a predicted eclipse failed to appear, or appeared at the wrong time, everyone could see it. Debates between schools frequently turned on eclipses, and the Kerala astronomer Parameśvara revised the parameters of his day after decades of comparing eclipse predictions with observation.

docs.title: 8.2.1 The myth
docs.text: The Ṛgveda (5.40) tells how the demon Svarbhānu pierced the Sun with darkness. In the later myth, told in the Mahābhārata and the Purāṇas, the demon Rāhu, disguised among the gods, drank some of the nectar of immortality produced by the churning of the ocean; the Sun and Moon exposed him, and Viṣṇu cut off his head with his discus. The immortal head, Rāhu, pursues the Sun and Moon and swallows them from time to time, but they emerge again through his severed throat. In some later forms of the story the headless body becomes Ketu. Rāhu became one of the nine “planets” (grahas) of Indian astrology.

docs.title: 8.2.2 The geometrical explanation
docs.text:
By the time of the classical siddhāntas the cause of eclipses was explained geometrically. Āryabhaṭa states it in a single line, the second half of a verse whose first half identifies the Moon with water, the Sun with fire and the earth’s shadow with darkness (Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 37):

Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 37 (second half)

chādayati śaśī sūryaṃ śaśinaṃ mahatī ca bhūcchāyā

“The Moon covers the Sun, and the great shadow of the earth covers the Moon.”

Varāhamihira devotes a chapter of the Bṛhatsaṃhitā to Rāhu and argues there that eclipses are caused by the Moon and the earth’s shadow, as the astronomers compute them, and not by a demon; he reconciles this with tradition by saying that Rāhu, by a boon, is present at eclipses to receive the offerings made then (Varāhamihira 1981–1982). Brahmagupta took a more conservative line and criticised astronomers who contradicted the scriptural account of Rāhu. Al-Bīrūnī, who read his work in the eleventh century, sharply criticised Brahmagupta for this, observing that he knew the true cause of eclipses perfectly well (al-Bīrūnī 1888). The episode shows an astronomer negotiating between technical knowledge and religious authority, a tension found at several points in the tradition (Minkowski 2002).

In the siddhāntas, Rāhu and Ketu were redefined as the two nodes of the Moon’s orbit, the points where it crosses the ecliptic, which move slowly backwards around the zodiac in about 18.6 years. Rāhu is the ascending node and Ketu the descending node, \(180^\circ\) away. The astronomers thus kept the mythological names and gave them a new, geometrical referent. (In older texts ketu also means a comet or meteor.)

docs.title: 8.3 When Eclipses Occur
docs.text:
A lunar eclipse can happen only at full moon, when the Moon is opposite the Sun, and a solar eclipse only at new moon. Since the Moon’s orbit is inclined to the ecliptic (by \(4^\circ 30'\) in the siddhāntas; about \(5^\circ 09'\) in reality), at most full and new moons the Moon passes above or below the earth’s shadow or the Sun. An eclipse occurs only when the syzygy (full or new moon) happens close enough to one of the nodes that the Moon’s latitude \(\beta\) is less than the sum of the relevant apparent radii:

\[\begin{align*} \text{lunar eclipse:}\quad |\beta| &< r_{\text{shadow}} + r_{\text{Moon}}, \\ \text{solar eclipse:}\quad |\beta_{\text{apparent}}| &< r_{\text{Sun}} + r_{\text{Moon}}, \end{align*}\]

where, for the solar eclipse, the Moon’s latitude must be corrected for parallax as seen from the observer’s place. In practice this means that the Moon must be within roughly one to one and a half degrees of the ecliptic, and the syzygy within some ten to eighteen degrees of a node. The siddhāntas first test whether this condition is met, and only then carry out the full computation.

Figure 8.1. Why eclipses need a node. The larger grey discs represent the earth’s shadow at the Moon’s distance, centred on the ecliptic opposite the Sun; the small discs are the Moon at full moon. Far from the node the Moon passes north or south of the shadow; near the node it enters it. The inclination of the Moon’s path is exaggerated.

Because the Sun passes each node once a year, there are two “eclipse seasons” each year, a little less than six months apart (the nodes move backwards, so the seasons come about nineteen days earlier each year). In every year there are at least two solar eclipses somewhere on the earth, and in some years as many as seven eclipses, solar and lunar, in all. Any given place, however, sees a total solar eclipse only rarely, on average once in several centuries, while lunar eclipses are frequently visible. The experience of eclipses on which Indian astronomers could draw was therefore mainly of lunar eclipses and of partial solar eclipses.

docs.title: 8.4 Computing a Lunar Eclipse
docs.text:
The procedure of the Sūryasiddhānta (chapter 4), which is typical, can be summarised as follows (Burgess 1860; Montelle 2011).

  1. Compute the true longitudes and daily motions of the Sun and Moon, and the longitude of the node, at the moment of full moon.

  2. Compute the apparent diameters of the Sun and Moon. The Sūryasiddhānta makes them proportional to the bodies’ true daily motions, so that a body appears larger when it moves faster (because it is nearer).

  3. Compute the diameter of the earth’s shadow at the Moon’s distance, from the diameters of the earth and Sun and their distances, by similar triangles.

  4. Compute the Moon’s latitude at the full moon from its distance from the node.

  5. From the latitude and the radii, compute the magnitude of the eclipse (the part of the Moon’s diameter covered, grāsa).

  6. Compute the half-duration (sthityardha): the time from first contact to mid-eclipse is the distance the Moon must travel relative to the shadow, divided by its relative speed \(v\):

    \[t_{1/2} = \frac{\sqrt{(r_{\text{shadow}} + r_{\text{Moon}})^2 - \beta^2}}{v}.\tag{8.3}\]

    The half-duration of totality uses \(r_{\text{shadow}} - r_{\text{Moon}}\) in the same way.

  7. Because the Moon’s latitude changes during the eclipse, repeat the computation of the times of first and last contact with the latitude at those times, until the results no longer change (an “iterative” or asakṛt procedure).

Figure 8.2. The geometry of a lunar eclipse (not to scale). The siddhāntas find the width of the earth’s shadow at the Moon’s distance (the short bar) from the sizes and distances of the Sun and earth by similar triangles.

Example 8.1 (An illustrative lunar eclipse)

The numbers in this example are rounded values chosen for illustration, of the right order of magnitude; they are not taken from a particular eclipse. Suppose that at the moment of full moon the angular radius of the earth’s shadow at the Moon’s distance is \(40'\), the Moon’s angular radius is \(16'\), the Moon’s latitude is \(20'\), and the Moon moves relative to the shadow at \(30'\) an hour.

The Moon’s centre must come within \(40' + 16' = 56'\) of the centre of the shadow for any part of it to be eclipsed. Since its least distance is \(20'\), it is eclipsed; the part of its diameter covered is \(56' - 20' = 36'\), more than the whole diameter of \(32'\), so the eclipse is total.

The half-duration from first contact to the middle of the eclipse is

\[\frac{\sqrt{56^2 - 20^2}}{30} = \frac{52.3'}{30'\text{ per hour}} \approx 1.74 \text{ hours} \approx 1 \text{ hour } 45 \text{ minutes},\]

and the half-duration of totality is

\[\frac{\sqrt{(40 - 16)^2 - 20^2}}{30} = \frac{13.3'}{30'\text{ per hour}} \approx 0.44 \text{ hours} \approx 27 \text{ minutes}.\]

The whole eclipse would last about three and a half hours, of which about 53 minutes would be total. A siddhānta astronomer would carry out the same steps with his own values, expressed in minutes of arc and nāḍikās, and would then refine the times of contact by iteration.

docs.title: 8.4.1 The vocabulary of an eclipse
docs.text: The siddhāntas and almanacs describe an eclipse with a fixed vocabulary. The first contact is sparśa (“touch”), the middle madhya, and the last contact mokṣa (“release”); the beginning and end of totality are called sammīlana (“closing”) and unmīlana (“opening”). The amount of the disc covered is the grāsa (“mouthful”), and a total eclipse is khagrāsa or sarvagrāsa. Almanacs still announce eclipses with the times of sparśa, madhya and mokṣa, the magnitude, and the direction of first contact, which determine the timing of the ritual observances described below.

docs.title: 8.5 Computing a Solar Eclipse
docs.text:
A solar eclipse is harder, because what matters is not the Moon’s position as seen from the centre of the earth but as seen from the observer on its surface. The Moon is close enough for this difference, the parallax, to amount to as much as a degree, twice the Moon’s apparent diameter. The siddhāntas divide the parallax into two components:

  • lambana, the component along the ecliptic, which changes the time of apparent conjunction;

  • nati, the component perpendicular to the ecliptic, which changes the Moon’s apparent latitude and hence whether, and how much, the Sun is eclipsed at that place.

Both are computed from the position of the point of the ecliptic that is highest above the horizon at that moment (the “nonagesimal”, vitribhalagna), which in turn depends on the observer’s latitude and the time. Since the parallax changes the time of conjunction, which changes the parallax, the computation must again be iterated. The Sūryasiddhānta devotes its fifth chapter to these computations, and later astronomers, from Brahmagupta to the Kerala school, refined them (Burgess 1860; Montelle 2011). Solar eclipses were the hardest phenomena to predict, and their predicted times and magnitudes were the least reliable.

docs.title: 8.6 Drawing the Eclipse
docs.text: The siddhāntas also teach how to draw a diagram of the coming eclipse (parilekha), showing the eclipsed disc, the shadow (or the Moon) and the directions from which the eclipse begins and ends. The direction depends on two angles of “deflection” (valana): one due to the observer’s latitude (akṣavalana) and one due to the inclination of the ecliptic to the equator (ayanavalana). Such diagrams appear in manuscripts and were drawn for patrons; they allowed the predicted eclipse to be compared with the real one, not only in time but in orientation.

docs.title: 8.7 Indian Eclipse Theory in Comparison
docs.text:
The Indian astronomers were not the first to predict eclipses, nor the only ones to explain them correctly. Babylonian astronomers were predicting possible lunar eclipses by the seventh century BCE, using numerical cycles, among them the 18-year cycle of 223 synodic months now called the Saros. Greek astronomers from the fifth century BCE knew that the Moon is eclipsed by the earth’s shadow, and Hipparchus and Ptolemy computed eclipses geometrically, with parallax (Montelle 2011; Neugebauer 1975). The Indian siddhāntas inherited the geometrical approach and developed it in their own way, with their own parameters, rules for apparent diameters, parallax algorithms and iterative methods.

Two cycles are often confused. The Saros of 223 synodic months (about 6585.3 days, or 18 years and 11 days) is an eclipse cycle: eclipses tend to recur after this interval. The Metonic cycle of 235 synodic months (almost exactly 19 years) is a calendar cycle that brings the phases of the Moon back to the same dates of the solar year; it is not an eclipse cycle. The siddhāntas do not use either cycle for prediction. They compute each eclipse from the positions of the Sun, Moon and node, which their integer period relations already contain.

docs.title: 8.8 Handbooks, Tables and Observation
docs.text:
Most eclipse predictions were made not from the full siddhānta rules but from handbooks (karaṇas) and tables. Brahmagupta’s Khaṇḍakhādyaka (665), Bhāskara II’s Karaṇakutūhala (1183) and Gaṇeśa Daivajña’s Grahalāghava (1520) were widely used; the last provides methods for screening possible eclipses quickly. In south India the vākya system gave the Moon’s position in memorised sentences (Chapter 10), and Tamil calendar-makers computed eclipses with counters and memorised tables, a method that a French astronomer saw demonstrated in the 1760s (Section 13.8).

Parameśvara of Kerala (c. 1360–1455) reports that he observed eclipses over a period of some five decades and found discrepancies between the times computed by the standard methods and those observed; his Dṛggaṇita of 1431 was designed to remove them (Sarma 1972). His pupil’s pupil Nīlakaṇṭha discussed eclipse observations in his Jyotirmīmāṃsā, insisting that the agreement of computation with observation is the test of an astronomical system (Chapter 10). This is the clearest evidence of a systematic link between observation and parameter revision in Indian astronomy.

How accurate the predictions were cannot yet be stated with precision, because few Indian eclipse predictions have been compared systematically with modern retrocalculation. Parameśvara’s own reports of discrepancies suggest that, as an estimate, errors of the order of tens of minutes in the times of lunar eclipses were not unusual when a text’s parameters had drifted, and solar eclipses, which depend on the difficult parallax computation, were harder still. That would be a respectable performance for naked-eye astronomy, of the same order as in other pre-modern traditions; claims of minute-level precision for ancient Indian eclipse predictions have no support in the evidence.

docs.title: 8.9 Eclipses in Religious and Social Life
docs.text:
The religious treatment of eclipses gave the astronomer’s prediction its public importance. The Dharmaśāstra texts and the later digests (nibandhas) treat an eclipse as a time of impurity and of great opportunity for merit. Before and during it, cooking and eating are avoided; at its end, people bathe, if possible in a river or sacred tank, and give gifts. Solar eclipses in particular drew crowds to sacred places: the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (10.82) tells of the Yādavas and others gathering at Kurukṣetra for a solar eclipse, and the eclipse pilgrimage to Kurukṣetra continues today. Kings and wealthy donors made grants on eclipse days, and the copper-plate charters that record them are among the main sources for the history of Indian kingdoms. Popular customs connected with eclipses, many of them concerning pregnant women, varied by region and community; they rest on belief, not on any physical effect of eclipses.

The same events had a place in other communities. Islamic practice prescribes a special prayer at an eclipse, and Muslim rulers in India employed astronomers who could announce them. Jain and Buddhist texts also discuss eclipses, the Jain cosmology explaining them by a dark planet passing in front of the Sun or Moon. Across these traditions the astronomer’s ability to say in advance when an eclipse would come, and how much of the Sun or Moon would be covered, was valued as a practical and religious service.

docs.title: 8.10 Eclipses and History
docs.text: Because inscriptions often record eclipses (as the occasion of a grant) together with the date in an Indian era, the month, the tithi and sometimes the weekday, eclipses are an important tool for verifying the dates of Indian historical documents. The tables of Sewell and Dikshit (1896) were designed partly for this purpose. Attempts to date much earlier texts (the Ṛgveda or the Mahābhārata) from the eclipses they mention have been less successful, because the references are mythic or literary and can be matched with many different eclipses.

docs.title: 8.10.1 Why grants record eclipses
docs.text: The Dharmaśāstra texts count gifts made at an eclipse, a saṅkrānti, an equinox or a solstice among the most meritorious, and kings and donors timed their grants of land and villages accordingly. Thousands of copper-plate charters and stone inscriptions therefore give, with the era and year, the month, the fortnight and the tithi, often the weekday and the nakṣatra, and the occasion: “on the occasion of an eclipse of the Sun”, “at the Uttarāyaṇa saṅkrānti”. For the historian these details are a gift in a second sense. A date in an era alone can be misread, because the epigraphist may not know whether the year is current or elapsed, in which month the year began, or whether the months are amānta or pūrṇimānta (Chapter 13); a date that also names a tithi, a weekday and an eclipse can be tested, because only a few days in a long span of years satisfy all the conditions together (Sircar 1965).

docs.title: 8.10.2 Verifying a date
docs.text:
The method was worked out by the epigraphists of the late nineteenth century, among them J. F. Fleet and Franz Kielhorn, who computed the details of hundreds of inscriptions; Sewell and Dīkṣit’s tables (Sewell and Dikshit 1896) and later L. D. Swamikannu Pillai’s Indian Ephemeris (1922) made the computation routine. The procedure is the reverse of making an almanac. One converts each candidate year into the Julian calendar, finds the day on which the stated tithi of the stated month was current, checks the weekday, then the nakṣatra, and finally whether an eclipse or saṅkrānti fell on that day. If all the details agree for one interpretation of the year, the date is regarded as verified, and the interpretation that fits (elapsed or current year, amānta or pūrṇimānta months) becomes evidence for the reckoning used in that region and period. Much of what is known about the regional usage of the eras in Table 13.4 was established in this way.

The test cuts both ways. A date whose details cannot be reconciled under any reasonable reading casts doubt on the document, and irregular dates are one of the criteria by which epigraphists have identified copper plates that were forged, or rewritten later, to support claims to land. Some of the eclipses named in grants cannot be found at all, or were not visible where the grant was made; whether such a date reflects the prediction of a local almanac, an error of the scribe or a later fabrication has to be decided case by case, and a mismatch is not by itself proof of forgery (Sircar 1965).

docs.title: 8.10.3 Eras and epochs in the inscriptions
docs.text: Inscriptions also show how the astronomers’ epochs entered public life. The best-known example is the Aihole inscription of the Cālukya king Pulakeśin II, composed by the poet Ravikīrti, which gives its date in two ways: 3735 years after the Bhārata war, and 556 years of the Śaka kings. Since Śaka 556 corresponds to 634/635 CE, the inscription places the war in 3102/3101 BCE, that is, at the beginning of the Kali age as the astronomers computed it (Chapter 6). The identification of the war with the Kali epoch was thus current in the Deccan within about a century and a half of Āryabhaṭa; it is evidence for the spread of the astronomers’ chronology, not for the date of the war. Later inscriptions sometimes give the Kali year beside the Śaka year, and Kerala authors occasionally dated their works by the number of days elapsed since the Kali epoch (the kalidina, Chapter 12), a direct transfer of the astronomer’s day-count into ordinary dating.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Montelle (2011) places Indian eclipse reckoning in the context of Babylonian and Greek methods. Burgess (1860) translates the eclipse chapters of the Sūryasiddhānta; Sarma (1972) describes Parameśvara’s work. Sircar (1965) explains how epigraphists use the astronomical details of inscriptions, and Sewell and Dikshit (1896) provide the tables for checking them.

docs.title: Chapter 9: Astronomers and Schools from Āryabhaṭa to Gaṇeśa Daivajña
9.1 Introduction
docs.text: This chapter follows the principal astronomers of the classical tradition outside Kerala, from Āryabhaṭa (499) to the handbook writers of the sixteenth century. Their mathematical work is treated more fully in Volume 11; here the emphasis is on their astronomy, their parameters, and the schools (pakṣas) that grew up around their texts. The Kerala school is the subject of Chapter 10, and the astronomers who engaged with Islamic astronomy appear in Chapter 11. Dates are those established from the texts’ own statements or from their epochs; for many authors only the century is known.

docs.title: 9.2.1 Life and work
docs.text:
Āryabhaṭa is the earliest Indian astronomer whose work survives complete and whose date is certain. He gives it himself (Āryabhaṭīya, Kālakriyāpāda 10):

Āryabhaṭīya, Kālakriyāpāda 10

ṣaṣṭyabdānāṃ ṣaṣṭir yadā vyatītās trayaś ca yugapādāḥ tryadhikā viṃśatir abdās tadeha mama janmano ’tītāḥ

“When sixty times sixty years and three quarter-yugas had passed, twenty-three years had then elapsed since my birth.”

Three thousand six hundred years of the Kali age were complete in 499 CE, so he was born in 476. He says that he set out his knowledge at Kusumapura, usually identified with Pāṭaliputra (Patna). The Āryabhaṭīya has 121 verses in four parts: the Gītikāpāda (13 verses), which gives the parameters in Āryabhaṭa’s alphabetic notation; the Gaṇitapāda (33), on mathematics; the Kālakriyāpāda (25), on time and planetary motion; and the Golapāda (50), on the sphere and eclipses (Āryabhaṭa 1976). A second work by Āryabhaṭa, using an epoch at midnight rather than sunrise, is lost but is known from Varāhamihira, Brahmagupta’s Khaṇḍakhādyaka and Bhāskara I; it became the basis of the Ārdharātrika (“midnight”) school.

docs.title: 9.2.2 The rotation of the earth
docs.text:
Āryabhaṭa is the only classical Indian astronomer who taught that the earth rotates on its axis. His parameters include 1,582,237,500 rotations of the earth in a yuga, and he illustrates the idea with an image (Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 9):

Āryabhaṭīya, Golapāda 9

anulomagatir nausthaḥ paśyaty acalaṃ vilomagaṃ yadvat acalāni bhāni tadvat samapaścimagāni laṅkāyām

“Just as a man in a boat moving forward sees stationary objects moving backward, so at Laṅkā the stationary stars are seen moving exactly westward.”

The next verse describes the daily rotation of the sky in the conventional way, as if driven by a cosmic wind, and later commentators debated whether Āryabhaṭa really meant the earth to move. The doctrine was rejected by most of his successors, including Varāhamihira and Brahmagupta, who raised physical objections (for example, that objects not attached to the earth would be left behind), and some later followers of Āryabhaṭa reinterpreted the verse (Plofker 2009). Āryabhaṭa’s rotating earth is a genuine and remarkable idea. The earth nevertheless stays at the centre of his universe, with the Sun and planets moving around it, so that his system is geocentric (Section 16.6).

docs.title: 9.2.3 Other contributions
docs.text:
The Sine table and its rule.

Āryabhaṭa gives the 24 Sine differences in a single verse and a rule for generating them (Chapter 6).

The circumference of the circle.

Gaṇitapāda 10 gives the ratio of circumference to diameter:

Āryabhaṭīya, Gaṇitapāda 10

caturadhikaṃ śatam aṣṭaguṇaṃ dvāṣaṣṭis tathā sahasrāṇām ayutadvayaviṣkambhasyāsanno vṛttapariṇāhaḥ

“One hundred plus four, multiplied by eight, and sixty-two thousand: this is the approximate circumference of a circle whose diameter is twenty thousand.”

That is, \(\pi \approx 62{,}832/20{,}000 = 3.1416\). Āryabhaṭa calls the value “approximate” (āsanna). The Kerala astronomer Nīlakaṇṭha, a thousand years later, explained the word by saying that the exact ratio cannot be expressed; this is Nīlakaṇṭha’s interpretation, and it should not be read back into Āryabhaṭa as a proof of irrationality.

The pulveriser.

The last verses of the Gaṇitapāda give the kuṭṭaka (“pulveriser”), a method for solving linear indeterminate equations in integers, used in astronomy to find, for example, the number of days elapsed from given remainders of planetary revolutions (Volume 11).

Parameters.

Āryabhaṭa’s sidereal year, 1,577,917,500 days divided by 4,320,000 years, is 365 days 6 hours 12 minutes 30 seconds; the modern sidereal year is 365 days 6 hours 9 minutes 10 seconds. His revolution numbers (Table 6.1) were fitted to observations of his own time (Billard 1971). He divided the mahāyuga into four equal quarters and made his kalpa 1008 yugas, departing from the Purāṇic scheme, for which Brahmagupta attacked him (Chapter 14).

docs.title: 9.2.4 Bhāskara I and the Āryabhaṭa school
docs.text: Bhāskara I (early seventh century) wrote the most important early commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya, completed in 629, and two works on astronomy in the Āryabhaṭa tradition, the Mahābhāskarīya and Laghubhāskarīya (Shukla 1976). His commentary explains Āryabhaṭa’s terse verses with many worked examples and is a rich source for the mathematics of the period. His rational approximation to the Sine has been given in Chapter 6. The Ārya school remained strong in south India, especially in Kerala, where the Āryabhaṭīya was studied and commented on until the eighteenth century.

docs.title: 9.3 Varāhamihira
docs.text: Varāhamihira, of the region of Ujjayinī, was active in the sixth century; a late tradition places his death in 587. His astronomical compendium, the Pañcasiddhāntikā (epoch 505), was described in Chapter 5. He is better known as the great systematiser of astrology and divination: the Bṛhajjātaka and Laghujātaka on nativities, the Yogayātrā on military expeditions, the Vivāhapaṭala on marriage, and the encyclopaedic Bṛhatsaṃhitā on omens and many related subjects (Chapter 15) (Varāhamihira 1981–1982). Varāhamihira’s works became the classical texts of Indian astrology, commented on by Bhaṭṭotpala in Kashmir in the tenth century. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā includes a nice combinatorial calculation: from sixteen perfume ingredients taken four at a time, 1820 different perfumes can be made.

docs.title: 9.4 Brahmagupta
docs.text:
Brahmagupta was born in 598. He tells us that he composed the Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta (“Corrected Treatise of Brahmā”) in 628, at the age of thirty, during the reign of King Vyāghramukha of the Cāpa dynasty, and he is associated with Bhillamāla (Bhinmal, in southern Rajasthan) (Sharma 1966; Plofker 2009). In 665 he wrote a handbook, the Khaṇḍakhādyaka, based on Āryabhaṭa’s midnight system rather than on his own.

The Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta, in twenty-four chapters, presents itself as a corrected version of an older Paitāmaha (“Brahmā”) siddhānta. Besides the full range of astronomical topics, it contains two chapters on mathematics, including the first systematic rules for computation with zero and with negative quantities, rules for quadratic and indeterminate equations, the composition rule (bhāvanā) for equations of the form \(Nx^2 + k = y^2\), and the formula for the area of a cyclic quadrilateral (Volume 11). Not every rule is correct by modern standards: Brahmagupta sets zero divided by zero equal to zero.

Brahmagupta was a sharp critic. A whole chapter (chapter 11) examines the errors of earlier systems, above all Āryabhaṭa’s, attacking his equal quarter-yugas, his rotating earth and several of his parameters. He defended the Purāṇic yuga scheme and, as noted in Chapter 8, made concessions to the scriptural account of Rāhu that al-Bīrūnī later criticised. Brahmagupta’s work was the foundation of the Brāhma school, dominant in north-western and western India and in Kashmir, and it was among the Indian sources of early Islamic astronomy (Chapter 16). The commentator Pṛthūdakasvāmin (864) wrote on both his main works.

docs.title: 9.4.1 The controversy with the Āryabhaṭa school
docs.text: Brahmagupta’s attacks on Āryabhaṭa set the terms of a long debate between the Brāhma and Ārya schools. His objections were of three kinds. Some concerned tradition: Āryabhaṭa’s equal quarter-yugas, his kalpa of 1008 yugas and his beginning of the Kali age contradicted the smṛtis. Some concerned physics: if the earth rotated, he argued, objects such as birds and clouds would be left behind. Some concerned accuracy: Brahmagupta claimed that Āryabhaṭa’s parameters gave wrong positions and wrong eclipses. The first kind of objection shows how the authority of scripture could be invoked in technical disputes; the third was the one that mattered for practice. Āryabhaṭa’s followers, notably Bhāskara I, defended him, and in the south the Ārya school prevailed. The disagreement was never simply settled; each school kept its parameters, corrected by bījas, for centuries (Pingree 1978; Plofker 2009).

docs.title: 9.5 From Lalla to Śrīpati
docs.text:
The centuries between Brahmagupta and Bhāskara II produced many siddhāntas and handbooks, most of which await full study (Pingree 1981, 1978).

  • Lalla (eighth century, the date disputed) wrote the Śiṣya­dhī­vṛddhida­tantra (“Treatise for increasing the understanding of students”), in the Ārya tradition, with a well-known chapter on “false knowledge” (mithyājñāna) refuting popular and Purāṇic beliefs about the earth and the heavens that conflict with the spherical astronomy of the siddhāntas.

  • Vaṭeśvara wrote the large Vaṭeśvarasiddhānta in 904, notable for its very detailed computational procedures.

  • Muñjāla wrote the short Laghumānasa (epoch 932). He is credited with an additional lunar correction and, according to Bhāskara II, with a steady rate of precession (Chapter 6).

  • Śrīpati wrote the Siddhāntaśekhara and a handbook, the Dhīkoṭidakaraṇa (1039), as well as astrological works. He worked in the Brāhma tradition.

  • Śatānanda of Puri wrote a much-used handbook, the Bhāsvatī (epoch 1099), with decimal rather than sexagesimal fractions.

docs.title: 9.6.1 Life and works
docs.text:
Bhāskara (called Bhāskara II or Bhāskarācārya to distinguish him from Bhāskara I) was born in 1114 and completed his Siddhāntaśiromaṇi (“Crest-jewel of Siddhāntas”) in 1150, at the age of thirty-six; both dates he gives himself. He came from a family of scholars associated with a place called Vijjaḍaviḍa, whose location is uncertain; his grandson Caṅgadeva was court astrologer to the Yādava king Siṅghaṇa and founded a college for the study of his grandfather’s works, recorded in an inscription of 1207 at Patna in Khandesh (Pingree 1978).

Bhāskara’s works became the standard textbooks of mathematics and astronomy in much of India:

  • Līlāvatī, on arithmetic and mensuration, and Bījagaṇita, on algebra, often treated as the first two parts of the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi;

  • Grahagaṇita, on the computation of the planets, and Golādhyāya, on the sphere, the two astronomical parts;

  • the Vāsanābhāṣya, his own commentary on these, with demonstrations;

  • the Karaṇakutūhala (1183), a handbook.

docs.title: 9.6.2 Astronomy
docs.text:
Bhāskara’s astronomy follows the Brāhma school, refined in many details (Bhāskara II 1861). He explains the procedures of planetary and spherical astronomy with demonstrations; discusses the instantaneous motion (tātkālika gati) of a planet, using in effect the rate of change of the Sine, and the condition that the equation of centre is greatest where its rate of change vanishes; adds the udayāntara correction to time (Chapter 6); reports Muñjāla’s steady precession alongside the oscillation of the Sūryasiddhānta; and describes instruments, including his own simple “board” instrument (phalakayantra). In the Golādhyāya he says that the earth has a power of attraction by which heavy objects in the air are drawn to it and appear to fall, and he uses the sphere’s lack of support to refute Purāṇic views that the earth rests on something. He also criticised the Purāṇic cosmology of a flat earth with Mount Meru at its centre, while reinterpreting parts of it to fit the sphere (Minkowski 2004).

The Golādhyāya is also a work of literature. It opens its account of the sphere with a defence of the study of astronomy, includes a poetic description of the seasons, and ends with a set of problems (praśnas) for the student, many of them requiring real ingenuity in spherical trigonometry. Bhāskara’s style, clear and elegant, explains much of the lasting popularity of his works, which were taught across India until the nineteenth century and translated into Persian at the Mughal court.

Bhāskara’s “attraction” is a qualitative explanation of why heavy things fall towards the earth. It states no relation between attraction and mass or distance and is not applied to the planets, whose motions in his system are still those of the epicycles; the modern claim that it amounts to a theory of gravitation is discussed in Section 16.6. His rules for instantaneous motion belong with the computation of planetary stations (Section 7.5).

docs.title: 9.6.3 The legend of Līlāvatī
docs.text: A well-known story makes Līlāvatī, whose name is the title of Bhāskara’s arithmetic, his daughter. Her horoscope, the story goes, showed that she would be widowed if she did not marry at a precise moment; her father set up a water clock to measure it, but a pearl from her ornaments fell into the bowl and blocked the hole, the moment passed unnoticed, and she was widowed soon after. To console her Bhāskara named his book after her. The story is told in the preface to Fayḍī’s Persian translation of 1587 (Section 11.3) and became popular in modern retellings. It has no support in Bhāskara’s own works, in which “Līlāvatī” is the name of the book and, in its examples, an addressee (“O beautiful one”), and it should be treated as legend. It is nevertheless revealing: it combines the water clock, the horoscope and the dangers of a woman’s “ill-starred” marriage, the very themes discussed in this volume.

docs.title: 9.7 After Bhāskara
docs.text:
After the twelfth century the most influential astronomical works in northern and western India were handbooks and tables rather than full siddhāntas: the tables of Mahādeva (early fourteenth century) and the Makaranda (Vārāṇasī, 1478), the Grahakautuka (1496) of Keśava of Nandigrāma and the Grahalāghava (1520) of his son Gaṇeśa Daivajña. How these worked, and who used them, is the subject of Chapter 12. Rāma Daivajña’s Muhūrtacintāmaṇi (1600), on electing auspicious times, became the most influential astrological handbook of its kind (Chapter 15).

Full siddhāntas continued to be written. The best documented of the early sixteenth century is the Siddhāntasundara of Jñānarāja, completed in 1503. Jñānarāja belonged to a family of astronomers at Pārthapura on the Godāvarī, in Maharashtra, and his son Sūryadāsa wrote commentaries on Bhāskara II’s Līlāvatī and Bījagaṇita. The Siddhāntasundara is written in ornate verse, and it is notable for the length at which it treats cosmology: Jñānarāja set out to reconcile the Purāṇic account of the earth, with Mount Meru at its centre, with the spherical earth of the siddhāntas, a problem that occupied astronomers for the next two centuries (Section 14.5). The work has been translated in part, with a detailed study, by Knudsen (2014).

docs.title: 9.8 Jain and Buddhist Astronomers
docs.text:
Jain scholars contributed to astronomy both within their own cosmological tradition and in the common siddhānta tradition. The canonical astronomical texts and Malayagiri’s twelfth-century commentaries on them have been described in Section 3.6. Jain monks and laymen wrote in the siddhānta tradition: the mathematician Mahāvīra (ninth century), whose Gaṇitasārasaṅgraha served astronomers among others; Mahendra Sūri, author of the first Sanskrit treatise on the astrolabe (1370), and his pupil Malayendu Sūri; and a number of authors of handbooks and astrological works in western India. Jain libraries in Gujarat and Rajasthan are among the richest repositories of astronomical manuscripts (Pingree 1981).

Buddhist authors are rarer in the siddhānta tradition, for the monastic rules discouraged monks from making a living by astrology (Chapter 15), and the early Buddhist sources are calendrical rather than mathematical (Section 3.7). The great exception is the Kālacakratantra (“Wheel of Time”), composed in the early eleventh century, whose first chapter, with its commentary the Vimalaprabhā, contains a complete calendrical astronomy; the tantra as a whole is described in Volume 4, Buddha–Jina Prabhā. Its methods are those of a handbook (Chapter 12): mean motions counted from a recent epoch with small integer ratios, short tables for the equations of the Sun and Moon, the five elements of the almanac, the true planets and eclipses, together with the sixty-year cycle. The tantra was taken to Tibet, where the first sixty-year cycle of the Tibetan calendar is counted from 1027, and Tibetan almanacs are still computed by rules derived from it (Henning 2007). The Kālacakra thus preserves, in a Buddhist setting and outside India, a form of Indian handbook astronomy that has been in continuous use for nearly a thousand years.

docs.title: 9.9 The Commentators
docs.text:
Much of the history of Indian astronomy after the major authors is a history of commentary. Commentators explained the root texts, supplied worked examples and demonstrations, compared them with other systems, and sometimes corrected them. Some of the most important are listed in Table 9.1.

Table 9.1. Some important commentaries on astronomical texts Root text Commentator Date and remarks Āryabhaṭīya Bhāskara I 629; the fundamental early commentary Āryabhaṭīya Sūryadeva Yajvan born 1191; south Indian Āryabhaṭīya Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī c. 1500; extensive, with new theory (Chapter 10) Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta Pṛthūdakasvāmin 864 Khaṇḍakhādyaka Pṛthūdakasvāmin; Bhaṭṭotpala 9th–10th c. Varāhamihira’s works Bhaṭṭotpala 10th c., Kashmir; the standard commentaries on the astrological works Sūryasiddhānta Raṅganātha 1603, Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka Siddhāntaśiromaṇi Bhāskara II himself Vāsanābhāṣya, with demonstrations Siddhāntaśiromaṇi Nṛsiṃha Daivajña 1621, Vāsanāvārttika Tantrasaṅgraha Śaṅkara Vāriyar 16th c., Yuktidīpikā and Laghuvivṛti

docs.title: 9.10 Astronomers and Their Patrons
docs.text: The texts let us glimpse the social world of the astronomers. Authors name their fathers, teachers and places, and sometimes their kings: Brahmagupta the Cāpa king Vyāghramukha, Bhāskara II’s descendants the Yādava court of Devagiri, Mahendra Sūri the Delhi sultan, Nityānanda the Mughal emperor. Inscriptions record land granted to astrologers and the endowment of a school for the study of Bhāskara’s works. A family of astronomers could serve the same court for generations, and some families, like that of Gaṇeśa Daivajña or the astronomers of Vārāṇasī in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, produced a whole series of authors over several generations (Pingree 1981; Minkowski 2004). The astronomer’s main source of income, then as now, was usually not research but the almanac, the casting of horoscopes and the choice of auspicious times; the most famous mathematical astronomers also wrote on astrology.

docs.title: 9.11 The Schools
docs.text:
By the end of the first millennium Indian mathematical astronomy had settled into a small number of schools, each defined by its basic parameters and associated with particular regions (Pingree 1978, 1981).

Table 9.2. The principal schools (pakṣas) of Indian mathematical astronomy School Basis Main region Brāhma Brahmagupta’s Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta (628); later Bhāskara II north-west and west; Kashmir; Rajasthan and Gujarat Ārya Āryabhaṭa’s Āryabhaṭīya (499), sunrise epoch south India, especially Kerala Ārdharātrika Āryabhaṭa’s lost midnight system; Brahmagupta’s Khaṇḍakhādyaka (665) north India in the earlier period Saura the Sūryasiddhānta north and east India; widely used later Gaṇeśa Gaṇeśa Daivajña’s Grahalāghava (1520) Maharashtra, Gujarat and beyond

The schools were not sects: astronomers read each other’s works, criticised and borrowed from them, and the boundaries shifted. But the differences in parameters were real and could produce different dates for festivals and different predictions of eclipses, which made the choice of school a matter of practical consequence.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: For the individual astronomers see Pingree (1970–1994) and Pingree (1981); Plofker (2009) discusses their mathematics and astronomy; Āryabhaṭa (1976), Shukla (1976), Sharma (1966) and Bhāskara II (1861) are editions and translations of their works.

docs.title: 10.1 Astronomy on the Malabar Coast
docs.text: From the late fourteenth to the seventeenth century, a succession of astronomers working in a small area of central Kerala, between the Bhāratappuḻa (Nila) river and the region of Thrissur, produced some of the most original work in the history of Indian astronomy and mathematics. They are usually called the “Kerala school”. Most were Nampūtiri Brahmins or members of temple-service communities (Vāriyar, Piṣāraṭi), attached to temples and to the households (illams) of their families. They wrote in Sanskrit, and some of their most important explanations in Malayalam. Their work was known in Kerala until the nineteenth century but hardly outside it, and it reached modern scholarship only in 1834 (Whish 1834). The standard history is that of Sarma (1972); much of the source material has since been edited and translated.

docs.title: 10.2 Earlier Kerala Astronomy: Parahita and Vākya
docs.text:
Kerala astronomy belonged to the Ārya school. By tradition, the Parahita system of Haridatta was promulgated in 683 CE at the great festival at Tirunāvāya. It corrected the parameters of Āryabhaṭa by a correction proportional to the elapsed years of the Śaka era, and it used the kaṭapayādi notation (Chapter 1) to state its numbers.

The vākya (“sentence”) system, used in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, went further in making computation easy. For the Moon, the best-known set of vākyas (traditionally ascribed to Vararuci) consists of 248 short phrases, each encoding in kaṭapayādi the Moon’s true longitude on successive days of a cycle of 248 days. The cycle works because 248 days are almost exactly nine anomalistic months (9 × 27.5546 = 247.99 days), so that after 248 days the Moon’s irregularity repeats. Combined with a few corrections, the vākyas allowed the Moon’s position to be found with little arithmetic. Similar vākyas were composed for the Sun and planets, and the vākya almanac remains in use in parts of Tamil Nadu.

docs.title: 10.3 The Lineage
docs.text:
The school is defined by a chain of teachers and pupils (Sarma 1972; Plofker 2009).

Table 10.1. Principal members of the Kerala school. Dates are approximate except where a work’s own date is known. Astronomer Dates Principal works and contributions Mādhava of Saṅgamagrāma c. 1340–1425 Veṇvāroha (lunar computation); series for \(\pi\), sine, cosine and arctangent attributed to him by later authors Parameśvara of Vaṭaśśeri c. 1360–1455 Dṛggaṇita (1431); Goladīpikā; commentaries; decades of eclipse observation Dāmodara 15th c. son of Parameśvara; teacher of Nīlakaṇṭha and Jyeṣṭhadeva Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī 1444–c. 1545 Tantrasaṅgraha (1500); commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya; Golasāra; Jyotirmīmāṃsā; revised planetary model Jyeṣṭhadeva c. 1500–1610 Yuktibhāṣā (Malayalam, c. 1530): demonstrations of the school’s results Citrabhānu 16th c. algebraic work Śaṅkara Vāriyar c. 1500–1560 commentaries on the Tantrasaṅgraha and (with Nārāyaṇa) on the Līlāvatī (Kriyākramakarī) Acyuta Piṣāraṭi c. 1550–1621 Sphuṭanirṇaya; reduction of the Moon’s position to the ecliptic Putumana Somayājī date uncertain (17th–18th c.?) Karaṇapaddhati Śaṅkara Varman 19th c. Sadratnamālā (1819 or 1823; sources differ), a late summary

docs.title: 10.4 Observation and Revision
docs.text: The Kerala astronomers were unusually explicit about the relation between computation and observation. Two figures stand out: Parameśvara, who put the principle into practice, and Nīlakaṇṭha, who reflected on it (Sarma 1972; Minkowski 2002).

docs.title: 10.4.1 Parameśvara
docs.text: Parameśvara of Vaṭaśśeri (Alathur), on the Nila river, was the most prolific author of the school. Having compared eclipse predictions with what he saw over several decades, he introduced a new set of parameters, the dṛk (“seen”) system of his Dṛggaṇita (1431), to replace the Parahita system where it had become inaccurate. He also wrote a short treatise on the sphere (Goladīpikā), works on eclipses, and commentaries on the Āryabhaṭīya, on Bhāskara I’s works, on the Sūryasiddhānta and on the Līlāvatī, among others. His commentaries often record his own views and corrections. His career is the best example in the Indian tradition of a sustained programme of comparing computation with observation, and his work was the starting point for his successors (Sarma 1972).

docs.title: 10.4.2 Nīlakaṇṭha’s Jyotirmīmāṃsā
docs.text: Nīlakaṇṭha’s Jyotirmīmāṃsā is unusual in Indian astronomy because it is about the nature of astronomical knowledge itself. Written in a style influenced by the Mīmāṃsā school of scriptural interpretation, it asks how the parameters of the siddhāntas, which some held to be revealed or infallible, can be known and justified. Nīlakaṇṭha’s answer is that they rest on observation and reasoning, not on revelation; that every system becomes inaccurate in time; that the authors of the classical texts themselves derived and revised them in this way; and that the astronomers of every age must do the same. He recommends, in particular, the careful observation of eclipses as the decisive test (Sarma 1972; Minkowski 2002).

docs.title: 10.5.1 The results
docs.text:
The most celebrated achievement of the school is a set of infinite series for the circumference of the circle and for trigonometric quantities. Later Kerala authors (Nīlakaṇṭha, Śaṅkara Vāriyar, Jyeṣṭhadeva) attribute them to Mādhava, whose own surviving works do not contain them (Plofker 2009; Sarma et al. 2008). In modern notation they include:

\[\begin{align*} \frac{\pi}{4} &= 1 - \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7} + \cdots \\ \sin\theta &= \theta - \frac{\theta^3}{3!} + \frac{\theta^5}{5!} - \cdots \\ \cos\theta &= 1 - \frac{\theta^2}{2!} + \frac{\theta^4}{4!} - \cdots \\ \arctan x &= x - \frac{x^3}{3} + \frac{x^5}{5} - \cdots \quad (|x| \le 1) \end{align*}\]

The texts state these in words and with the Sine and arc in a circle of radius \(R\), not with modern functions; the formulae above are modern translations. The series for \(\pi\) converges very slowly, and the Kerala astronomers devised “end corrections” (antyasaṃskāra), rational expressions added at the point where the series is cut off, which greatly improve the result, and transformed series that converge faster. With such methods they obtained values of \(\pi\) of high accuracy. The verse attributed to Mādhava and analysed digit by digit in Section 1.8 gives the circumference of a circle of diameter \(9 \times 10^{11}\) as 2,827,433,388,233, which corresponds to \(\pi \approx 3.14159265359\), correct to eleven decimal places.

In Europe the series for the arctangent and for \(\pi/4\) were found by James Gregory (1671) and Leibniz (1673–74), and the sine and cosine series by Newton (1669). The Kerala results are earlier, a fact now generally recognised.

docs.title: 10.5.2 Purpose and demonstration
docs.text:
The series were not ends in themselves. They served to compute the Sine and arc more accurately than the old tables, and Mādhava is credited with a table of Sines at the traditional 24 intervals, given to fractions of a second of arc. The demonstrations of the series are preserved in the Malayalam Yuktibhāṣā of Jyeṣṭhadeva and in Śaṅkara Vāriyar’s commentaries. They proceed by dividing a quantity (for example, an arc of a circle) into a large number of small parts, expressing the contribution of each, and summing using results on the sums of powers of integers (saṅkalita), which for a very large number of parts can be approximated by simple expressions (Sarma et al. 2008; Divakaran 2018).

Modern readers naturally see in these arguments ideas related to integration and to limits. The comparison is legitimate if it is made carefully. The Kerala demonstrations are rigorous within their own framework and are a major achievement; but they concern particular geometrical quantities, they do not formulate the general concepts of derivative and integral, and they are not “calculus” in the sense of Newton and Leibniz, still less a “Riemann integral”. The results are best described in the terms historians of mathematics now use: power series for trigonometric functions and \(\pi\), derived by methods of discretisation and summation. Their mathematics is examined in Volume 11.

docs.title: 10.5.3 From series to tables
docs.text: The series made it possible to compute the Sine of any arc, and the radius itself, to much higher precision than before. With an accurate value of \(\pi\), the radius of a circle whose circumference is \(21{,}600'\) is \(21{,}600/2\pi = 3437;44,48\) minutes, that is, \(3437'\) \(44”\) \(48”'\), instead of the traditional round \(3438'\). Mādhava’s table of Sines, at the traditional intervals of \(3^\circ 45'\), gives its values to thirds (sixtieths of a second) of arc and is accurate in almost every entry to the last place given (Plofker 2009). Such tables, and the series for interpolating between their entries, were used in the computation of the vākyas and of planetary positions. The mathematics of the school was thus driven by, and served, the needs of astronomical computation.

docs.title: 10.5.4 Discovery and recognition
docs.text: Charles Whish, an official of the East India Company in Malabar, described the series of the Tantrasaṅgraha, Yuktibhāṣā, Karaṇapaddhati and Sadratnamālā in a paper read in 1832 and published in 1834 (Whish 1834). His work attracted little attention for a century. The Kerala results were brought back into view by Indian scholars in the mid-twentieth century, and the critical editions of K. V. Sarma and the translations of Ramasubramanian, Srinivas and Sriram have since made the texts accessible (Sarma 1972; Sarma et al. 2008; Ramasubramanian and Sriram 2011). The Kerala series now appear in standard histories of mathematics, though popular accounts often still credit them only to their European rediscoverers.

docs.title: 10.6.1 The revision
docs.text:
In the classical models (Chapter 7) the inferior planets, Mercury and Venus, are treated differently from the superior ones: their mean planet is the mean Sun, and their own heliocentric motion is assigned to the śīghrocca. One consequence is that the classical rule for the latitude of Mercury and Venus, computed from the mean planet, gives wrong results. In the Tantrasaṅgraha (1500) Nīlakaṇṭha changed the model for the inferior planets: he took as the planet’s mean motion the motion that the older texts assigned to the śīghrocca (the motion around the Sun), applied the manda correction to this, and treated the mean Sun as the śīghrocca. The inferior planets were thus handled in the same way as the superior planets, and the latitudes came out correctly (Ramasubramanian and Sriram 2011). Figure 10.1 shows the change.

Figure 10.1. Nīlakaṇṭha’s revision of the model for an inferior planet, shown for Venus. In both panels the mean Sun moves around the earth, and Venus lies on a circle around it whose radius, about 0.72 of the Sun’s, is that of the śīghra epicycle (Table 7.2). What changes is which motion counts as the mean planet, and therefore which motion receives the manda (eccentric) correction and is used to compute the latitude. Mercury is treated in the same way. The eccentricity in (b) is exaggerated.

docs.title: 10.6.2 The “geo-heliocentric” interpretation
docs.text: K. Ramasubramanian, M. D. Srinivas and M. S. Sriram have argued that passages in Nīlakaṇṭha’s later writings (his commentary on the Āryabhaṭīya and the Golasāra) describe a picture in which the five planets move in eccentric orbits around the mean Sun, while the Sun moves around the earth: a geometrical arrangement like the one Tycho Brahe proposed in 1588 (Ramasubramanian et al. 1994). This is an important finding about Nīlakaṇṭha’s understanding of the geometry of his model. It should be stated with three qualifications. First, Nīlakaṇṭha’s system remained geocentric: the earth was at rest at the centre, and the Sun moved around it. Second, the interpretation of the relevant passages, and how far Nīlakaṇṭha meant a physical arrangement rather than a computational one, is discussed by historians. Third, there is no evidence of any connection between Nīlakaṇṭha’s model and Tycho’s. Calling the model “heliocentric” or saying that it “anticipated Copernicus” is therefore misleading. Its achievement was to make the treatment of all five planets consistent and to correct a long-standing error in the theory of latitudes.

docs.title: 10.7 Other Contributions
docs.text: The Kerala astronomers also refined the theory of the Moon, adding corrections to its true position; treated the reduction of the Moon’s position from its inclined orbit to the ecliptic (Acyuta Piṣāraṭi); computed eclipses and the visibility of the lunar crescent with new care; and wrote large numbers of commentaries, in Sanskrit and Malayalam, on the Āryabhaṭīya, the Līlāvatī and their own texts. The Karaṇapaddhati of Putumana Somayājī shows how the parameters of the vākya system could be derived from those of the siddhāntas using the school’s mathematics; it has been translated with a full commentary by Pai et al. (2018). Many of these works were edited by K. V. Sarma, among them the Tantrasaṅgraha with Śaṅkara Vāriyar’s two commentaries (Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī 1977; Sarma 1972).

docs.title: 10.8 Did the Kerala Series Reach Europe?
docs.text: Jesuit missionaries were active in Kerala from the mid-sixteenth century, learned Malayalam and Sanskrit, and were interested in Indian calendrical methods. George Gheverghese Joseph and C. K. Raju have argued that Kerala mathematics may have been transmitted to Europe through them and influenced the development of the calculus (Joseph 2011; Raju 2007). The hypothesis is plausible as a possibility, since the routes existed. But no document has been found showing that any European knew of the Kerala series before Whish’s paper of 1834, and the European discoveries of the seventeenth century can be traced through their own sources. Most historians of mathematics therefore regard transmission as unproven (Plofker 2009). The value of the Kerala achievement does not depend on the answer.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Sarma (1972) is the basic history. Ramasubramanian and Sriram (2011) translate the Tantrasaṅgraha with a detailed commentary, Sarma et al. (2008) the Yuktibhāṣā and Pai et al. (2018) the Karaṇapaddhati. Plofker (2009) and Divakaran (2018) discuss the mathematics; Ramasubramanian et al. (1994) present the interpretation of Nīlakaṇṭha’s model.

docs.title: Chapter 11: Instruments, Islamic Astronomy and the Observatories of Jai Singh
11.1 Instruments in the Siddhāntas
docs.text: Most siddhāntas contain a chapter on instruments (yantrādhyāya), and the instruments they describe have been surveyed by Ōhashi (1994); the surviving physical instruments, most of them from the last four centuries, by Sarma (2008). The classical instruments were simple, made of wood, metal or clay, and mostly small. They were used for teaching, for timekeeping, and for observations of the Sun’s altitude, the time of day and night, and the positions of stars and planets. The texts rarely report the results of observations made with them, which is one reason why the observational basis of Indian astronomy has been debated (Chapter 1).

docs.title: 11.1.1 The gnomon
docs.text:
The oldest and most important instrument was the gnomon (śaṅku), a vertical rod conventionally 12 aṅgulas high, set up on level ground. Its shadow gives the cardinal directions, the time of day, the Sun’s altitude and, from the noon shadow at the equinox, the latitude (Chapter 6). Its use goes back to the Vedic altar manuals and is described in all the siddhāntas.

Figure 11.1. The gnomon (śaṅku). The Sun’s altitude \(a\) follows from the ratio of the gnomon to its shadow.

docs.title: 11.1.2 Water clocks
docs.text: At night, and on cloudy days, time was measured with water clocks. The usual Indian form (ghaṭī or ghaṭikāyantra) was a hemispherical copper bowl with a small hole in the bottom, floated in a vessel of water; it filled and sank in one ghaṭikā (24 minutes), after which it was emptied and set floating again, and an attendant struck a gong. The Sūryasiddhānta and other texts describe it, and such bowls were used at temples and courts until recent times (Ōhashi 1994; Sarma 2008). The size of the hole was found by trial against a sundial or the stars, not by a hydraulic formula.

docs.title: 11.1.3 The armillary sphere and other instruments
docs.text:
The golayantra or armillary sphere, a model of the heavens made of rings representing the horizon, meridian, equator, ecliptic and other circles, is described in the Sūryasiddhānta (chapter 13), by Āryabhaṭa (who mentions a sphere turned by water) and by most later authors. It served above all for teaching and for demonstrating the relations among the circles of the sphere.

Figure 11.2. A nineteenth-century European armillary sphere of wood and printed paper, with rings for the horizon, meridian, equator, tropics and zodiac. The Sanskrit texts describe armillary spheres (golayantra) of the same general kind; no Indian example of comparable age is shown here. Photo: Rama, CC BY-SA 3.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons (object: Musee d'histoire des sciences, Geneve, MHS 1344)

The chapters on instruments in Brahmagupta’s Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta, Lalla’s Śiṣya­dhī­vṛddhida­tantra and Bhāskara II’s Golādhyāya describe how each instrument is made and used.
