Bhāskara lists the sphere (gola), the equatorial ring (nāḍīvalaya), the staff (yaṣṭi), the gnomon (śaṅku), the water clock (ghaṭī), the circle (cakra), the semicircle (cāpa), the quadrant (turya) and his own board (phalaka), and praises above all the “instrument of the intellect” (dhīyantra), meaning the astronomer’s understanding, without which no instrument is of use. Most of these are simple devices for measuring the altitude of the Sun or a star, or the time, and many could be improvised from wood or bamboo. Ōhashi’s survey shows that the classical instruments were quite adequate for the measurements on which the siddhānta parameters could have been based (Ōhashi 1994).

Other texts add the hemispherical bowl (kapāla) and various shadow instruments. Bhāskara’s “board” (phalakayantra) is a graduated rectangular board with a pointer, for finding time from the Sun’s altitude (Bhāskara II 1861; Ōhashi 1994). Several authors, including Brahmagupta, Lalla and Bhāskara II, also describe “self-moving” devices (svayaṃvaha), wheels said to turn perpetually with the help of mercury or water; these belong to the history of speculation about perpetual motion, not of working instruments.

docs.title: 11.2 The Astrolabe in India
docs.text:
The planispheric astrolabe, the characteristic instrument of medieval Islamic astronomy, reached India with the Delhi Sultanate. It projects the celestial sphere onto a flat plate, and with it the user can find the time from the altitude of the Sun or a star, the rising and setting of stars, the ascendant, and much else. Its main parts are the body (mater), plates engraved for particular latitudes, the openwork “rete” carrying pointers for bright stars and the ecliptic, and a sighting rule on the back.

The first Sanskrit treatise on the astrolabe, the Yantrarāja (“King of Instruments”), was written in 1370 by the Jain monk Mahendra Sūri, astronomer at the court of Sultan Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq, and was commented on by his pupil Malayendu Sūri. It was followed by other Sanskrit works on the instrument. Astrolabes were made in India in large numbers, especially in Lahore from the late sixteenth century, with Arabic or Persian inscriptions; others were made with Sanskrit inscriptions in Devanāgarī, giving the nakṣatras and Indian units. S. R. Sarma’s studies of these instruments show the astrolabe as a shared Indo-Islamic instrument, adapted to Indian needs (Sarma 2008).

docs.title: 11.3.1 The zīj tradition
docs.text: Islamic astronomy, which had absorbed Indian methods in eighth-century Baghdad (Chapter 16) and then developed on a largely Ptolemaic basis, returned to India with the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals. Its characteristic product was the zīj, a handbook of astronomical tables with instructions for their use. The Zīj-i Sulṭānī compiled at the observatory of Ulugh Beg in Samarqand (completed around 1440) was widely used in Mughal India, and Mughal astronomers produced their own versions, such as the Zīj-i Shāh Jahānī under Shāh Jahān. Astronomers and astrologers trained in Persian and Arabic served at the courts alongside Sanskrit-trained jyotiṣīs.

docs.title: 11.3.2 The Delhi Sultanate
docs.text: Islamic astronomy in India before the Mughals is much less well known than the Sanskrit tradition beside it or the Mughal astronomy that followed. Persian chroniclers show that the sultans of Delhi, from the thirteenth century, kept astrologers at court and consulted them on the timing of campaigns and ceremonies, and these astrologers presumably computed with Persian and Arabic zījes brought from Iran and Central Asia. Fīrūz Shāh Tughluq (r. 1351–1388) is the best-documented patron: the chroniclers of his reign report that Sanskrit books taken from the temple library of Nagarkot (Kangra) were translated into Persian, among them works on astronomy and astrology, and it was at his court that Mahendra Sūri wrote the first Sanskrit treatise on the astrolabe (Section 11.2). Most Sultanate-period Persian astronomical writing, however, survives only in manuscript or is known only by title, and it has not yet been studied in enough detail to support a fuller account; this chapter therefore follows the Islamic tradition in India mainly where it met the Sanskrit one.

docs.title: 11.3.3 Astronomy and astrology at the Mughal court
docs.text: The Mughal emperors and their nobles took a keen interest in the heavens. Astrologers, both Muslim and Hindu, were consulted on the timing of coronations, campaigns and journeys, and Mughal memoirs and histories mention their predictions, sometimes with scepticism. Humāyūn was devoted to astronomy and astrology and is said to have organised aspects of his court according to the planets; Akbar’s court employed astrologers of both traditions and sponsored translations from Sanskrit into Persian, among them the poet Fayḍī’s Persian version of Bhāskara II’s Līlāvatī (1587), whose preface is the source of the legend of Līlāvatī (Section 9.6); Shāh Jahān’s reign saw the Zīj-i Shāh Jahānī and its Sanskrit version by Nityānanda. Persian-language astronomy and astrology flourished alongside Sanskrit, and many scholars worked in both. This environment, rather than any single translation, is the setting for the Sanskrit response to Islamic astronomy (Plofker 2009; Sarma 2008).

docs.title: 11.3.4 Persian-language astronomy in India
docs.text: Astronomy written in Persian in India deserves to be counted as part of Indian astronomy, not only as a foreign presence. The Zīj-i Shāh Jahānī, compiled by Mullā Farīd al-Dīn Masʿūd Dihlawī, adapted Ulugh Beg’s tables to the Mughal capital and its calendar. Abū al-Faḍl’s Āʾīn-i Akbarī, the great survey of Akbar’s empire written in the 1590s, includes an account of Hindu learning in which the Indian calendar, eras and astronomy are described for Persian readers, as al-Bīrūnī had done five centuries earlier. Movement also ran the other way: Sanskrit manuals explained the Islamic calendar and Persian astronomical terms to Indian astronomers, among them the Pārasīprakāśa of Vedāṅgarāya (1643), written at Shāh Jahān’s court (Pingree 1981). Instrument-making was another meeting point: the Lahore workshops mentioned above, among them a family of makers active over several generations, supplied astrolabes and celestial globes to patrons across the Mughal world (Sarma 2008). The history of these Persian texts and instruments is still less studied than that of the Sanskrit tradition, and much of it remains in manuscript.

docs.title: 11.3.5 Sanskrit responses
docs.text:
The encounter produced a substantial Sanskrit literature (Pingree 1978; Plofker 2009).

  • Translations. Nityānanda, at Shāh Jahān’s court, translated the Zīj-i Shāh Jahānī into Sanskrit as the Siddhāntasindhu (1628) and wrote the Sarvasiddhāntarāja (1639), presenting Islamic (Ptolemaic) astronomy in the form of a Sanskrit siddhānta. Later a Sanskrit version was made of al-Birjandī’s commentary on part of Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī’s Tadhkira, a major work of Islamic theoretical astronomy (Kusuba and Pingree 2002).

  • Debate. In Vārāṇasī in the mid-seventeenth century, Kamalākara’s Siddhānta­tattva­viveka (1658) adopted elements of Islamic and Greek astronomy and criticised his rivals, while Munīśvara, author of the Siddhāntasārvabhauma (1646), defended the traditional siddhānta. Their debates also concerned the place of Purāṇic cosmology (Minkowski 2004).

  • Astrology. Perso-Arabic astrology was translated into Sanskrit as tājika, used especially for annual horoscopes; the Tājikanīlakaṇṭhī (1587) of Nīlakaṇṭha Daivajña (not the Kerala astronomer of the same name) became its standard text (Chapter 15).

Overall, Sanskrit astronomers took over Islamic instruments, tables and some models while keeping their own framework of computation and their sidereal reckoning. Pingree judged that the encounter changed traditional practice less than might have been expected; more recent work has emphasised the range and seriousness of the exchange (Minkowski 2004; Sarma 2008).

docs.title: 11.4 Sawai Jai Singh and His Observatories
11.4.1 The project
docs.text:
Sawai Jai Singh II (1688–1743), ruler of Amber and founder of Jaipur and a high noble of the Mughal empire, was the most ambitious patron of astronomy in early modern India. Finding that the positions computed from the existing tables, both Sanskrit and Islamic, disagreed with observation, he decided to make new observations and new tables. To do so he built five observatories in the 1720s and 1730s: at Delhi (the first, around 1724), Jaipur (the largest), Ujjain, Vārāṇasī and Mathurā. The Mathurā observatory has disappeared; the others survive, restored to various degrees. The Jaipur observatory was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010 (Sharma 1995).

Jai Singh’s circle was learned in three traditions. His astronomer Jagannātha Samrāṭ translated into Sanskrit Ptolemy’s Almagest, from al-Ṭūsī’s Arabic recension, as the Samrāṭsiddhānta (1732), and Euclid’s Elements as the Rekhāgaṇita. Persian-writing astronomers worked on the Zīj-i Muḥammad Shāhī, the tables produced by the project and named after the emperor Muḥammad Shāh. Jai Singh was also in contact with Jesuit astronomers, obtained European astronomical tables, including those of Philippe de La Hire, and sent a mission to Portugal (Sharma 1995).

docs.title: 11.4.2 The instruments
docs.text:
Jai Singh’s distinctive idea was to build instruments in masonry on a huge scale, so that their graduations could be finely divided and their alignment would not change. Several of the designs were his own or were developed in his circle from traditional instruments.

Table 11.1. Principal instruments of Jai Singh’s observatories (Sharma 1995) Instrument Description and use Samrāṭ yantra equinoctial sundial: a great triangular wall whose upper edge points to the celestial pole, with graduated quadrants on either side in the plane of the equator; time and the Sun’s declination Jaya Prakāśa a pair of complementary hemispherical bowls sunk in the ground, their inner surfaces engraved with coordinate circles; the shadow of a cross-wire stretched over the rim shows the Sun’s position directly Rāma yantra a pair of complementary open cylindrical structures with a central pillar; altitude and azimuth Rāśivalaya yantras twelve dials, one for each zodiacal sign, each oriented so as to measure ecliptic coordinates when the beginning of its sign is on the meridian Nāḍīvalaya two dials in the plane of the equator, facing north and south Digaṃśa yantra circular walls around a central pillar; azimuth Ṣaṣṭhāṃśa sixty-degree arcs in the meridian inside a darkened chamber, with a pinhole image of the Sun; noon altitude and the Sun’s diameter Kapāla yantra hemispherical dials for conversion between coordinate systems Cakra yantra large rings mounted parallel to the earth’s axis; declination and hour angle

docs.title: 11.4.3 How two of the instruments work
docs.text:
The Samrāṭ yantra.

The gnomon is a right-angled triangle of masonry standing in the plane of the meridian, its base running north–south and its upper edge (the hypotenuse) rising towards the north at an angle to the horizontal equal to the latitude of the place, so that it is parallel to the earth’s axis. On each side of the gnomon a quadrant of a circle is built, lying in the plane of the celestial equator, with its centre on the hypotenuse. As the sky turns, the shadow of the hypotenuse moves across the quadrants at a uniform rate of \(15^\circ\) an hour, so that equal divisions of the quadrants mark equal intervals of time; the eastern quadrant serves in the morning and the western in the afternoon. The Sun’s declination can be read from the position of the shadow along scales marked on the face of the hypotenuse (Figure 11.3).

Figure 11.3. Schematic side view (from the east) of a Samrāṭ yantra at latitude \(\phi\) (here about \(27^\circ\), as at Jaipur). The quadrants, seen edge-on, lie perpendicular to the hypotenuse, in the plane of the equator. Not to scale.

The Jaya Prakāśa.

Each of the two bowls is a hemisphere sunk into the ground, with its rim level with the ground, representing the visible half of the sky turned inside out. A pair of cross-wires is stretched over the rim so that their intersection lies at the centre of the sphere. The shadow of the intersection falls on the inner surface at the point diametrically opposite the Sun, and lines engraved on the surface (hour circles, declination circles, the horizon system and the signs of the ecliptic) allow the Sun’s coordinates to be read directly. The surface is cut into alternate strips, removed in one bowl and kept in the other, so that the observer can walk within the bowl to read the scales; together the two bowls make one complete hemisphere (Sharma 1995).

Figure 11.4. Schematic cross-section of a Jaya Prakāśa bowl. The shadow of the intersection of the cross-wires marks the point of the inner surface opposite the Sun, where the Sun’s coordinates are read. Not to scale. Figure 11.5. The great Samrāṭ yantra at the Jaipur observatory. The sloping upper edge of the triangular wall points to the celestial pole; the shadow it casts on the curved quadrants (one is visible at the left) indicates the time. Photo: Jakub Hałun, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Samrāṭ yantra at Jaipur is among the largest sundials ever built; its gnomon wall rises about 27 metres. Its scale allows very fine graduation, and it is often said that time can be read on it to a few seconds. In practice the edge of the shadow is blurred by the Sun’s finite disc, and the accuracy achievable with the masonry instruments, discussed by Sharma (1995), was limited also by the precision of construction and by settling of the masonry.

Figure 11.6. Panorama of the Jaipur observatory. In the foreground are several of the twelve Rāśivalaya yantras, with their sloping gnomon walls; at the right of centre is the Nāḍīvalaya (the dial with a red face); the City Palace and the Nahargarh hills are behind. Photo: Marcin Białek (correction: Aleks G), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons Figure 11.7. The Jaipur observatory from above, looking towards the City Palace. Visible are the smaller Samrāṭ yantra (the red stepped triangle at centre), the Nāḍīvalaya (right of centre) and, at left, the ring instruments. Photo: Knowledge Seeker (2002), public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

docs.title: 11.4.4 Jai Singh and his predecessors
docs.text: Jai Singh’s project belongs to a tradition of royal observatories in the Islamic world. The observatory of Marāgha in north-western Iran, founded in 1259 under Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī, and that of Ulugh Beg at Samarqand, built in the 1420s, used large fixed instruments, including a huge meridian arc at Samarqand, to obtain new parameters for new zījes. Jai Singh knew Ulugh Beg’s tables and sought to improve them. His instruments, however, differ from those of his predecessors: most are not meridian instruments but dials and bowls that give coordinates directly at any hour, combining the principles of the sundial, the armillary sphere and the astrolabe in masonry. Several, such as the Jaya Prakāśa and the Rāma yantra, have no exact precedent.

docs.title: 11.4.5 Assessment
docs.text: Jai Singh’s observatories are monuments of the last great project of naked-eye astronomy, carried out when the telescope had already transformed European astronomy. The Zīj-i Muḥammad Shāhī, completed in the 1730s, was based in large part on the tables of Ulugh Beg, corrected by the new observations (Sharma 1995). It improved on the older tables available in India, but it did not match the best European tables of its time, and Jai Singh’s programme did not continue after his death in 1743. Nevertheless, the project is remarkable for its scale, for its deliberate combination of Indian, Islamic and European learning, and for the instruments themselves, several of which are original designs. Those achievements, rather than its tables, are its legacy.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Ōhashi (1994) surveys the instruments of the siddhāntas; Sarma (2008) the history of instruments, including astrolabes; Sharma (1995) Jai Singh and his observatories; Minkowski (2004) and Kusuba and Pingree (2002) the Sanskrit response to Islamic astronomy.

docs.title: Chapter 12: Handbooks, Tables and the Working Astronomer
12.1 From Treatise to Handbook
docs.text:
The great siddhāntas described in the preceding chapters were not, for the most part, the books from which almanacs, horoscopes and eclipse warnings were actually computed. A siddhānta counts its days from the beginning of the kalpa or of the Kali age, so that the astronomer who follows it must multiply a day-count of seven digits or more by revolution numbers of up to ten digits and divide by a number of civil days of ten digits, keeping the remainder. The work is long and errors are easy. From the seventh century onwards the practical astronomer worked instead with a handbook (karaṇa) or with tables (sāraṇī), and it was in these forms that most of the tradition reached most of its users (Pingree 1981; Plofker 2009).

Later writers classified astronomical works by the epoch from which they count: a siddhānta in the strict sense counts from the beginning of the kalpa, a tantra from the beginning of the current yuga, in practice usually the Kali age (Chapter 1), and a karaṇa from a recent date, usually in the author’s own lifetime. The recent epoch is the defining feature of the handbook, and most of its other features follow from it:

  • the handbook states the mean positions of the Sun, Moon, planets, apogees and nodes at its epoch (the initial values, called kṣepaka or dhruva), so that only the days elapsed since then need to be counted;

  • the long period relations of the siddhānta are replaced by small ratios or by motions per day, month or year, chosen to give nearly the same results over a few centuries;

  • the rules are shortened: Sine tables are reduced or replaced by approximations, iterations are cut to a single step, and the theoretical chapters on the sphere and on cosmography are omitted or reduced;

  • the contents are those that practice required: true positions, the elements of the almanac, eclipses, the visibility of the Moon and planets, conjunctions and the shadow of the gnomon.

The titles of the handbooks advertise their convenience. Khaṇḍakhādyaka names a sweetmeat made with sugar, presumably a promise that the subject will go down easily; Laghumānasa is “the short Mānasa”; Karaṇakutūhala means something like “the delight of computation”; and Grahalāghava, “lightness in the planets”, promises ease in computing them. Judging by the manuscripts recorded in Pingree’s Census, the most successful handbooks and tables were copied far more often than all but a few siddhāntas (Pingree 1970–1994). This chapter describes how they worked, how the astronomers who used them earned their living and handed on their knowledge, and how the tradition dealt with the slow drift of computation away from the sky.

docs.title: 12.2 The Khaṇḍakhādyaka
docs.text:
The oldest surviving handbook, and one of the most influential, is the Khaṇḍakhādyaka of Brahmagupta, whose epoch falls in Śaka 587 (665 CE). Brahmagupta was then sixty-seven, and thirty-seven years had passed since his Brāhma­sphuṭa­siddhānta (Chapter 9). The handbook has a surprising basis. It does not follow Brahmagupta’s own system but Āryabhaṭa’s midnight (ārdharātrika) system, the very school Brahmagupta had criticised at length in his siddhānta. The usual explanation is practical: the midnight system was the one in common use in the region where he worked, and a handbook was useful only if its results agreed with the almanacs and the eclipse times that its users already knew. Brahmagupta added a supplement, the Uttarakhaṇḍakhādyaka, in which he corrected some of the rules of the first part, partly in the direction of his own earlier work (Sengupta 1934; Pingree 1978).

The Khaṇḍakhādyaka shows how a handbook compresses a siddhānta. In a siddhānta the number of intercalary months that have accumulated is found by multiplying the elapsed solar months by the number of intercalary months in the yuga (1,593,336) and dividing by the number of solar months (51,840,000). Brahmagupta’s handbook does the same with small numbers. In effect it multiplies the elapsed solar months by 2 and divides by 65, with a small additive constant that fixes the epoch; in the same way it finds the omitted tithis by multiplying the elapsed tithis by 11 and dividing by 703. (The rules in the text are worded with their own multipliers and epoch constants, but these are the ratios they amount to.) The approximations are excellent:

\[\begin{alignat*} {2} \frac{2}{65} &= 0.030769 &\qquad& \text{against}\quad \frac{1{,}593{,}336}{51{,}840{,}000} = 0.030736,\\ \frac{11}{703} &= 0.0156472 && \text{against about}\quad 0.015647, \end{alignat*}\]

the second value being the proportion of omitted tithis implied by the period relations of the Āryabhaṭa school. Both fractions are successive approximations of the kind produced by the continued-fraction methods of Indian arithmetic, though the handbook does not say how they were found. The first gains one intercalary month on the exact ratio only in about 2,500 years; with the epoch constant reset by each new handbook, the error never matters.

Other parts of the work were equally practical. Its rule for interpolating in a table by second differences is described in Chapter 6. Its eclipse rules were used for centuries, and its commentators, among them Pṛthūdakasvāmin (864) and Bhaṭṭotpala (tenth century), wrote worked examples for students (Table 9.1). The book also travelled: an Arabic version made in Sind and known as the Zīj al-Arkand, from Sanskrit ahargaṇa, was among the first Indian astronomical works in Arabic (Chapter 16). P. C. Sengupta’s English translation (Sengupta 1934) remains the most accessible version.

docs.title: 12.3 Later Handbooks
docs.text:
Table 12.1 lists some of the principal handbooks. Their authors and epochs are well established; their schools and regions of use are given only where the texts or their manuscript tradition make them clear. Several of these authors have already appeared in Chapter 9; here the interest is in what their handbooks did.

Table 12.1. Some Sanskrit astronomical handbooks (karaṇas). Epochs are the years from which the handbooks count. Handbook Author Epoch Remarks Khaṇḍakhādyaka Brahmagupta 665 Ārdharātrika school; Arabic Zīj al-Arkand Laghumānasa Muñjāla 932 very short; an additional lunar correction Rājamṛgāṅka attributed to King Bhoja of Dhārā 1042 a handbook issued in a king’s name Karaṇaprakāśa Brahmadeva 1092 Ārya school Bhāsvatī Śatānanda, Purī 1099 Saura parameters of the Pañcasiddhāntikā; decimal fractions Karaṇakutūhala Bhāskara II 1183 Brāhma school; also called Brahmatulya Grahalāghava Gaṇeśa Daivajña, Nandigrāma 1520 cycles of 4016 days; no Sine table Vākyakaraṇa anonymous, Tamil country c. 14th c. vākya system (Chapter 13) Karaṇapaddhati Putumana Somayājī, Kerala uncertain derivation of the vākyas (Chapter 10)

Three of them show the range of the genre.

The Bhāsvatī.

Śatānanda, writing at Purī in Odisha, based his handbook of 1099 on the old Sūryasiddhānta as summarised five centuries earlier in Varāhamihira’s Pañcasiddhāntikā (Chapter 5), not on the later text of that name. His innovation was arithmetical. Instead of sexagesimal fractions he expressed the motions in hundredths, so that most of the computation became a matter of multiplying, adding and shifting decimal places. The handbook was much copied and commented on, which shows that an archaic set of parameters could live on for centuries if it was packaged conveniently.

The Karaṇakutūhala.

Bhāskara II wrote his handbook in 1183, at the age of sixty-nine, thirty-three years after his Siddhāntaśiromaṇi. Its alternative title, Brahmatulya (“equal to the Brāhma [system]”), states its claim: it reproduces the results of the Brāhma school by easier methods. It was used for almanacs in parts of western and northern India.

The Grahalāghava.

Gaṇeśa Daivajña, son of Keśava of Nandigrāma on the western coast, wrote in 1520 the most radical simplification of all, and one of the most widely used handbooks. It has two famous devices: it does without a Sine table, replacing trigonometric functions by algebraic approximations, and it counts days in cycles (cakras) of 4016 days. The choice of cycle is ingenious. Four thousand and sixteen days are very nearly 136 synodic months (4016.2 days) and eleven sidereal years less about two days (11 × 365.26 = 4017.8 days). After one cycle, therefore, the mean Sun and the mean Moon each fall only a few degrees short of their starting positions, and the tithi has nearly returned to its starting value. The user divides the days elapsed since the epoch by 4016, multiplies the number of complete cycles by small corrections stated in the text (about \(-1.8^\circ\) for the Sun and \(-3.8^\circ\) for the Moon), and adds the motion for the remaining days, never handling a number of more than four or five digits. To take an illustration with the rates of the Sūryasiddhānta (the Grahalāghava’s own differ slightly), a count of 175,000 days from the epoch is 43 cycles and 2312 days. The Sun’s correction for one cycle is \(-1^\circ 49' 11”\), so for 43 cycles it is \(-78.25^\circ\); the motion for 2312 days is \(118.71^\circ\) after whole revolutions are removed; and the sum, \(40.46^\circ\), added to the Sun’s position at the epoch, is exactly what the long multiplication \(175{,}000 \times 0;59,8,10\) would give. The Grahalāghava remained the basis of many almanacs in Maharashtra, Gujarat and Karnataka into the twentieth century (Chapter 13).

docs.title: 12.4 Counting the Days: A Worked Example
docs.text:
The first step of every computation, in siddhānta and handbook alike, is the ahargaṇa, the number of civil days from the epoch to the day required (Chapter 6). An almanac-maker did not start from a modern calendar date. He started from the date as his own calendar expressed it, a lunar month, a tithi and a year of an era, and converted it into days by the period relations of his system. The worked computation of Appendix A takes its ahargaṇa from modern tables; the example below shows how the same number is obtained by the rules of the Sūryasiddhānta itself (Burgess 1860).

Example 12.1 (The day-count for 1 January 2000 by the rules of the Sūryasiddhānta)

At midnight beginning 1 January 2000, Kali year 5100 had elapsed (Kali years \(\approx\) CE \(+ 3101\), the year beginning in March–April), and in the current lunar year eight months, Caitra to Kārttika, had elapsed. The current month was Mārgaśīrṣa (in the amānta reckoning), and its twenty-fifth tithi, the tenth of the dark fortnight, was running, so that 24 tithis of the month were complete. The Sūryasiddhānta gives, for a mahāyuga, 51,840,000 solar months, 1,593,336 intercalary months, 1,603,000,080 lunar days (tithis) and 1,577,917,828 civil days, so that 25,082,252 tithis are omitted.

  1. Elapsed solar months: \(5100 \times 12 + 8 = 61{,}208\).

  2. Intercalary months: \(61{,}208 \times 1{,}593{,}336 / 51{,}840{,}000 = 1881.27\); the integer, 1881, is kept.

  3. Lunar months: \(61{,}208 + 1881 = 63{,}089\).

  4. Elapsed tithis: \(63{,}089 \times 30 + 24 = 1{,}892{,}694\).

  5. Omitted tithis: \(1{,}892{,}694 \times 25{,}082{,}252 / 1{,}603{,}000{,}080 = 29{,}615.11\); the integer, 29,615, is kept.

  6. Civil days: \(1{,}892{,}694 - 29{,}615 = 1{,}863{,}079\).

This is exactly the value obtained in Appendix A from the Julian day numbers. Astronomers checked such a result against the weekday. The Kali epoch fell on a Friday; \(1{,}863{,}079 = 7 \times 266{,}154 + 1\), so the day is one weekday after a Friday, a Saturday, which is correct. Had the check failed, a day would have been added or subtracted, since rounding at steps 2 and 5 can leave the count one day out.

Mean positions.

With the ahargaṇa known, the mean longitude follows from Equation (6.2). For the Sun, \(1{,}863{,}079 \times 4{,}320{,}000 / 1{,}577{,}917{,}828 = 5100.7100\) revolutions; the fraction \(0.7100\) of a revolution is \(255.61^\circ\), or \(15^\circ 37'\) in Dhanus. For the Moon, the same computation with 57,753,336 revolutions gives \(68{,}190.5138\) revolutions and a mean longitude of \(184.98^\circ\). These agree with Table A.1. In practice the multiplication was done with the daily motions in sexagesimal form (0;59,8,10 for the Sun, 13;10,34,52 for the Moon; Table 6.2), keeping as many places as the desired accuracy required.

The handbook’s shortcut.

A handbook avoids the large numbers. Suppose an author had fixed his epoch at midnight beginning 17 April 1999, day 1,862,820 of the Kali era, a few hours after the mean Sun had entered Meṣa. He would compute once, and record in his book, the mean positions at that moment: for the Sun \(0^\circ 20'\), for the Moon \(12^\circ 18'\). A user wanting 1 January 2000 needs only the 259 days elapsed since the epoch. The Sun moves \(259 \times 0;59,8,10 = 255^\circ 16'\), so its mean longitude is \(0^\circ 20' + 255^\circ 16' = 255^\circ 36'\); the Moon moves \(259 \times 13;10,34,52 = 3412^\circ 41'\), which is \(172^\circ 41'\) after removing whole revolutions, so its mean longitude is \(12^\circ 18' + 172^\circ 41' = 184^\circ 59'\). The results are the same as before, but every number now has at most four digits before the fractional part. This is what a karaṇa offered: the same astronomy, at a fraction of the labour, valid for as long as its epoch values and rates stayed close to the sky.

The day-count outside astronomy.

The ahargaṇa was familiar enough to serve as a date. In Kerala the number of days elapsed since the beginning of the Kali age (kalidina) was often recorded in a kaṭapayādi phrase (Chapter 1). The best-known example closes Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭatiri’s devotional poem Nārāyaṇīyam, whose last words, āyurārogyasaukhyam (“long life, health and happiness”), are traditionally read as the day of its completion. The syllables give the digits 0 (the initial vowel), 1 (yu), 2 (rā), 2 (ro), 1 (gya, whose last consonant is ya), 7 (sau) and 1 (khya); read from right to left they make 1,712,210. Counted from the Kali epoch used in the example above, that day falls in late 1586 CE. The phrase is at once a blessing, a date and a small exercise in the arithmetic of the almanac.

docs.title: 12.5 Tables
docs.text:
Tables (sāraṇī; the cells of a table are koṣṭhakas, “compartments”) went one step further than handbooks. A handbook gives rules to be applied; a table gives the results of applying them, so that the user enters with an argument, reads off a value, and interpolates. Sanskrit tables became common in the second millennium and survive in large numbers, mostly on paper, laid out in grids of sexagesimal numbers in Devanāgarī or other regional numerals (Montelle and Plofker 2018).

The main kinds are tables of mean motion (the motion of each body in so many years, months and days, to be added together); tables of the equations (phala) of the manda and śīghra corrections against the anomaly; tables for the elements of the almanac, which give the tithi, nakṣatra and yoga almost directly; and tables for eclipses and for the visibility of the Moon and planets. The Makaranda tables of Vārāṇasī (epoch 1478), based on the Sūryasiddhānta, became the standard basis of almanacs in much of northern and eastern India, and Gaṇeśa Daivajña, besides his handbook, produced tables for the tithis (the Tithicintāmaṇi, 1525). Many such sets were compiled by almanac-makers for their own use and never circulated widely. Pingree catalogued the Sanskrit tables in the collections of the United States and of England (Pingree 1968, 1973), and Montelle and Plofker (2018) have given the first general account of their types and construction.

An equation table shows both the convenience and the limits of the form. Table 12.2 gives, at intervals of \(15^\circ\) of anomaly, the equation of the centre of the Sun computed from the rules of the Sūryasiddhānta, whose epicycle for the Sun shrinks from \(14^\circ\) at the apsides to \(13^\circ 40'\) at the quadrants (Chapter 7).

Table 12.2. The equation of the centre of the Sun at intervals of \(15^\circ\) of anomaly, computed from the parameters of the Sūryasiddhānta. A traditional table would give the values to the nearest second, usually at smaller intervals. Anomaly Epicycle Equation \(0^\circ\) \(14^\circ 0'\) 0;0,0 \(15^\circ\) \(13^\circ 55'\) 0;34,23 \(30^\circ\) \(13^\circ 50'\) 1;6,3 \(45^\circ\) \(13^\circ 46'\) 1;32,57 \(60^\circ\) \(13^\circ 43'\) 1;53,25 \(75^\circ\) \(13^\circ 41'\) 2;6,12 \(90^\circ\) \(13^\circ 40'\) 2;10,32

For an anomaly of \(50^\circ\) the user interpolates between the entries for \(45^\circ\) and \(60^\circ\). The difference is \(20'28”\), a third of which, \(6'49”\), added to \(1;32,57\) gives \(1;39,46\). The exact value is \(1;40,34\), so simple interpolation over so wide an interval is out by \(48”\), because the equation does not grow linearly. A table-maker could reduce the error by tabulating at intervals of a few degrees, or the user could apply a second-difference rule like Brahmagupta’s (Chapter 6). The choice between larger tables and better interpolation is one that every table-making tradition faced.

docs.title: 12.6 The Jyotiṣī and the Profession
docs.text:
The people who computed with these books had many names. The Sanskrit gaṇaka (“calculator”), daivajña (“knower of fate”), sāṃvatsara (“man of the year”, that is, the calendar-maker) and jyotiṣī survive in regional forms and in family names: the Marathi and Gujarati jośī or Joshi is the jyotiṣī, and Tamil kaṇiyaṉ, “astrologer”, comes from gaṇaka. The word is old in Tamil: the Caṅkam poet Kaṇiyaṉ Pūṅkuṉṟaṉ bears it as part of his name. In Kerala the Kaṇiyār (Kaṇisan) community were hereditary astrologers, and in the Tamil country the Vaḷḷuvar (Chapter 13); the profession was thus not exclusively Brahmin, although the authors of Sanskrit astronomical texts almost always were (Chapter 1).

The working jyotiṣī lived from services, not from research. He computed and sold the year’s almanac, and in many regions read it aloud on New Year’s day, a custom still kept in the Telugu and Kannada country as pañcāṅga-śravaṇa, “hearing the almanac”. He fixed the auspicious times (muhūrtas) for weddings, journeys, house-building and the sowing of crops, cast and interpreted horoscopes, announced eclipses with their ritual times of beginning and end, and advised on the dates of festivals and fasts. A few served courts or temples for a stipend or a grant of land; most served a clientele of households. In the villages of the Deccan the jośī was often counted among the hereditary village servants (balutedār) who received a customary share of the harvest in return for their services, which included reading the almanac and fixing the times of household rites. From the later nineteenth century printed almanacs, issued by family firms and publishing houses, carried the computations of a few such families to very large numbers of readers (Chapter 13), and the village calendar-maker increasingly became a reader and interpreter of an almanac computed elsewhere. Astrology was therefore the economic base of astronomy, and the most technically accomplished astronomers wrote astrological works too (Chapter 15).

Skill and books passed within families. Chapter 9 has described the family of Bhāskara II and the school endowed for his descendants. The pattern can be followed in more detail in western India and Vārāṇasī in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, where the authors’ own statements allow genealogies to be reconstructed (Pingree 1981; Minkowski 2004). Keśava of Nandigrāma was the father and teacher of Gaṇeśa Daivajña. A family from Golagrāma in Maharashtra, descended from Divākara, who had studied with Gaṇeśa, produced authors over four generations, among them Nṛsiṃha (born 1586), who wrote a commentary on the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi, and his son Kamalākara. A rival family from Dadhigrāma, also in Maharashtra, included Raṅganātha, author of a commentary on the Sūryasiddhānta (1603), and his son Munīśvara. Both families settled in Vārāṇasī, and the controversy between Kamalākara and Munīśvara (Chapter 11) was in part a rivalry between lineages. Such families kept their own manuscripts, trained their sons with them, and wrote commentaries full of worked examples (udāharaṇa) for the next generation; several members of the Golagrāma family are credited with such example-commentaries on the handbooks.

The tradition had its own ideal of the practitioner. The second chapter of Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā describes the sāṃvatsara a king should employ: of good family and conduct, truthful, learned in all three branches of the science, and able to answer questions on any part of it before a learned assembly; and it warns against the ignorant pretender, whose predictions do harm (Varāhamihira 1981–1982). The ideal combined mathematical competence with moral standing, because the practitioner’s computations governed other people’s rites and decisions.

In practice training was more modest. A pupil memorised a handbook, learned its rules on worked examples, and computed under supervision; mastery of a full siddhānta, of spherical astronomy and of the demonstrations (upapatti) was the mark of a learned astronomer rather than a requirement of the trade. Bhāskara II, at the opening of his Golādhyāya, warns that an astronomer who computes without knowing the demonstrations will neither win respect in learned assemblies nor be free of doubt himself; the warning was needed because many practitioners computed by rote.

docs.title: 12.7 Manuscripts and Collections
docs.text:
The whole of this literature survives in manuscript copies, and its history is in large part the history of copying (Chapter 1). Astronomical manuscripts have two features that make them unusual. First, their colophons are often precisely dated by the copyist in the terms of the calendar itself: an era year, a lunar month and fortnight, a tithi, a weekday and sometimes a nakṣatra. Because these elements are redundant, the date can be checked by computation, and the tables of Sewell and Dikshit (1896) were designed partly for verifying such dates in inscriptions and manuscripts. Second, they are full of numbers. A copyist who misreads a digit in a table or a word-numeral in a verse leaves no grammatical trace of his error; commentaries, with their worked examples, are therefore an essential control on the text, and modern editors have often had to restore parameters by recomputing them. Manuscripts were written in the scripts of their regions, Devanāgarī in the north and west, Śāradā in Kashmir, the Bengali and Oriya scripts in the east, and Grantha, Malayalam, Telugu and Kannada scripts in the south, and the numbers in tables were written with the regional forms of the decimal digits. A table copied from one script into another was therefore exposed to a further kind of error.

Example 12.2 (Checking a colophon date (a hypothetical case))

Suppose a colophon is dated on the first tithi of the bright half of Caitra in Śaka year 1500, a Sunday. With the rules of Example 12.1, Kali year 4679 (Śaka \(+\,3179\)) has elapsed and no months of the new year: \(4679 \times 12 = 56{,}148\) solar months; \(56{,}148 \times 1{,}593{,}336 / 51{,}840{,}000 = 1725.7\), so 1725 intercalary months; \(57{,}873\) lunar months and \(1{,}736{,}190\) tithis; \(1{,}736{,}190 \times 25{,}082{,}252 / 1{,}603{,}000{,}080 = 27{,}166.3\), so 27,166 omitted tithis; and \(1{,}709{,}024\) civil days. Since \(1{,}709{,}024 = 7 \times 244{,}146 + 2\), the day falls two weekdays after a Friday, on a Sunday, and the colophon is consistent. The day is 9 March 1578 in the Julian calendar, the day after a new moon. Had the colophon named a Wednesday, the historian would ask whether the scribe counted the year as current rather than elapsed, used another reckoning of the months, or simply erred. The tables of Sewell and Dikshit (1896) make such checks routine.

Manuscripts were kept by families, by temples and monasteries, and by rulers. The Jain libraries (bhaṇḍāras) of Gujarat and Rajasthan preserved astronomical and astrological works of all communities; the library assembled for Sawai Jai Singh’s astronomers at Jaipur survives and has been catalogued (Pingree 2003); and many Kerala texts were preserved on palm leaf in the households of the families who wrote them, until collectors and editors such as K. V. Sarma brought many of them to light (Sarma 1972). In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries large numbers of manuscripts entered public libraries in India and Europe through purchase, colonial searches for Sanskrit manuscripts, and gifts. Today the largest holdings of astronomical manuscripts are divided among public libraries and research institutes in Vārāṇasī, Pune, Jaipur, Bikaner, Thiruvananthapuram, Chennai and Kolkata, among the Jain libraries, and among libraries in Britain, Germany and the United States; many remain in private hands. The National Mission for Manuscripts, set up by the Government of India in 2003, has been surveying and cataloguing them.

The indispensable guide to this scattered material is David Pingree’s Census of the Exact Sciences in Sanskrit (Pingree 1970–1994). Arranged by author, it records for each the works attributed to him, the manuscripts of each work in the catalogues of collections throughout the world, and the editions. Five volumes appeared between 1970 and 1994; the series was not completed before Pingree’s death in 2005. With his separate catalogues of tables and of the Jaipur collection, it showed for the first time the true size of the literature, and in particular how much of it consists of handbooks, tables, commentaries and astrological works rather than the few famous siddhāntas.

docs.title: 12.8 Computation, Observation and Correction
docs.text:
A handbook fixed a set of epoch values and rates. Like every set of parameters, it drifted slowly away from the sky, and its users found out when an eclipse began at the wrong time or a planet rose earlier than computed. How the tradition responded to such failures reveals how it understood its own authority.

Some of the standard texts claimed more than human authority. The Sūryasiddhānta presents itself as the teaching of the Sun, revealed at the end of the Kṛta age, and Brahmagupta presented his siddhānta as a corrected restoration of the system of Brahmā (Burgess 1860; Pingree 1978). If the parameters were revealed, a discrepancy with the sky was a problem for the observer, not for the text. The Sūryasiddhānta itself offers one way out near its beginning: the science is the same as the one the Sun first taught, and the differences arise only from the passing of the ages. The way most widely taken was the bīja (Chapter 6): a small change in the revolution numbers, added to the text rather than replacing it, which brought its results back into line while leaving the authority of the root text intact. From about 1500 the Sūryasiddhānta was generally used with such a bīja, and Sewell and Dikshit (1896) took this into account in their tables.

The handbook-makers were the people most exposed to the sky, and several of them claimed to have adjusted their parameters by observation. In Kerala the Parahita system added a correction proportional to the years elapsed since a fixed date in the Śaka era, and Parameśvara rebuilt the parameters after decades of eclipse observations (Chapter 10). In western India Keśava of Nandigrāma, in his Grahakautuka (1496), stated that he had corrected his parameters to agree with what was seen, and his son built such corrections into the Grahalāghava. The test was almost always the same: eclipses, conjunctions of planets with each other and with bright stars, and the first and last visibility of the planets, the events that a careful practitioner could time with a water clock and a gnomon.

The justification of such corrections was argued explicitly by Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī, for whom all parameters rest on observation and must be revised from time to time (Chapter 10), and was contested in the seventeenth-century debates of Vārāṇasī (Chapter 11). Against it stood a view that the times required for ritual are those computed by the authoritative text, whatever the sky may show, since the ritual’s efficacy is unseen. Both positions were reasoned, and both had defenders among learned astronomers (Minkowski 2002). The same disagreement returned in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, now between almanacs computed from modern ephemerides and those computed from the traditional texts (Chapter 13). The reformers, too, often worked in the old genre. Veṅkaṭeśa Bāpūjī Ketkar (1854–1930), one of the leading advocates of dṛk almanacs in western India, set out modern parameters and methods in Sanskrit verse handbooks of his own, so that the karaṇa form outlived the parameters for which it had been invented.

docs.title: 12.9 Handbooks in a Wider Perspective
docs.text:
Every pre-modern astronomy that computed a calendar had to turn its theory into a practical instrument. Ptolemy followed his Almagest with the Handy Tables (Neugebauer 1975); the Islamic astronomers organised their practical astronomy in the zīj, a book of tables with rules for their use; Chinese official calendars were issued as computational procedures. The Indian handbook shares the aim of all these. Its distinctive features are two. First, its primary form was a set of rules in verse, meant to be memorised and applied with small arithmetic, rather than a set of tables; tables became common later, alongside the rules. Second, its authors sought simplification by arithmetic as much as by tabulation: the small ratios of the Khaṇḍakhādyaka, the decimal fractions of the Bhāsvatī and the cycles and algebraic approximations of the Grahalāghava replace tables by rules that are easy to carry in the head. The working astronomer’s mathematical skill, as much as his books, was the instrument of his trade.

The handbook was also the form in which Indian astronomy travelled most readily. The Arabic Zīj al-Arkand was built on the Khaṇḍakhādyaka (Section 12.2); the calendrical astronomy of the Kālacakratantra, still used in Tibet, is of the handbook type (Section 9.8); and the luni-solar calendars of Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, counted from an era beginning in 638 CE, were computed by rules derived from Indian handbooks (Chapter 16). A set of rules with a recent epoch, small numbers and no need for the full theory behind them could be learned, carried and adapted far more easily than a siddhānta. In that portability lies much of the historical importance of the karaṇa.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Pingree (1981) surveys the handbooks and tables genre by genre, and Pingree (1978) gives their parameters and schools. Sengupta (1934) translates the Khaṇḍakhādyaka. On tables, Montelle and Plofker (2018) is the standard account, with Pingree (1968, 1973) for the manuscripts. Pingree (1970–1994) is the guide to manuscripts and authors, and Pingree (2003) describes the Jaipur collection. On the reasons astronomers gave for their parameters and corrections, see Minkowski (2002); on the families of Vārāṇasī, Minkowski (2004). Sewell and Dikshit (1896) explain the calendar computations that the almanac-makers performed.

docs.title: Chapter 13: The Pañcāṅga and the Indian Calendars
13.1 The Almanac
docs.text: For most people in most periods of Indian history, astronomy meant the almanac. The pañcāṅga (“five limbs”) is the traditional almanac, published each year in many regional versions and languages. It gives, for each day, five elements derived from the positions of the Sun and Moon, together with the times of sunrise and sunset, the solar and lunar months, festivals and fasts, eclipses, planetary positions and astrological information. Computing it was the main practical task of the jyotiṣī, and it remains the chief living use of the siddhānta tradition (Sewell and Dikshit 1896; Yano 2003).

docs.title: 13.2 The Five Limbs
docs.text: Table 13.1. The five elements (aṅgas) of the pañcāṅga. \(\lambda_\odot\) and \(\lambda_M\) are the sidereal longitudes of the Sun and Moon. Element Meaning Definition tithi lunar day the time in which the Moon gains \(12^\circ\) on the Sun; 30 in a synodic month vāra weekday the seven days named after the seven planets nakṣatra lunar asterism the division of \(13^\circ 20'\) occupied by the Moon yoga “addition” the division of \(13^\circ 20'\) reached by the sum \(\lambda_\odot + \lambda_M\) karaṇa half-tithi the time in which the Moon gains \(6^\circ\) on the Sun; 60 in a month

docs.title: 13.2.1 Tithi
docs.text:
The tithi, first defined in the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, is the basic unit of the religious calendar. The number of the current tithi is

\[\text{tithi} = \left\lfloor \frac{\lambda_M - \lambda_\odot}{12^\circ} \right\rfloor + 1 .\tag{13.1}\]

The thirty tithis of a month are divided into the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), from new moon to full moon, and the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), from full moon to new moon. Each fortnight has fifteen tithis, numbered and named Pratipad (1), Dvitīyā, Tṛtīyā, Caturthī, Pañcamī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Saptamī, Aṣṭamī, Navamī, Daśamī, Ekādaśī, Dvādaśī, Trayodaśī, Caturdaśī, and Pūrṇimā (full moon, the fifteenth of the bright half) or Amāvāsyā (new moon, the fifteenth of the dark half).

Because the Moon’s speed varies, a tithi lasts between about 20 and 27 hours. The tithi current at sunrise gives its name to the civil day. When a tithi begins after one sunrise and ends before the next, no day bears its name and it is called “lost” (kṣaya); when a tithi includes two sunrises, two consecutive days bear the same name (adhika or vṛddhi). The rules for fixing festivals when this happens differ between regions and traditions, which is one reason why the same festival is sometimes celebrated on different days.

Figure 13.1. The tithis as positions of the Moon relative to the Sun. Each tithi corresponds to \(12^\circ\) of elongation; the ticks mark the thirty tithis, and the bright fortnight runs from new moon (Moon in the direction of the Sun) to full moon.

docs.title: 13.2.2 Vāra
docs.text:
The seven-day week came to India with Hellenistic astrology (Chapter 5). The days are named, in the same order as in the West, after the Sun (Ravivāra or Ādityavāra, Sunday), Moon (Somavāra), Mars (Maṅgalavāra), Mercury (Budhavāra), Jupiter (Guruvāra or Bṛhaspativāra), Venus (Śukravāra) and Saturn (Śanivāra). The Indian civil day runs from sunrise to sunrise. Since the siddhāntas count days from the Kali epoch, which fell on a Friday in their reckoning, the weekday of any day follows from the ahargaṇa by division by seven.

The order of the weekdays, which seems arbitrary, follows from the Hellenistic scheme of planetary hours. Arrange the seven planets in the order of their supposed distances, from the farthest: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, Moon. Give the first hour of a day to the Sun, the second to Venus, the third to Mercury, and so on round the list. Since \(24 = 3 \times 7 + 3\), the twenty-fifth hour, the first hour of the next day, falls to the planet three places further on, the Moon; the next day begins with Mars, and so on. The lords of the first hours give the sequence Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, the order of the week used in India and Europe alike. The scheme is Hellenistic; the Indian texts preserve it in the rules for the “lords of the hours” (horeśas).

docs.title: 13.2.3 Yoga and karaṇa
docs.text:
The yoga has no simple astronomical meaning: it is the division of \(13^\circ 20'\) reached by the sum of the longitudes of the Sun and Moon. Its twenty-seven names are Viṣkambha, Prīti, Āyuṣmān, Saubhāgya, Śobhana, Atigaṇḍa, Sukarman, Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Vṛddhi, Dhruva, Vyāghāta, Harṣaṇa, Vajra, Siddhi, Vyatīpāta, Varīyas, Parigha, Śiva, Siddha, Sādhya, Śubha, Śukla, Brahman, Indra and Vaidhṛti. The yogas are used almost entirely for astrological purposes.

The karaṇa is half a tithi. There are eleven karaṇas. Seven “movable” ones (Bava, Bālava, Kaulava, Taitila, Gara, Vaṇij and Viṣṭi, also called Bhadrā) repeat eight times in each month, occupying 56 of its 60 half-tithis. Four “fixed” ones occupy the remaining four: Kiṃstughna the first half of the first tithi of the bright fortnight, and Śakuni, Catuṣpada and Nāga the last three half-tithis of the dark fortnight.

docs.title: 13.3.1 Lunar months
docs.text:
The lunar month (cāndramāsa) runs from one new moon to the next or from one full moon to the next. In the amānta reckoning, used in most of south and western India, the month ends at new moon; in the pūrṇimānta reckoning, used in most of north India, it ends at full moon. The dark fortnight of a pūrṇimānta month therefore bears the name of the following amānta month. The twelve months, named after nakṣatras (Chapter 4), are listed in Table 13.2.

Table 13.2. The lunar months and their approximate position in the Gregorian year (amānta reckoning) No. Month Approx. No. Month Approx. 1 Caitra Mar–Apr 7 Āśvina Sep–Oct 2 Vaiśākha Apr–May 8 Kārttika Oct–Nov 3 Jyaiṣṭha May–Jun 9 Mārgaśīrṣa Nov–Dec 4 Āṣāḍha Jun–Jul 10 Pauṣa Dec–Jan 5 Śrāvaṇa Jul–Aug 11 Māgha Jan–Feb 6 Bhādrapada Aug–Sep 12 Phālguna Feb–Mar

docs.title: 13.3.2 Intercalation
docs.text:
Twelve lunar months make about 354.4 days, some eleven days less than a solar year. The calendar keeps the lunar months in step with the seasons by inserting an extra month about every two and a half to three years. The rule of the siddhānta calendar is astronomical, not a fixed cycle. A solar month is the time the Sun spends in one sign of the sidereal zodiac, and the Sun’s entry into a sign is a saṅkrānti. An amānta lunar month in which no saṅkrānti occurs is intercalary (adhika), and takes the name of the following month with the prefix adhika; it is regarded as unsuitable for many rites. Rarely, when the Sun moves fastest (around January) a lunar month may contain two saṅkrāntis; one month is then omitted (kṣaya), and an intercalary month falls in the same year. Such years are rare, traditionally said to recur at intervals of 141 or 19 years (Sewell and Dikshit 1896).

Because 235 synodic months are almost exactly nineteen years, this rule produces on average seven intercalary months in nineteen years, the same proportion as the Greek and Babylonian nineteen-year cycle. The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, with its two intercalations in five years, intercalated too often, which is one reason why its calendar needed periodic resetting (Chapter 3).

docs.title: 13.3.3 Solar calendars
docs.text:
In Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Bengal, Odisha, Assam and Punjab the civil months are solar: each begins at, or on the day after, a saṅkrānti, and the months have 29 to 32 days because the Sun’s apparent speed varies. The solar year in these calendars begins at the Sun’s entry into sidereal Aries (Meṣa saṅkrānti, now around 14 April), except in Kerala, where the Malayalam (Kollam) year begins with the entry into Leo (Siṃha) in August. The festivals of the solar new year (for example Puthandu, Vishu, Pohela Boishakh, Bohag Bihu, Baisakhi) fall in mid-April for this reason.

The solar months take their names from the signs, from the lunar months, or from local traditions. Table 13.3 gives the month names of three regional solar calendars alongside the sign that the Sun occupies.

docs.title: 13.3.4 The drift of the solar calendar
docs.text: The Indian solar year is the sidereal year of the siddhāntas (about 365.2588 days in the Sūryasiddhānta), which is about twenty-four minutes longer than the tropical year of the seasons (the true sidereal year exceeds it by about twenty minutes; Section 2.4). Over many centuries the solar months have therefore moved against the seasons by more than three weeks. Makara Saṅkrānti, the Sun’s entry into sidereal Capricorn, which once coincided with the winter solstice, now falls on 14 or 15 January, more than three weeks after it; Meṣa Saṅkrānti, once close to the spring equinox, now falls around 14 April. The festivals linked to these moments have drifted with them. The reform of 1957 stopped the drift only for the new civil calendar; the religious calendar it recommended keeps the sidereal reckoning, and the drift continues (Section 13.9).

docs.title: 13.4 Eras
docs.text:
Many eras have been used in India; dates in inscriptions and manuscripts must be converted with care, since an era’s year may be counted as “current” or “elapsed”, and may begin in different months (Sewell and Dikshit 1896).

docs.title: 13.4.1 The sixty-year cycle
docs.text: Besides eras, Indian calendars use a cycle of sixty named years (saṃvatsaras), beginning with Prabhava and Vibhava and ending with Akṣaya. In its astronomical form the cycle is “Jovian” (bārhaspatya): a year of the cycle is the time Jupiter takes, in mean motion, to pass through one sign, a little less than a solar year, so that five revolutions of Jupiter (about 59.3 years) make up the sixty years. In this form a name is occasionally skipped to keep the cycle in step with Jupiter. In south India, however, the sixty names are simply attached to successive solar years, without omission, and the Tamil and Telugu–Kannada years are still named in this way.

docs.title: 13.5 Other Calendars in India
docs.text: The Hindu calendars were never the only ones in India. The Islamic lunar calendar (Hijri), with its twelve months of 29 or 30 days and no intercalation, has been used since the arrival of Islam for religious purposes, and the new crescent Moon marks the beginning of Ramaḍān and the festivals. The Mughal emperor Akbar introduced a solar “divine era” (tārīkh-i ilāhī, 1584), with Persian month names, dated from his accession in 1556; and the revenue year called faslī (“of the harvest”), derived from it, survived in several regions into the twentieth century. The Parsis keep the Zoroastrian calendar, in more than one reckoning; Jains reckon dates in the era of Mahāvīra’s nirvāṇa as well as in the Vikrama era; Buddhists in some regions use an era from the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; and in 2003 the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee adopted for Sikh observances a solar “Nānakshāhī” calendar with an era from the birth of Guru Nānak (1469), later modified. A modern Indian almanac often gives the dates in several of these calendars side by side.

docs.title: 13.6 Festivals
docs.text:
Most Hindu festivals are fixed by the lunar calendar (a tithi in a given month), a few by the solar calendar. Because the lunar year is shorter than the solar, lunar festivals move by about eleven days from year to year and jump back by about a month after an intercalation. The same calendar fixes the many fasts and vows (vratas) of household religion. Some, such as the Ekādaśī fasts, are kept by men and women alike; many others, among them those undertaken for the welfare of a husband or of children, are kept mainly by women, who were thus among the most regular users of the almanac’s tithis, though hardly ever among its makers.
