docs.title: 13.6.1 Festivals fixed by Jupiter
docs.text:
A few of the largest gatherings in India are fixed not by the Sun and Moon alone but by Jupiter, whose passage through the twelve sidereal signs takes about a year each and the whole zodiac about twelve years (11.86 years in mean motion). The same slow motion underlies the Jovian sixty-year cycle described above.

The best known are the great bathing fairs called Kumbha Melā, held in rotation at four places, each roughly once in twelve years: Haridvāra on the Gaṅgā, Prayāga at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, Ujjayinī on the Kṣiprā, and Nāsik and Tryambak on the Godāvarī. Their times are defined by the signs occupied by Jupiter and the Sun. In the usual statement of the rules, the Haridvāra fair falls when Jupiter is in Kumbha (Aquarius) and the Sun enters Meṣa; the Prayāga fair when Jupiter is in Vṛṣabha and the Sun in Makara, in the month of Māgha; the Nāsik fair when Jupiter is in Siṃha, which gives it its other name, Siṃhastha; and the Ujjayinī fair when Jupiter is in Siṃha and the Sun in Meṣa. The name and the scheme of four sites are better documented in the last few centuries than earlier; the annual Māgha fair at Prayāga, for example, is much older than its designation as a Kumbha, which historians have traced to the nineteenth century (Maclean 2008). The astronomy, however, is straightforward.

Because Jupiter’s period is a little less than twelve years, a festival held every twelve years slowly falls behind the planet. In each twelve-year interval Jupiter goes \(360^\circ \times 12/11.86 \approx 364.2^\circ\), about \(4^\circ\) more than a full circuit; after seven or eight such intervals, roughly eighty-five years, the accumulated lead reaches a whole sign, and the condition recurs after only eleven years. This is why the Haridvāra fair was held in 2010 and again in 2021.

In the south the same principle governs the Puṣkaram festivals (Telugu Puṣkaralu), in which each of twelve sacred rivers is honoured for twelve days when Jupiter enters the sign assigned to it: the Godāvarī when Jupiter enters Siṃha, the Kṛṣṇā when it enters Kanyā, and the Kāverī when it enters Tulā, as in the successive years 2015, 2016 and 2017. Since the moment at which Jupiter enters a sign depends on the almanac’s parameters and on its ayanāṃśa, traditional and dṛk almanacs (Section 13.7) can disagree about the dates of these festivals by days or weeks, a disagreement that has practical consequences when millions of pilgrims and the administration of their gathering depend on it.

docs.title: 13.7.1 Traditional methods
docs.text:
A traditional almanac-maker computed the true longitudes of the Sun and Moon at sunrise each day, using a siddhānta or, more often, a handbook or table (Chapter 12), and from them found the five elements and the moments at which each changed. The elements follow simply from the two longitudes:

  • tithi \(= \lfloor(\lambda_M - \lambda_\odot)/12^\circ\rfloor + 1\);

  • nakṣatra \(= \lfloor\lambda_M/13^\circ 20'\rfloor + 1\);

  • yoga \(= \lfloor(\lambda_\odot + \lambda_M)/13^\circ 20'\rfloor + 1\) (modulo 27);

  • karaṇa: the half-tithi \(\lfloor(\lambda_M - \lambda_\odot)/6^\circ\rfloor + 1\), mapped onto the eleven names;

  • vāra: from the day count modulo 7.

The hard part is the true longitude of the Moon, whose errors translate directly into errors in the times of tithis and nakṣatras. In south India the vākya tables made this easy (Chapter 10).

docs.title: 13.7.2 The printed almanac
docs.text: A printed almanac of the twentieth or twenty-first century usually opens with the name of the year in the sixty-year cycle and in one or more eras, a list of the year’s festivals and eclipses, and astrological forecasts for the year. The body of the almanac then gives, for each lunar fortnight or month, a table with one line per day. A typical line gives the date in the lunar calendar (month, fortnight and tithi), the weekday, the time at which the tithi ends, the nakṣatra and the time at which it ends, the yoga and karaṇa with their ending times, the times of sunrise and sunset for the place for which the almanac is computed, the solar date, and the corresponding Gregorian date. Times are traditionally given in ghaṭikās and palas counted from sunrise, and in modern almanacs also in hours and minutes of standard time. Further columns or pages give the daily positions of the planets, the times at which the ascendant enters each sign, the auspicious and inauspicious periods of the day, and the festivals, fasts and religious observances of each day. Because the times depend on the place, almanacs are computed for particular cities, and the user is instructed how to correct them for other places.

docs.title: 13.7.3 Finding an intercalary month: a schematic example
docs.text: The rule that an amānta month containing no saṅkrānti is intercalary can be illustrated with a schematic sequence of events (the dates are invented for illustration). Suppose that the Sun enters Mithuna (Gemini) on 15 May and Karka (Cancer) on 15 June, and that new moons fall on 10 May, 8 June and 7 July. The lunar month from 10 May to 8 June contains the saṅkrānti of 15 May, and the month from 8 June to 7 July contains that of 15 June; both are ordinary months. Now suppose instead that the new moons fall on 16 May and 14 June, while the Sun enters Mithuna on 15 May and Karka on 15 June. The lunar month from 16 May to 14 June then contains no saṅkrānti at all: the Sun is in Mithuna throughout. That month is intercalary, and it takes the name of the month that follows, with the prefix adhika. Since the solar months are about 30.4 days long and the lunar months about 29.5, such a situation arises roughly every 32 or 33 months.

docs.title: 13.7.4 Dṛk and traditional almanacs
docs.text: In the nineteenth century, as the discrepancies between traditional almanacs and the sky (for example in the times of eclipses) became widely known, reformers in western India and elsewhere began to compute almanacs from modern European astronomical tables while retaining the traditional calendar framework. Such almanacs are called dṛk or dṛggaṇita (“observation-based”) almanacs, in contrast to the traditional ones computed from the Sūryasiddhānta, the Grahalāghava or the vākyas. The debate between the two kinds of almanac, which can differ by hours in the time of a tithi and therefore sometimes by a day in the date of a festival, has continued ever since. Today almost all dṛk almanacs use modern ephemerides with an ayanāṃśa to obtain sidereal longitudes (Chapter 4).

docs.title: 13.7.5 Astrological content of the almanac
docs.text: Almanacs have always carried astrological information along with the astronomical, and today this part is often the most consulted. Besides the auspicious times (muhūrtas) for marriages, journeys and other undertakings, many almanacs mark for each day periods regarded as inauspicious. In south India the best known is rāhukāla, one-eighth of the daytime, whose place in the day is fixed by the weekday; others are yamagaṇḍa and gulikakāla. These periods are astrological conventions (Chapter 15), not astronomical phenomena: rāhukāla has nothing to do with the position of the lunar node called Rāhu. Their observance is a matter of custom and belief.

docs.title: 13.8 A Regional Tradition: The Tamil Almanac
docs.text:
The regional almanacs of India are not local copies of a single Sanskrit model. Each has its own language, conventions, festivals and history of computation, and the Tamil almanac (pañcāṅkam) shows this especially clearly.

Nakṣatras in Tamil.

The asterisms have been part of Tamil culture since the classical (Caṅkam) poetry, which names several of them and mentions festivals tied to them, apparently including the festival of lamps in the month of Kārttikai. Their Tamil names are partly adapted from Sanskrit (Kārttikai for Kṛttikā, Rōkiṇi, Pūcam for Puṣya, Makam for Maghā, Cittirai, Cuvāti, Vicākam, Mūlam) and partly distinctively Tamil: Tiruvātirai for Ārdrā and Tiruvōṇam for Śravaṇa, with the honorific prefix tiru; Āyilyam for Āśleṣā, Kēṭṭai for Jyeṣṭhā, Aviṭṭam for Dhaniṣṭhā and Catayam for Śatabhiṣaj; and paired forms such as Pūram and Uttiram for the two Phalgunīs and Pūrāṭam and Uttirāṭam for the two Āṣāḍhās.

Festivals by nakṣatra and solar month.

A characteristic southern pattern is to fix a festival not by a tithi in a lunar month, as in most of the north, but by the day on which the Moon is in a given nakṣatra within a given solar month (Table 13.3). Thus Kārttikai Tīpam falls when the Moon is in Kārttikai during the solar month Kārttikai, Tai Pūcam on the day of Pūcam in Tai, Paṅkuṉi Uttiram on the day of Uttiram in Paṅkuṉi, and the Tiruvātirai festival of Śiva in Mārkaḻi; in Kerala, Ōṇam is the day of Tiruvōṇam in the solar month Ciṅṅam. Birthdays, too, are traditionally kept on the birth nakṣatra (Chapter 4). Such festivals depend on the Moon’s true position and the Sun’s entry into the signs, and so on exactly the computations described in this chapter.

Vākya and tirukkaṇitam.

Tamil almanac-makers kept the vākya system (Chapter 10) longer than anyone else. Its main handbook, the Vākyakaraṇa, was probably composed in the Tamil country around the fourteenth century, and its commentator Sundararāja, in the early sixteenth century, exchanged questions and answers with the Kerala astronomer Nīlakaṇṭha (Pingree 1981; Sarma 1972). Two kinds of Tamil almanac are published today: the vākya pañcāṅkam, computed by the traditional sentences and still followed by many temples, and the tirukkaṇita pañcāṅkam (from Sanskrit dṛggaṇita), computed from modern ephemerides. Like the dṛk and traditional almanacs elsewhere, they can differ by hours in the ending time of a tithi or nakṣatra, and occasionally by a day in the date of a festival.

Calculation without writing.

Tamil calendar-makers were known for computing with counters laid out on the ground and with memorised tables rather than written arithmetic. The French astronomer Le Gentil, during his stay at Pondicherry in 1768–69, had the computation of a lunar eclipse demonstrated to him in this way and published the procedure; Otto Neugebauer later analysed his account and showed how the method worked (Neugebauer 1952). Some decades later John Warren recorded the same kind of computation, made with shells laid out on the ground, in his Kala Sankalita (Section 16.4.4). The episode is a reminder that the living practice of Indian astronomy was largely oral and manual, carried by people whose names rarely entered the written record. In the Tamil country these included not only Brahmin specialists but also hereditary astrologers of other communities, such as the Vaḷḷuvar.

docs.title: 13.9 The Reform of 1957
docs.text:
In 1952 the Government of India appointed a Calendar Reform Committee, chaired by the astrophysicist Meghnad Saha, to examine the more than thirty calendars then in use and to propose a unified one. Its report (1955) recommended (Calendar Reform Committee 1955):

  • for civil use, a national calendar based on the tropical solar year, with the Śaka era, in which the year begins on 22 March (21 March in leap years) and the months have fixed lengths of 30 or 31 days, in step with the Gregorian calendar;

  • for religious use, the continued use of lunar and solar months, but computed from accurate modern data, with the sidereal longitudes obtained by a single, fixed definition of the ayanāṃśa (the Citrā-pakṣa value, with Spica at \(180^\circ\)).

The two recommendations had different consequences for the seasons. The civil calendar is tropical and stays in step with them. The religious calendar remained sidereal: since the ayanāṃśa grows with precession, the saṅkrāntis and the solar months, and with them festivals such as Makara Saṅkrānti, continue to move later in the seasonal year, by about one day in seventy years. Only the civil calendar was reformed in this respect.

The national calendar came into official use on 22 March 1957 (1 Caitra 1879 Śaka) alongside the Gregorian calendar. It is used in the Gazette of India and in some official documents, but has not displaced either the Gregorian calendar in civil life or the regional calendars in religious life. The Positional Astronomy Centre in Kolkata, part of the India Meteorological Department, publishes an annual Rāṣṭrīya Pañcāṅga (national almanac) on the principles recommended by the Committee. The great majority of almanacs, however, are still published privately, by traditional families and publishing houses, according to regional traditions and choices of school.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Sewell and Dikshit (1896) remains the standard reference for converting Indian dates and explains the calendar rules in detail. Calendar Reform Committee (1955) is the report of the Calendar Reform Committee. Yano (2003) is a short modern account. Neugebauer (1952) analyses an eighteenth-century account of Tamil eclipse computation.

docs.title: Chapter 14: Cosmic Time and the Shape of the Cosmos
14.1 Two Kinds of Cosmology
docs.text: Indian astronomers worked with two pictures of the universe. One, inherited from the Purāṇas and shared in different forms by Hindu, Jain and Buddhist traditions, describes a flat earth of concentric continents and oceans around the world mountain Meru, with the heavens above and the underworlds below, existing through immense cycles of creation and dissolution. The other, that of the siddhāntas, describes a spherical earth at the centre of a spherical cosmos, with the Sun, Moon and planets moving on circles at measurable distances. The two pictures shared the cycles of time, which the siddhāntas used as the frame of their computations, but disagreed about space. How astronomers negotiated between them is one of the most interesting themes of the tradition (Minkowski 2004).

docs.title: 14.2.1 The four ages
docs.text:
The Purāṇic scheme, already present in the Mahābhārata and in the Manusmṛti (1.68–73; the text is dated c. 2nd century CE), divides time into four ages (yugas) of declining virtue: Kṛta (or Satya), Tretā, Dvāpara and Kali. Their lengths are stated in “divine years”, each equal to 360 human years, and each age is preceded and followed by a “twilight” (sandhyā and sandhyāṃśa) of one-tenth of its length.

Table 14.1. The four yugas of the Purāṇic scheme. Lengths include the twilights. One divine year = 360 human years. Age Core + twilights Divine years Human years Kṛta \(4000 + 400 + 400\) 4800 1,728,000 Tretā \(3000 + 300 + 300\) 3600 1,296,000 Dvāpara \(2000 + 200 + 200\) 2400 864,000 Kali \(1000 + 100 + 100\) 1200 432,000 Mahāyuga (all four) 12,000 4,320,000

docs.title: 14.2.2 Larger cycles
docs.text:
Seventy-one mahāyugas make a manvantara, the reign of a Manu. Fourteen manvantaras, with fifteen intervening twilights each as long as a Kṛta age, make a kalpa of 1000 mahāyugas, or 4,320 million years. A kalpa is a “day of Brahmā”, followed by a night of equal length in which the worlds are dissolved; 360 such days and nights make a year of Brahmā, and Brahmā lives a hundred such years, some 311 million million human years.

The tradition also locates the present. We are said to be in the fifty-first year of the present Brahmā, in the kalpa called Śvetavarāha, in the seventh manvantara (that of Manu Vaivasvata), in the twenty-eighth mahāyuga, in its Kali age, which began in 3102 BCE. On this reckoning, used in traditional almanacs and in the formulae recited before rituals, nearly 1,973 million years of the present kalpa have elapsed. The Sūryasiddhānta, which allows a period for creation at the beginning of the kalpa, counts somewhat differently (Burgess 1860).

docs.title: 14.2.3 The cycles in astronomy
docs.text: The siddhāntas adopted these cycles for a practical reason (Chapter 6): stating the number of revolutions of every planet in a mahāyuga or a kalpa makes every mean motion a ratio of integers, and if all the mean planets are assumed to be together at the beginning of the cycle, any mean position can be computed from the number of days elapsed. Brahmagupta’s system, following the Purāṇic scheme, assumes a conjunction of all the mean planets, their apogees and nodes at the beginning of the kalpa. Āryabhaṭa took a different course. He made the four ages equal (1,080,000 years each) and the kalpa 1008 mahāyugas (14 manvantaras of 72 mahāyugas each), so that his mean planets were in conjunction at the beginning of every quarter-yuga, including the beginning of the Kali age. Brahmagupta condemned this departure from tradition at length.

docs.title: 14.2.4 Jain and Buddhist cycles
docs.text: The Jain and Buddhist traditions have their own cycles of cosmic time, equally vast but differently organised. In Jain cosmology the “wheel of time” (kālacakra) turns through two half-cycles, an ascending one (utsarpiṇī) in which conditions improve and a descending one (avasarpiṇī) in which they decline, each divided into six “spokes” (aras) of unequal length; the twenty-four Tīrthaṅkaras of our world appear in the third and fourth spokes of each half-cycle, and we live in the fifth spoke of a descending half. The units of this scheme are counted in innumerable years (palyopama, sāgaropama) defined by thought-experiments rather than by multiplication. Buddhist texts describe a great aeon (mahākalpa) of four “incalculable” aeons, through which a world system forms, endures, is destroyed and remains empty. These schemes share with the Purāṇic one the ideas of immense duration, recurrence and moral decline, but unlike it they were never tied to astronomical computation.

docs.title: 14.2.5 The number 432,000
docs.text: The Kali age of 432,000 years recalls the 432,000 years that the Babylonian priest Berossus (early third century BCE) assigned to the kings who ruled before the Flood. Whether the Indian numbers have a Mesopotamian origin, as some historians have suggested, or arose from the internal arithmetic of the Indian scheme (432,000 is \(1200 \times 360\)), is not settled (Pingree 1981).

docs.title: 14.2.6 Modern comparisons
docs.text: The kalpa of 4.32 billion years is of the same order of magnitude as the modern age of the earth and solar system (about 4.57 billion years), and this is often presented as a remarkable anticipation. It is a coincidence. The Purāṇic numbers were obtained by multiplying a schematic age of 1200 divine years by successive factors (360, 10, 1000); they were not derived from any evidence about the age of the earth, and the larger figures of the same scheme (the life of Brahmā, some \(3 \times 10^{14}\) years) bear no relation to any modern quantity. The Purāṇic cycles express religious and cosmological ideas of immense duration, recurrence and decline, and their importance lies there.

docs.title: 14.3 The Purāṇic Earth
docs.text:
In the Purāṇic cosmography the earth (bhūloka) is a vast flat disc. At its centre is the continent Jambudvīpa, in the middle of which rises Mount Meru. Around Jambudvīpa lie six further ring-shaped continents (dvīpas), separated by seven oceans of salt water, sugar-cane juice, wine, clarified butter, curds, milk and fresh water. India (Bhāratavarṣa) is the southern part of Jambudvīpa. Above the earth are the spheres of the Sun, Moon, nakṣatras and planets, and higher heavens; below it are the netherworlds. Day and night are produced by the Sun’s circling Meru. Jain and Buddhist cosmologies share the general structure with different details; the Jain version, with two suns and two moons, was described in Chapter 3.

In this cosmography the distances are enormous and schematic (the continents and oceans double in size outward), and the Moon is farther than the Sun. It explains religious geography and the moral order of the worlds; it was not designed to predict celestial phenomena. Purāṇic and Jain cosmography, and the siddhāntas’ geography of the spherical earth, are treated more fully in Volume 21, Bhūgola.

docs.title: 14.4 The Spherical Cosmos of the Siddhāntas
docs.text:
The siddhāntas, by contrast, place a spherical earth, suspended without support, at the centre of the universe. Around it revolve, at increasing distances, the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and the stars. The whole is enclosed in the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), whose size the Sūryasiddhānta computes from its principle of equal linear velocities (Chapter 7).

The siddhāntas kept some Purāṇic names by giving them new places on the sphere. Meru became the north pole of the earth, where the gods live and see the Sun continuously for six months, so that their “day” is half a human year; the asuras live at the south pole. Laṅkā became a point on the equator on the prime meridian, and three other cities (Yavakoṭi, Romaka and Siddhapura) were placed on the equator at intervals of \(90^\circ\), so that when the Sun rises at one it is noon, sunset and midnight at the others (Burgess 1860).

Figure 14.1. The spherical earth of the siddhāntas, with Purāṇic names given new places: Meru at the north pole, and four cities on the equator at intervals of \(90^\circ\) (Laṅkā on the prime meridian, Siddhapura opposite it, Yavakoṭi and Romaka between). Schematic.

The siddhānta writers drew out the consequences of the spherical earth with evident pleasure. At Meru, on the pole, the Sun is visible continuously for the six months in which it is north of the equator and invisible for the other six, so that the gods’ day and night each last half a year; at the south pole the reverse holds for the asuras. At Laṅkā, on the equator, day and night are always equal. Between them, the length of the day depends on latitude and season, as the rules of the ascensional difference describe (Chapter 6). The “day of the gods” of Purāṇic chronology, a human year, was thus given an astronomical meaning.

This re-use of Purāṇic names made the new cosmography easier to accept, and it allowed the astronomers to claim that their sphere was consistent with tradition.

docs.title: 14.5 Conflict and Accommodation
docs.text:
The two cosmologies could not both be literally true, and astronomers said so. Lalla, in the eighth century, devoted a chapter to refuting “false knowledge” (mithyājñāna): that the earth is flat or supported, that the Moon is beyond the Sun, that night is caused by Meru, and that Rāhu swallows the Sun and Moon. Bhāskara II, in the Golādhyāya, argued against the support of the earth and discussed how the Purāṇic statements could be understood. Some astronomers took the view that the Purāṇas describe things that astronomy does not (and need not) explain, or that they are true in a different sense; others proposed that the Purāṇic descriptions were meant for a different purpose.

The debate continued in the early modern period. Jñānarāja’s Siddhāntasundara (1503) gave long chapters to reconciling the Purāṇic earth with the sphere (Knudsen 2014), and Kamalākara and Munīśvara in seventeenth-century Vārāṇasī disagreed about how far the astronomer may depart from scripture, and later scholars wrote treatises reconciling the two pictures. In the nineteenth century, when European astronomy was taught in Indian schools, the same questions were asked again about the relation between the heliocentric system and the siddhāntas (Minkowski 2004, 2002). In these debates Indian astronomers reflected explicitly on the nature and authority of their own knowledge.

docs.title: 14.6 Time in Indian Philosophy
docs.text: The philosophical schools also discussed the nature of time (kāla): whether it is a substance (as the Vaiśeṣikas held) or a construction from the succession of events, whether it is continuous or made of discrete instants (the Buddhist doctrine of momentariness), and how it relates to causality. These discussions, treated in Volume 3, were largely independent of the astronomers’ practical time-reckoning, although both shared the vocabulary of units and cycles.

docs.title: Further Reading
docs.text: Minkowski (2004) studies the debates between Purāṇic and siddhāntic cosmology; Burgess (1860) translates the cosmographical chapter of the Sūryasiddhānta; Pingree (1981) discusses the cycles.

docs.title: Chapter 15: Horā and Saṃhitā: Astrology and Omens in Historical Perspective
15.1 Scope and Approach
docs.text: This chapter describes the two branches of jyotiḥśāstra other than mathematical astronomy: horoscopic astrology (horā) and the interpretation of omens (saṃhitā). Both have long histories, large literatures and great social importance in India, and both were practised by the same people who computed the planets. They are described here as historical and social phenomena: what the texts teach, where their ideas came from, how they were used, and how they have been judged. Describing a technique is not endorsing it. The predictive claims of astrology and omen literature have no known physical basis, and where they have been tested under controlled conditions they have not been confirmed (Section 15.7).

docs.title: 15.2.1 Omens and auspicious times
docs.text: The oldest Indian astral beliefs concern omens and auspicious times. The Vedic ritual texts prescribe particular nakṣatras for particular rites, and the domestic ritual manuals do the same for marriage, the first feeding of a child, and other life-cycle rites. Collections of omens, celestial and terrestrial, appear in the supplements (pariśiṣṭas) of the Atharvaveda and in the Gārgīya Jyotiṣa. Pingree argued that a part of this omen material derives from the Mesopotamian celestial omen series Enūma Anu Enlil, transmitted through the Achaemenid empire, alongside native Indian traditions (Pingree 1997).

docs.title: 15.2.2 Greek horoscopy
docs.text: Horoscopic astrology, which interprets the configuration of the planets in the twelve signs and twelve “places” at a moment (above all the moment of birth), is Hellenistic in origin. It was developed in Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt and reached India in the early centuries CE, notably through the Yavanajātaka (Chapter 5). Its technical vocabulary in Sanskrit is full of Greek words (horā, kendra, drekkāṇa, jāmitra, paṇaphara, āpoklima). Indian astrologers then developed it in their own directions, adding the nakṣatras, new systems of planetary periods, and many other techniques. From the thirteenth century a second wave of foreign astrology, the Perso-Arabic, entered Sanskrit as tājika (Pingree 1981, 1997).

docs.title: 15.3 Saṃhitā: The Bṛhatsaṃhitā
docs.text:
The classic text of the omen branch is Varāhamihira’s Bṛhatsaṃhitā (sixth century), in more than a hundred chapters (Varāhamihira 1981–1982). It is a compendium of almost everything that a royal astrologer might be asked about, and its range is remarkable:

  • the courses of the Sun, Moon and planets, the seven sages (Ursa Major), Canopus and comets, and what their appearances portend for kingdoms and crops;

  • eclipses (with the geometrical explanation discussed in Chapter 8);

  • weather: the “pregnancy” of the clouds, by which signs observed in certain months are said to bring rain a fixed number of days later; the measurement of rainfall in a vessel; winds, halos, rainbows and other atmospheric signs;

  • earthquakes, classified according to the deity (Wind, Fire, Indra or Varuṇa) presiding over the asterism in which they occur, with their portents;

  • the finding of underground water (dakārgala) from plants, termite mounds, soils and stones;

  • building sites and house plans (vāstuvidyā), the making of images, the planting of trees;

  • gems, perfumes (with the combinatorial calculation noted in Chapter 9), and the characteristics of men, women, horses, elephants, cows and dogs;

  • omens from birds and animals (śakuna), and much else.

The Bṛhatsaṃhitā is a precious source for the material culture, technology and beliefs of sixth-century India. It also contains genuine observation, especially of weather and of the natural signs of groundwater, together with much that is lore or divination. Its chapters on earthquakes, for example, contain no theory of their cause and classify them by the asterism of their occurrence. Modern claims that the text anticipated meteorology, seismology or hydrology, or that its methods have been “validated”, go beyond the evidence: a few of its rules for finding water may reflect real associations between vegetation and groundwater, but this has not been systematically established, and its rain forecasts have not been shown to work.

docs.title: 15.4 Comets, Meteors and Other Transient Lights
docs.text: The siddhāntas computed only what returns: the Sun, Moon, planets, nodes and fixed stars. Everything that appears unannounced in the sky (comets, meteors and fireballs, halos, rainbows, mock suns, the red glow of the horizon) belonged to the omen branch. The Bṛhatsaṃhitā groups most of these phenomena in a run of short chapters: in the numbering of the standard editions, chapter 11 on comets, then chapters 30 to 38 on the twilights (sandhyā), the “burning of the quarters” (digdāha, an unexplained glow at the horizon), earthquakes, meteors (ulkā), halos (pariveṣa), the rainbow (indrāyudha, “Indra’s weapon”), the “cities of the Gandharvas” (gandharvanagara, cloud-forms and mirages), mock suns (pratisūrya) and thunder from a clear sky (nirghāta), with a general chapter on portents (utpāta) later in the work (Varāhamihira 1981–1982).

docs.title: 15.4.1 The theory of portents
docs.text:
The chapter on portents, which Varāhamihira says he takes from Garga, gives the theory behind all of these. A portent is defined as a change in the natural order (prakṛter anyatvam). Calamity comes from the accumulated wrongdoing of human beings; the gods, offended by human misconduct, produce the portents, which announce it; and the king should therefore have rites of appeasement (śānti) performed in the kingdom to avert it. Portents are of three kinds. The celestial are anomalies of the planets and stars; the atmospheric are meteors, thunder from a clear sky, unusual winds, halos, “cities of the Gandharvas”, rainbows and the like; the terrestrial are those arising from moving and fixed things on earth. Some authorities held that terrestrial portents are quelled by śānti, atmospheric ones only softened, and celestial ones not at all; Varāhamihira answers that even the celestial are quelled by large gifts of gold, food, cows and land, by a sacrifice of ten million oblations, or by milking cows on the ground at a temple of Rudra. The effects fall, in eight ways, on the king himself, his son, treasury, vehicles, city, wives and priest, and on the people.

This framework explains the place of the transient phenomena in jyotiṣa. They were not curiosities to be catalogued but messages addressed to the king, and the practical response to them was ritual, not further observation. It also explains a classification that seems strange today: a meteor, which falls through the air, is an atmospheric portent, whereas an unusual colour or course of a planet is a celestial one; comets, as the chapter on them says, could be of any of the three kinds.

docs.title: 15.4.2 Comets
docs.text:
The Sanskrit word for a comet, ketu, means a sign or banner; a comet is also called śikhin, “the crested one”, and dhūmaketu, “smoke-bannered”, a word that in the Ṛgveda is an epithet of fire. In the siddhāntas, as Chapter 8 explains, Ketu also became the name of the Moon’s descending node, the ninth of the astrological “planets”. The two senses are different things, the one a portent that cannot be computed, the other a mathematical point, and confusing them has produced modern claims that Indian texts “predicted” comets.

Varāhamihira’s chapter on the “course of comets” (ketucāra) opens by naming its sources, the comet lore of Garga, Parāśara and Asita Devala “and many others”. It then states a principle: the appearance and disappearance of comets cannot be determined by calculation, because comets are of three kinds, celestial, atmospheric and terrestrial. Celestial comets are those seen among the nakṣatras; atmospheric ones appear on banners, weapons, houses, trees, horses and elephants; terrestrial ones are the rest. Fireflies, gems and similar shining things are explicitly excluded, but the category is evidently wide enough to include luminous phenomena that would now be classed quite differently. Some authorities, Varāhamihira reports, count 101 comets, others a thousand, while the sage Nārada held that there is only one comet, appearing in many forms; his own view is that, whether one or many, their effects must be stated.

The rest of the chapter, sixty-odd verses in the standard text, is a classification by appearance, with the omen attached to each class. A comet that is short, thin, clear, glossy, straight, white and quickly gone brings plenty and well-being; its opposite brings misfortune. The effects mature over as many months as the comet was seen for days; for a comet seen longer than three fortnights, years are counted instead of months. Then come named types: twenty-five “ray” comets, said to be sons of the Sun, glittering like necklaces, gems or gold and seen in the east or west; types called Kumuda, Maṇiketu, Jalaketu, Bhavaketu, Padmaketu and Saṃvarta, each described by the colour and shape of its crest, the direction and time of night of its appearance and the length of its visibility; and finally the peoples and kings who suffer when a comet touches or obscures particular nakṣatras. These last verses name Andhras, Madrakas, Kāśi, Yaudheyas, Śibis, Kekayas, Siṃhala, Vaṅga, Kirātas, Colas, Hūṇas and Cīnas, which makes them, like other lists in the work, a source for the historical geography of sixth-century India. The tenth-century commentator Bhaṭṭotpala quotes at length from the earlier comet lists that Varāhamihira summarised, and his commentary is one of the two main witnesses to that lost literature (Pingree 1981). The other is the Adbhutasāgara (“Ocean of marvels”), a vast compendium of portents begun by the Sena king Ballālasena of Bengal in the later twelfth century and completed under his son Lakṣmaṇasena. Under each class of portent, comets among them, it arranges quotations from Garga, Parāśara, Vṛddhagarga, Varāhamihira and many authors whose works are otherwise lost. Its royal authorship is a reminder of whom the omen literature served: the king, whose fortunes the sky was believed to announce.

docs.title: 15.4.3 Meteors
docs.text: The chapter on meteors (ulkā) begins with an explanation that is religious, not physical: meteors are the forms of beings who have enjoyed the fruits of their good deeds in heaven and are now falling, an idea familiar from the Bhagavadgītā (9.21), where those who have enjoyed heaven return to the world of mortals when their merit is spent. Varāhamihira distinguishes five kinds: dhiṣṇyā, ulkā, aśani (the thunderbolt), vidyut (lightning) and tārā (“star”, the small shooting star), and assigns to each a time within which its effect matures (a fortnight for the ulkā proper, three fortnights for the dhiṣṇyā and the thunderbolt, six days for lightning) and a measure of its strength: the shooting star gives a quarter of the effect, the dhiṣṇyā half, the other three the full effect. The grouping of lightning and thunderbolts with meteors is a reminder that the categories are those of an observer of signs, not of a physicist: everything that flashes and falls from the sky is one class.

docs.title: 15.4.4 Halos, rainbows and mock suns
docs.text:
The chapters on the optical phenomena of the atmosphere are short, but they are the place where the omen literature comes closest to physical explanation. The halo chapter opens by defining its subject: halos are rays of the Sun and Moon which, condensed by the wind, take the form of a circle in a thin cloud; they are of many colours, and each colour is assigned to a deity. The rainbow chapter similarly defines “Indra’s bow” as the variously coloured rays of the Sun, struck by the wind in a clouded sky, which appear in the shape of a bow, and then reports that some teachers derive it instead from the breath of the serpents of Ananta’s family. The short chapter on mock suns (pratisūrya) ends by relating them, too, to water and wind. These are not theories in the sense of Greek or Islamic optics: there is no geometry of reflection or refraction, and the explanation serves only to define the class before its omens are listed. But they show that the authors of the omen literature did think about the causes of what they classified, and that for some phenomena they preferred a natural cause, sunlight, wind and moisture, to a mythical one, which they recorded as the opinion of others. The pattern is the same as in Varāhamihira’s treatment of eclipses, where the shadow theory is affirmed and the role of Rāhu reduced to a matter of ritual (Chapter 8). The chapters on the “cities of the Gandharvas” and the “burning of the quarters”, by contrast, give only the omens, by colour and direction, with no word about the cause.

The omens themselves follow a few simple rules of correspondence. The eight colours of halos (red, blue, pale, dove-grey, cloud-coloured, variegated, green and white) are made, in that order, by Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, Nirṛti, the Wind, Īśa, Brahmā and the Waters; a rainbow that faces a king on the march foretells his defeat; a mock sun of the colour of the season, glossy and clear like beryl, brings safety and plenty, a yellow one disease; a yellow glow at the horizon threatens the king, a fiery one the country, a red one with an adverse wind the crops. In the chapter on the cities of the Gandharvas the colours white, red, yellow and black are assigned to the destruction of the four varṇas in order, and the directions to the king’s priest, the king, the commander and the crown prince. The sky was read, in other words, through the same grid of colours, directions and social ranks that organised the rest of the omen literature, and the observations were valued for what they could be made to signify.

docs.title: 15.4.5 The problem of identification
docs.text:
None of this literature records an event. It describes types of comet and meteor, not the comet of a particular year, and it gives no dates, positions or durations that could be checked. In this it differs sharply from Chinese astronomy, whose official records of “guest stars” and “broom stars” over two thousand years have been used to compute the orbits of comets and to identify the remnants of supernovae (Chapter 16). No Indian record has yet been securely identified of the supernovae of 1006 and 1054, which were recorded in East Asian and, for 1006, in Arabic sources; nor of any return of Halley’s comet before the modern period. The silence is not evidence that nobody looked; it reflects the genre. Omen texts were manuals for interpreting what might be seen, and court records that might have noted particular events have largely not survived.

For the same reason, attempts to identify a particular comet in an Indian text should be treated with caution. The portents that the Mahābhārata lists before the great battle, including a “white planet” and a comet afflicting Puṣya, have been used to date the war; but they are literary lists drawn from the repertoire of the omen literature, they contradict one another, and they contain no information that would single out one comet among the many that appear in any century (see Volume 7, Itihāsa–Purāṇa). An identification requires at least a date, a position and a description, and these the Sanskrit sources do not give.

The first Indian observations of comets that can be dated come from the Mughal court and from European observers in India. The emperor Jahāngīr recorded in his memoirs two comets seen during a royal journey in his thirteenth regnal year; they have been identified with the two great comets of November 1618, which the Jesuit Venceslaus Kirwitzer was observing at the same time at Goa, with what appears to be the first astronomical use of a telescope in India (Kapoor 2016; Thackston 1999). Jahāngīr also describes the fall of a meteorite near Jalandhar in April 1621, after which he had the iron forged into two swords, a dagger and a knife; the knife survives. Later comets were observed by Jesuits at Pondicherry (1689, Chapter 16) and Surat (1695), and by the astronomers of the Madras Observatory. The most curious of the Madras observations links comets and meteors directly. After the great meteor shower of 27 November 1872, which seemed to come from the region of the lost comet of Biela, the German astronomer Klinkerfues telegraphed to N. R. Pogson at Madras to search for the comet in the southern sky. Pogson found a tailless comet there in the early morning of 3 December. Whether it was Biela’s comet is still debated, and the object is now catalogued under Pogson’s name.

The contrast is instructive. The omen literature was a systematic classification of what could be seen, by colour, shape, direction and duration, and in that sense it encouraged attentive watching of the sky. But it attached each class to a prediction about kings and harvests rather than to a cause, and its own principle, that comets cannot be computed, set the transient phenomena outside the domain in which Indian astronomy made its advances. Comets became objects of computation only when their orbits could be calculated, in Europe at the end of the seventeenth century.

docs.title: 15.5.1 The texts
docs.text: After the Yavanajātaka (third century) and Mīnarāja’s Vṛddhayavanajātaka, the classical works are Varāhamihira’s Bṛhajjātaka and Laghujātaka (sixth century), Kalyāṇavarman’s Sārāvalī (probably ninth century), Śrīpati’s astrological works (eleventh century), Vaidyanātha’s Jātakapārijāta and Mantreśvara’s Phaladīpikā (both late medieval, their dates uncertain). The Bṛhatpārāśarahorāśāstra, ascribed to the ancient sage Parāśara and now very popular, is a compilation whose date is uncertain and probably late; it is not an ancient text in its present form (Pingree 1981). Kerala produced its own tradition of horary astrology, of which the Praśnamārga (seventeenth century) is the best-known text.

docs.title: 15.5.2 The shape of a classical manual
docs.text: Varāhamihira’s Bṛhajjātaka shows how a classical manual of nativities is organised. It begins with definitions: the signs and their divisions (horā, drekkāṇa, navāṃśa and others), with their Greek names; the planets, their natures, friendships and strengths; and the places of the horoscope. It then deals with the conception and birth of the child, with rules for deciding whether a child will live and how long, and with the effects of each planet in each sign and place, alone and in combination with others. Further chapters concern the native’s character, appearance, wealth and profession, the horoscopes of women, death, and the techniques for determining the periods in which each planet gives its effects. The same order of subjects, with variations and additions, is found in later manuals. The horoscopes of women were treated in a separate chapter, largely concerned with marriage, chastity and widowhood, which reflects and reinforced the norms of the society for which the texts were written.

docs.title: 15.5.3 Techniques
docs.text:
A horoscope (jātaka, janmapatrī, kuṇḍalī) records the positions of the planets in the signs, the ascendant (lagna: the sign rising on the eastern horizon), the twelve “houses” (bhāvas) counted from it, and the nakṣatra of the Moon. The astrologer judges the “strength” of each planet, the houses it occupies and rules, the aspects between planets, and the presence of particular combinations (yogas). The computation of the ascendant requires real spherical astronomy, and the demand for horoscopes was one of the reasons why accurate planetary positions mattered.

Casting a horoscope in the traditional way involved the following steps, each drawing on the mathematical astronomy of the siddhāntas: (1) convert the time of birth, usually recorded in ghaṭikās after sunrise, into a moment of the astronomer’s reckoning; (2) compute the ahargaṇa and the true sidereal longitudes of the Sun, Moon and planets, and the position of the lunar node; (3) compute the ascendant from the rising times of the signs at the latitude of the birthplace (Chapter 6); (4) divide the ecliptic into houses counted from the ascendant, by one of several conventions; (5) find the nakṣatra and quarter of the Moon, from which the planetary periods are started; and (6) compute the various divisional charts (such as the navāṃśa, in which each sign is divided into nine parts). Only after this computation did the work of interpretation begin. In north India the result was drawn as a diamond-shaped chart, in south India as a square of twelve cells (Figure 15.1), and in Bengal and Odisha in other forms.

Figure 15.1. The two commonest layouts of the horoscope chart. (a) In the north Indian chart the twelve houses (bhāvas) are fixed: the first house, that of the ascendant, is the upper central diamond, and the houses follow anticlockwise, as numbered here; the astrologer writes in each house the number of the sign that occupies it, and the planets’ names. (b) In the south Indian chart the signs are fixed, Meṣa (Aries) in the second cell of the top row and the others following clockwise; the cell containing the ascendant is marked, and the planets are written in their signs. The central space is left empty or used for the native’s details.

Characteristic Indian developments include the systems of planetary periods (daśās), which divide a life into periods ruled by successive planets. In the most widely used, the viṃśottarī (“120-year”) system, the sequence starts from the lord of the Moon’s birth nakṣatra (Table 15.1).
